events.text: Deep in the sealing-room you find a seal of the Ministry of Winds, dissolved four thousand years ago. It is warm. Clerk Meiru, who keeps the room, goes pale and asks you, very quietly, whether it is possible not to have found it.

choices.text: Hand it back and forget it

effects.log: Meiru takes the seal and puts it in a drawer that locks twice. You are owed something now, and you both know it.

effects.log: Bo Quen thanks you for your diligence, and the seal is gone by morning. So, a little later, is Meiru's seat.

effects.log: Meiru's answer is long, and bad, and true. By the end you hold half of a secret that wants two people.

events.text: An edict arrives on a low isle, stamped with the seal of the Ministry of Winds. The isle's wind-farmers do as it commands, because it is the only edict that has ever promised them anything. Bo Quen is furious. {b3_elder} asks, mildly, who has the key to the drawer.

effects.log: You say you do not know. It is true of the key, and not of the drawer, and {b3_elder} lets the difference stand.

choices.text: Go to Meiru before anyone else does

effects.log: Meiru is waiting, with tea. The edict was Meiru's, and it is, you find, a good one. You help them draft the second.

choices.text: Lay the matter before the Ministries

effects.log: You lay it before the Ministries, and the room goes very quiet. Meiru is not named. The drawer is searched, and you are thanked for a century of service.

events.text: Meiru is a Celestial Officer now, and the Ministry of Winds has been quietly revived under another name. At the opening, Meiru looks for you in the crowd and nods once, as to an old colleague. The wind-farmers of the low isle have sent a wreath of reeds, and an invoice.

choices.text: Accept a seat at the new Ministry

effects.log: You take a place at the Ministry that should not exist. It is the quietest, best-fed post you have held in a thousand years.

choices.text: Tell Meiru you were never sure it was legal

effects.log: Meiru agrees that it was not, and that it works. The conversation goes on until the lamps need oil, and neither of you wins.

events.text: Marshal Ouyang Lan has been told to audit the isles' registers and wants someone who can count without wanting anything. That is you, apparently. The first ledger you open lists a hundred and four isles. The sky outside has a hundred and three.

choices.text: Count them again, from the roof

effects.log: You count from the roof of the Hall, twice. A hundred and three. The hundred and fourth was a mountain top that sank in the Age of Fog and was never struck off.

choices.text: Ask Lan to look at the ledger

effects.log: Lan looks at it for a long moment and asks you to note a hundred and three, quietly, and to say nothing of the fourth.
You write a hundred and three. Lan, reading it, says that is the first honest ledger in the Ministries' history, and takes a day to recover.

events.text: Years on, Ouyang Lan sends for you again. The hundred and fourth isle is not sunk: someone is paying its tithes. The money arrives in old coin, from no isle, to the Ministry of Granaries, in a different brush each year. Lan wants you to find who, and does not say why.

choices.text: Follow the coin down to the low isles

effects.log: The coin leads down to a little drowned market that sells fog by the jar. The seller says only that the isle is 'owed' and the tithes are what they owe it.

choices.text: Ask the Ministry of Granaries who receives it

effects.log: The Granaries do not know. They have been banking it for four thousand years and think of it as weather.

choices.text: Tell Lan it is better left unsolved

effects.log: Lan nods slowly. Both of you have heard the sound a mystery makes when it is finally solved, and neither wants to hear it twice.

events.text: You find the payer: an old woman on a drowned peak, the last of the isle's people, who has kept the tithes up since the sinking out of pure stubbornness and a belief that the Ministries would one day return the favour. Lan is with you. Lan does not know what to say, and says it.

choices.text: Have the isle struck from the register with honours

effects.log: The Ministries strike it with honours and a plaque. The old woman asks what she is to do with the plaque. You have no answer, and she keeps it anyway.

choices.text: Have the isle restored to the register

effects.log: It takes a decade and is the proudest paperwork of your life. The old woman lives to see the first tithe paid back to her.

choices.text: Leave the tithes running, and say nothing

effects.log: Lan agrees. Some debts are kinder left unpaid, and a book that is never balanced is a book that is never closed.

events.text: The Court of Remonstrance is asking for names to put on a letter to the Jade Court: a complaint about the cost of cloud-lamps on the White Stairs. It is a small matter and a large risk. The lamp-minister has a very long memory and a very short temper. Minister Zhao Linfeng asks you for yours.

effects.log: You sign. A hundred and twelve names follow yours. The lamp-minister is displeased, and the lamps are cheaper by a third within the century.
You sign last, in a small hand. Zhao Linfeng notes that you could have signed first, and that you did not.

choices.text: Decline, citing the cost of the paper

effects.log: Zhao Linfeng thanks you with great courtesy. The letter goes without you, and arrives with a margin where your name might have been.

events.text: The lamp-minister has not forgotten. A notice arrives in the Ministries: a review of those who 'disturbed the harmony of the White Stairs'. The lamps are cheaper. The review is not. {b3_peer}, who signed first, has been summoned. Zhao Linfeng looks across the hall at you.

effects.log: You stand beside {b3_peer}, and then others do, one at a time, and the review dissolves like salt in a very long afternoon.

choices.text: Send a note to the lamp-minister

effects.log: The note is polite and clever and mostly flattery. The review becomes a reprimand, and your name is quietly lifted off the list.

choices.text: Stay away and let it pass

effects.log: You stay away. It passes. {b3_peer} is demoted a seat for nine years, and does not speak of it, and does not forget who was absent.

events.text: A century later the lamps of the White Stairs are lit by a new rule that bears no author's name. Zhao Linfeng, long retired, stands at the lowest step with a little cup of tea, watching them come on one by one. They turn to you and say that it was never about the lamps, and has not been since the second year.

effects.log: It was about whether anyone would stand for a small thing when a large thing was easier. They say it took them four hundred years to find a name for it.

choices.text: Say nothing and share the tea

effects.log: You share the tea. It is bad tea, as old ministers' tea always is, and it is the best thing you drink all century.

choices.text: Offer to remember it for them

effects.log: They accept with grave courtesy. Years later a lamp on the stairs is lit in a certain pattern, and you are the only one who knows why.

events.text: Two ministers, Zhao Linfeng and Examiner Gu Wen, have each sat to the right of the Celestial Lord for four hundred years, in alternating months, by an arrangement nobody remembers agreeing. The Lord is ill. Both come to you, separately, in the same hour, each sure of being the heir.
events.arc: The Right Hand of the Lord

choices.text: Hear them both and promise nothing

effects.log: You hear them both and promise nothing, which both take as agreement. This is the most diplomatic thing you will do for a century.
Zhao Linfeng is moved, and writes a debt in a small neat hand. Gu Wen learns of it within the week.
Gu Wen is moved, and says nothing at all, which is Gu Wen's way of putting a thing in the ledger. Zhao Linfeng learns of it within the week.

events.text: The Celestial Lord dies, as the very old do, in the middle of a sentence. The ministries stand in the hall in order of rank, and nobody speaks. Zhao Linfeng and Gu Wen both look at you. It seems you have been counted.
events.arc: The Right Hand of the Lord

effects.log: Zhao Linfeng is carried to the seat on a tide of sleeves. Gu Wen bows to the new Lord first, and stays in the room an hour longer than anyone, and it is the most frightening thing you see that year.
Gu Wen is carried to the seat, and Zhao Linfeng bows and does not look at you again for eighty years.

choices.text: Propose that the seat stays empty a year

effects.log: It is unheard of and entirely within the rules. For a year the Ministries are governed by the minutes, which turns out to work disturbingly well.

events.text: The ministers have settled, as the old do, into respect. The one you did not name comes to you in the quiet hour and says it was well done, that they would have chosen the same, and that they will not forgive it. Both statements are true, and both are meant, and you carry them out of the hall like a pair of hot stones.
events.arc: The Right Hand of the Lord

choices.text: Accept the thanks and the grudge

effects.log: You accept both. You will carry the grudge for three hundred years, and it will be, in all that time, the most honest relationship you have in the Ministries.
You offer, and it is refused with the exquisite politeness of someone who would very much like you to have offered. Nothing is undone. Everything is understood.
You tell the hall. It causes a scandal that lasts a season and a reform that lasts a millennium. You are pleased, and slightly sick.

events.text: The Ministries train their young with a heron's quill that writes slowly, so the writer must think of every word. You are to supervise a class of five. Four write. One, Little Pei, stares at the page for the full three hours and produces a single line. It is a good line, and it is not what the lesson asked for.

effects.log: You praise the line. Pei looks stunned, and then writes ten more. They are not very good, but they are theirs.
You correct Pei to the form. Pei writes the form perfectly forever after, and never another line of their own.
You keep the line in a drawer. It is the best sentence in the Ministries, and you do not mention that to anyone for four hundred years.

events.text: Pei is a Court Attendant now, a famous drafter of edicts. Nobody understands why their edicts are always a little too humane. A minister complains of it at dinner and asks if you taught them. The room goes quiet, waiting to see if this is blame or credit.

effects.log: You take the credit and the blame together. It becomes known, in time, as the Ministries' oldest joke and its best policy.
You say you taught them nothing. It is true, in its way. Pei, hearing of it later, writes you a short, polite and unforgettable letter.

choices.text: Say they will be a Minister within a century

effects.log: The minister laughs, and the table laughs, and in ninety-two years it comes to pass, and that table is remembered by exactly the ones who laughed.

events.text: Minister Pei sends for you. The Ministries have grown too tidy, Pei says, and have forgotten how to be surprised. They want a single clerk, chosen at random, to write one sentence a year that is not in any form. They want you to choose who. You are, apparently, the right sort of person to be trusted with a risk.

effects.log: The youngest clerk is bewildered, then delighted, then terrified. The Ministries read their first sentence aloud, and it makes an old minister weep.
The oldest clerk, who has not written an unscripted word in nine thousand years, writes a sentence so odd and so exact that it is copied onto a wall.
Pei accepts, drily. Your sentences are read for a century and never discussed. You find that is the best kind of fame.

events.text: An edict from the Jade Court arrives with a single misspelled character, and the Ministries cannot decide whether to obey the edict, correct it, or declare the spelling itself an order. The matter has gone to the third floor. You are on the third floor.

effects.log: You obey it as written. The misspelling is the word 'dissolve' where 'resolve' was meant, and a small bureau vanishes by noon.

choices.text: Send it back with a polite note

effects.log: You send it back. It returns in sixty years, correct, and with a note of thanks from a clerk who has long since retired.

choices.text: Declare the spelling intended and carry on

effects.log: You declare it intended, and it becomes precedent. Three centuries on, the word is spelled that way throughout the isles and nobody can say why.

events.text: The Ministries keep a lost-and-found for isles. It has a shelf of small floating rocks, a drawer of lost harbours, and a tray of weather nobody collected. An old clerk takes a wrapped parcel out and puts it before you: an isle, the size of a plum, from a petition lodged before you were born.

effects.log: You sign the receipt. It is the smallest isle you will ever own, and it is, on clear days, the only thing you can see from your window.
It takes nine years and three isles to find them. They are very old, and they hold the plum in both hands and do not speak for some time.

choices.text: Put it back on the shelf

effects.log: You put it back. The clerk nods as if that were the right answer, and writes it down, and does not say what the right answer was.

events.text: Bells in the Hall of Precedence are for hours of audience, and each rank has its own bell. The bell of the sixth rank has not rung since the sixth rank was abolished. Today it rings, once, by itself, and every head in the Hall turns toward an empty row of seats.

choices.text: Take the sixth seat, as a joke

effects.log: You sit in it, and the bell rings again, softly, as if satisfied. The Ministries do not laugh. They begin, over the next decade, to consider restoring the rank.

choices.text: Ask the archivist what it means

effects.log: The archivist says only that the bell is bronze, and that bronze has a long memory, and that someone has been moved. Nobody can say who.
The bell is wrapped in felt. It rings anyway, inside the felt, once a year, on a day nobody has chosen.

events.text: A star marshal's retirement is a grave matter: forty thousand cloud-soldiers must be assigned to someone, and nobody wants them. Ouyang Lan asks you to take the farewell parade. It is held on the underside of a cloud, so that those below might see it, and be reminded.

effects.log: You march at the head of forty thousand silent men and women, and for one hour you understand why people have always followed flags.
You watch. The retiring marshal passes you, salutes, and says in an ordinary voice that they would give a great deal not to be going.
Your speech is short and, for once, plain. The old marshal is moved to tears, which in a star marshal is a kind of weather.

events.text: A demon of the Demon Realm has come to the Ministries with a petition, in all the right forms. It is the first in nine hundred years. Registrar Bo Quen would like to know if there is a precedent, and there is, and it says 'refuse'. The demon is waiting, with a polite face and very long hands.

effects.log: You refuse. The demon thanks you in perfect form, and leaves a card with a name on it, which will be useful, one day, to someone.

choices.text: Accept the petition and write a new precedent

effects.log: You accept it, and write the precedent yourself. It is the longest and most careful document of your career, and the demon reads every line.

choices.text: Quietly forward it to the Jade Court

effects.log: The Jade Court will take eleven years to say no, which is the closest the isles come to saying yes.

events.text: There is a rule in the Ministries that nothing is ever repeated, only referred to. Registrar Bo Quen has been asked a question for the eleventh time and has answered, for the eleventh time, 'see item nine of the first minute'. You have the minute. There is no item nine.

effects.log: You say so. Bo Quen goes very still, and then asks, quite gently, whether you would like to write one.
You write item nine. By the end of the year it is quoted by three ministers, and attributed to the first minute, and everyone is satisfied.
You let the matter go. It will return, with a twelfth question, in a year or a thousand, and you will be somewhere else by then.

events.text: The tax of dawn is the Ministries' oldest levy: every isle must send up, each year, a single jar of its first light. The jars line the lower corridor. One jar from the isle of Hanmei is dark. An inspector asks you to witness the opening, because a witness has to be somebody.

effects.log: You open it. The light inside is not gone, only shy, and it comes out slowly, looking around. The inspector stamps it 'accepted' with trembling hands.

choices.text: Seal it and enter a fine

effects.log: A fine is entered against Hanmei. It will be remitted in the next amnesty, and cost the isle a little pride and the inspector a little sleep.

choices.text: Declare the dark a valid dawn

effects.log: You declare it valid, on the ground that Hanmei has had a hard year. The Ministries do not like it. They accept it, which is a different thing.

events.text: A minister falls asleep standing, in the middle of an audience, with the speech unfinished. It is considered rude to wake a minister and rude to leave. A hundred officials stand around the sleeper. Your rank puts you nearest. It is a long afternoon.

effects.log: You finish the speech in their voice, from memory of their other speeches. When they wake, they say they always did say it that way.
They wake at dusk, apologetic. You have stood nine hours. The Ministries will remember who stayed.

choices.text: Quietly rearrange the audience around them

effects.log: By morning there is a small screen, a tea tray, and a new seating plan. Nobody mentions it. It is considered the best audience the minister ever held.

events.text: Your name was entered in the register of the Ministry of Granaries by mistake, as someone else, three hundred years ago. That someone has been receiving your stipend. A letter arrives from them, in the Granaries' style, asking whether you could kindly stop being them, as it is awkward.

effects.log: You write back and apologise, at some length, to a stranger. They reply with a recipe for rice-cakes. It is the best correspondence of your century.
The Granaries take eleven years, and pay you in grain, which you give away. The other 'you' sends a note: 'Well played.'

choices.text: Take their name and let them take yours

effects.log: You swap, officially. Nothing changes except the paperwork, which becomes a small and cheerful mess for two hundred years.

events.text: A very young Court Attendant is learning how to bow. There are eleven depths, and the correct one depends on the other person's rank, age, mood and the time of day. The attendant has bowed to a pillar by mistake and is now stuck at the lowest depth, red-faced, afraid to rise. They look at you, upside down.

effects.log: You bow back, the same depth, and hold it. For a full minute the two of you are the most polite thing in the Ministries. The attendant straightens, grinning.

choices.text: Tell them the pillar is a minister

effects.log: You say the pillar is a retired minister, in a fine disguise. They giggle. It becomes a legend that the pillar is still being bowed to.
You walk past. They rise in your wake. It is the first lesson of the Ministries: nobody helps, and everyone is watching.

events.text: A minister's portrait in the Gallery of Precedence has been looking, since last autumn, slightly to the left. Nobody can say who, or what, it is looking at. The minister in question is long dead, and is not helpful about it. The Gallery has begun to arrange a viewing party, with tea.

effects.log: You stand where it looks. It is a small window, with a view of an isle that does not appear on any register. You write the isle down.
You turn it around. The following morning it has turned itself back, and a small note is pinned to the frame: 'Rude.'

choices.text: Ask the minister, through the seance room

effects.log: The seance room produces a very short reply: 'Left, you fool.' It is taken, solemnly, as an instruction.

events.text: By long tradition, one day each century the Ministries sit in silence for twelve hours, as a rest for the whole order. It is the loudest day of the year. Clerks write notes, ministers pass them under desks, and the Registrar is caught eating a steamed bun with an expression of pure guilt.

choices.text: Pass a note of your own

effects.log: You pass a note. It says 'Good bun?' and is answered in a firm hand: 'Excellent.' It is the only conversation you have in the Ministries that nobody ever forgets.
You keep it honestly, twelve hours without a word or a thought. Afterwards you feel eleven years younger and are very hungry.

choices.text: Use the silence to read the archive

effects.log: You read in the dark, in a corner. By dusk you have learned what the Ministries have hidden from themselves, and you wish, a little, you hadn't.

events.text: A set of mourning bells rings through the Ministries: a Star Marshal is dead, a very old one, in the high isles. Protocol requires every officer of your standing to attend, in white, for nine days. A mourner of the Ministries is expected to say something, and the something is expected to be true.

choices.text: Say what the marshal was like

effects.log: You say it plainly. It includes a joke, which is considered shocking and is repeated for a decade at every funeral thereafter.
You list the deeds. It is a very long list, and by the sixth hour half the hall has remembered something they had forgotten.
You stand. The Ministries read silence as respect, and silence from you as something rather more.

events.text: A very ancient case file comes up from the lowest vault because it has begun, in the damp, to rewrite itself. The case is about a boundary of water and cloud, argued for two thousand years between two isles. The file now says the boundary does not exist, and has said it for a month.

choices.text: Accept the file as it is now

effects.log: You accept it. The two isles are astonished to find themselves agreed. Peace holds for a century, and nobody knows to thank a damp vault.
You restore the old text from a backup. The argument resumes with relief and vigour, and the isles say they were beginning to worry.

choices.text: Ask the isles what they think of the new file

effects.log: They both say it is nonsense and neither wants it changed. The file is left to its own devices. It continues to improve.

events.text: A Celestial Officer comes to you after hours, to ask your advice about a disagreement with a superior. The officer is correct. The superior is powerful. The officer is young enough to think those two facts have anything to do with each other. They sit very upright, with a folder.

effects.log: You tell them to push, with the folder. They do. It costs them nine years and wins them a better post than the one they lost.
You tell them to wait. They do. The superior falls, as the powerful do, and the officer is there to pick up the folder and the post.

choices.text: Tell them what it cost you

effects.log: You tell them. They listen. They push anyway, slightly differently, and you are surprised how little it hurts to be ignored.

events.text: The Wind-Seal is the Ministries' great stamp, which gives edicts their weight. It grows heavier by a grain each year, so that by now it takes two clerks to lift. Someone has proposed to retire it for a lighter one. A ministry-wide vote is called. A hundred hands rise, and a hundred hands do not.

choices.text: Vote to keep the heavy seal

effects.log: You vote to keep it. It is a very small cause and it feels like a huge one. The seal stays, and the clerks are given better lifting-poles.
You vote for the light one. It is lovely, and an edict signed with it floats off the table at the first breeze. The Ministries return to the heavy one within a year.

choices.text: Abstain, and watch who is watching

effects.log: You abstain. You note, in your private ledger, eleven hands that looked at yours before rising. It is a good ledger.

events.text: The Ministries hold annual examinations of officers, in which a hundred people sit in a hall and write about the isles they have never visited. You are on the panel. A young candidate's answer contains the line: 'A good ministry is one that does not need to exist.' The panel is divided.

effects.log: You pass them, over objections. Within a century they have dissolved a ministry, to general astonishment, and been decorated for it.
You pass them narrowly, as a compromise. They grin all the way out. It is the last compromise you make that year.
You fail them. They bow, perfectly, and leave. You learn, many years later, that they became a poet.

events.text: You are asked, as a favour, to teach a Celestial Lord's grandchild how to be ordinary. The child has never had to queue, apologise or carry anything. Lessons begin in the market of the lowest isle, in borrowed clothes. The child's first question is 'Who is the head of the market?'

effects.log: They do not believe you. They watch for an hour, and are astonished to find it works. They buy a plum, and carry it home like a trophy.
You teach them to queue. It takes four hours. They are stunned to find it ends in a bun.
The market does. By afternoon the child has been overcharged, undercharged and adopted by a fishmonger. They come home thoughtful.

events.text: The Ministries have no windows in the great archive, so that nothing might distract the readers. A window is discovered, bricked up, in the east wall. Under the plaster is a note from some earlier reader that says only 'Open this when it's needed.' Nobody can agree on whether it is needed.

effects.log: You open it. Light comes in over the old shelves, and the archive, after eleven thousand years, smells of rain. Some of the books have never looked so tired.
The vote takes a decade. The window is opened by a majority of one, and the one is not you, and everybody pretends not to know who.

choices.text: Leave it bricked, and keep the note

effects.log: You keep the note in your sleeve. On the hardest days of the century you take it out, and it says, still, 'when it's needed'.

events.text: A messenger from the Star Sea Pavilion delivers, to the whole Ministries, a prediction: that in nine years a certain minister will be dismissed. The Pavilion gives no name. The Ministries spend nine years being very, very nice to each other, and the prediction, when it comes true, is entirely about you.

effects.log: You accept it with a bow. You are reinstated in eleven years with a fuller title, and an apology that is too elaborate to be sincere.
You contest it. The Star Sea Pavilion sends a polite note: 'We said it would happen. We did not say it would stay.' You are cheered, slightly.
You quit, in style, at the Day of Precedence, with a very short speech. The prediction is recorded as having been 'fulfilled'.

events.text: A famous poet is stuck in the Ministries' waiting-room, summoned about a tax. The poet has been there nine days. Their lines have grown shorter, and graver, and they have started writing on the wall. The room, being under the Ministries, files the wall. You are sent to explain the fee.

effects.log: You explain it clearly. The poet listens, politely, and pays, and writes a verse about you that is not at all clear.
You waive it. The poet suspects, and is grateful, and does not say so. Their next book is dedicated to 'the clerk who was kind'.

choices.text: Ask for a poem as payment

effects.log: The poet gives you one. The Ministries file it as a receipt. It is the most beautiful receipt in the history of the isles.

events.text: The Ministry of Clouds has no staff. It has had no staff for thirty thousand years, and still produces, every month, a report on the state of the clouds, beautifully written, signed by nobody. A new clerk asks you who writes it, and you realise you have never thought to ask.

choices.text: Wait up one night and watch the desk

effects.log: You wait. At the third bell, a very small cloud settles on the desk and, with great effort, writes the report. You watch, and say nothing, and bring tea.
You say it is the Registrar. The new clerk believes you. The Registrar, hearing of it, confirms it, solemnly, and starts signing the report.
You tell them not to ask. It is the best advice you ever gave. The report continues, and nobody looks too closely, which is how it likes it.

events.text: A visiting official of the Nine Clouds Palace complains that the Ministries' hospitality is 'a performance'. It is true, and the Ministries are mortified. Marshal Ouyang Lan, who is never mortified, asks you to prepare a dinner that is not one. It is harder than it sounds.

choices.text: Serve plain rice and say little

effects.log: You serve plain rice, and the official eats three bowls. It is the first meal in a century in the Ministries that was not minuted.

choices.text: Invite them to a real quarrel

effects.log: You invite them to sit through a ministry argument. They are delighted. 'This,' they say, 'is a real place.'
You do it better, with such perfect formality it comes round to sincerity. The official bows to you and sighs, and you win.

events.text: The Ministries reward long service with a modest pension of a particular weather: a week of mild rain, a week of gold light, or a day of snow. You are offered your choice. The clerk who offers it asks, a little awkwardly, whether you would like to donate it to somebody who has never had any.

effects.log: You take the gold light. For a week your window is a different colour, and you do very little, and it is the best week of the century.

choices.text: Donate it to a clerk in the lowest office

effects.log: The lowest office sits under a sky of mild rain all week and is, by some accounts, never the same again.

choices.text: Take the snow day, and give it to the young

effects.log: You take the day of snow and open the gates. The young of the Ministries, who have never seen it, run out into the court with their hands up.

events.text: The humming blade on the Wall of Swords has chosen. It left its rack in the night and was found standing point-down in the yard before the door of Bai Xuan, an Outer Immortal of three hundred years who cannot yet draw a straight line with a brush. Elder Qin Haoran asks, tiredly, whether the Wall can be asked to reconsider.

choices.text: Say the blade chooses, and that is law

effects.log: You say the blade chooses. Qin Haoran sighs, because it is true, and has Bai Xuan fetched. Bai Xuan arrives holding a bowl of rice, and puts it down very slowly.

choices.text: Offer to hold the blade until Bai Xuan is ready

effects.log: You offer, and the blade is cold in your hand, and heavy with a patience that is not yours. After a month it quietly tugs back toward the yard.

choices.text: Suggest the blade be sent to a better bearer

effects.log: The Wall hums, in what sounds like contempt. The blade is returned to the yard, and set point-down, again, before Bai Xuan's door.

events.text: Bai Xuan has the blade a hundred years, and has not improved at anything else. At the Unsheathing, before the whole mountain, Bai Xuan draws, drops it, picks it up, and cuts the tassel off the Sect Ancestor's chair. The silence lasts a full minute. Elder Qin Haoran asks you whether this is a disgrace.

effects.log: You say the tassel was overdue. A few people laugh. Bai Xuan, who has gone the colour of rice, looks at you as if you had thrown a rope.

choices.text: Say it is a disgrace, and say it kindly

effects.log: You say it, kindly. Bai Xuan nods with the dignity of someone told the truth by the one person who might help. You begin to teach them that evening.
You say nothing. The mountain decides without you. Bai Xuan is sent to the lower terraces for sixty years, and the blade goes with them, as it would.

events.text: On the lower terraces, a landslide of cloud has trapped four hundred pilgrims below the Hall of Unsheathing. Nobody senior can reach them in time. Bai Xuan, now three centuries older and no better with a brush, draws the blade and cuts a stair out of the air itself, which is a thing the Wall was never meant to do. You were nearby.

choices.text: Stand with Bai Xuan on the new stair

effects.log: You stand beside them, on air, and all four hundred come up past you, one at a time. Bai Xuan, at the end, says that the blade did not choose them to be good with a sword.

choices.text: Cut a second stair beside theirs

effects.log: Your stair is cleaner, and Bai Xuan's is wider, and the pilgrims prefer Bai Xuan's, and say so, loudly, for centuries.

choices.text: Go to tell the Sect Ancestor

effects.log: The Sect Ancestor says only, 'Ah.' Within the year the Wall has a place carved for Bai Xuan's name, in a script nobody has used since the founding.

events.text: The mountain of white jade has been leaning, a hair a decade, since before the sect was founded, and nobody has minded. Sword-Warden Lian Shu has measured it with a plumb-line and a very expensive thread, and the lean has doubled. Lian Shu wants someone who is not a coward and not a fool to go and look underneath.

effects.log: Underneath is only cloud. But the cloud has a shape, and the shape is of a sword, a hundred miles long, pointed up at the mountain, quite still.
The disciple returns, white as paper, and says there is a very large thing under the mountain and that it is waiting. It will not say more.

choices.text: Tell Lian Shu the thread is wrong

effects.log: Lian Shu looks at you for a long minute and then buys another thread. It gives the same reading.

events.text: The lean is worse. The sect is worried in the way of the very old: with ceremony, and without haste. Elder Qin Haoran calls a council to ask whether the mountain should be propped, moved, or simply thanked. The Wall of Swords hums throughout, in a key that seems to mean something. You have been asked for a view.

effects.log: A thousand swords are driven into the mountain's base. It holds, for now, and the hum drops, and the whole sect sleeps worse than ever.
You propose a ceremony of thanks, and it is held, the whole sect on the lower terrace, in silence, for a day. The lean stops, for the first time in a thousand years.

choices.text: Move the sect and keep the mountain

effects.log: A third of the sect leaves. The mountain, relieved of the weight, slowly straightens. It is not, perhaps, what anyone intended.

events.text: A visiting Star Sea reader, passing through, glances at the mountain and says, with alarming ease, that it is leaning toward something, not away. It is leaning toward the Nine Clouds Palace. Qin Haoran goes grey. The sect has not been on good terms with the Palace for six hundred years, over a matter involving a sword, a furnace and a broken promise.

choices.text: Send word to the Palace at once

effects.log: The Palace answers, quickly, and with a surprising warmth. The mountain, it seems, has been leaning toward an old friend all along.

choices.text: Stay silent and see what happens

effects.log: The mountain leans another degree. The Palace, with magnificent dignity, sends a polite request that it please stop.

choices.text: Ask the Star Sea reader to look again

effects.log: The reader looks again, and says it is leaning toward you. It is not clear if that was a joke.

events.text: A visitor in the plum-coloured robes of the Verdant Archives arrives at the Hall of Unsheathing and bows. Nine hundred years ago, the sect lost a mountain to their ancestors on a point of grammar, and the visitor has come to ask, very politely, for the second half of it. They have a scroll and a smile.

effects.log: You say it is closed. The visitor says nothing is closed in grammar, and unrolls the scroll to a depth of nine feet.
You offer. They accept with a joyful look, and the argument begins at noon and does not stop for tea.
Qin Haoran enters, sees the scroll, and says a very short word. It is not grammatical.

events.text: The visitor's case has been fought for a decade, in the Hall, over tea. It turns on a single particle in the old deed that can be read as 'and' or as 'but'. The sect reads it as 'and'. The visitor reads it as 'but'. Elder Qin Haoran, driven to despair, asks you to settle it with a sword, in the old way, by cutting the particle off the page.

effects.log: You cut it, with one stroke. It falls to two halves, each with half a particle, which both sides immediately claim as a win.

choices.text: Propose a duel of grammar, not swords

effects.log: A duel of grammar is held, with swords on the table for form. It runs for three days. The visitor and the sect become friends, and are mortified.
You concede it. Qin Haoran is appalled, and then, slowly, relieved. The visitor is stunned, and says it is the first time anyone has conceded in grammar.

events.text: The half of the mountain changes hands, or does not, depending on which scroll you read. A single stone from it has been carved into a small bridge across the Verdant Archives' garden, and the sect has been invited to cross it. Qin Haoran refuses on principle. The visitor, now old, waits at the far end, holding a pot of tea, and watches you.

effects.log: You cross. The stone under your feet is warm, and has a faint grain, and says, if you read it, 'and'. You pour the tea yourselves.
You send a sword-cord. The visitor ties it to the bridge-rail, and it flutters there for a thousand years, a small knot of peace in a very long argument.

choices.text: Decline, and keep the quarrel alive

effects.log: You decline. Both sides are secretly glad. A good quarrel is a pillar of the sect, and a mountain is a small price for a pillar.

events.text: Elder Mu Ruoshui has been blind for four thousand years and teaches the Void Stance by walking among the students with a cup of tea, never spilling. They ask you to spar. You have the use of your eyes. They have a cup. Mu Ruoshui advises, politely, that you draw first.

effects.log: Your sword finds only air, and a little tea. Mu Ruoshui is behind you, cup steady, and says that your breath announces everything.
You close your eyes. For a long minute neither of you moves, and then something in the air moves for you, and you step aside by instinct. Mu Ruoshui says: 'Better.'
You bow. Mu Ruoshui smiles toward your voice and says there will be other afternoons. There are, and they are not as polite.

events.text: Mu Ruoshui asks a strange favour. The sword-cords of the sect must be braided by a person with sight, once a century, and the old hands have gone. Mu Ruoshui will tell you the knot by touch, and you will tie it. It takes a month, in a room that smells of pine, and a thousand questions, mostly about the colour of the light.

choices.text: Describe the light as exactly as you can

effects.log: You describe it, every day, in detail. By the end the elder says they can nearly see it, and thanks you in a voice that has too many years in it.

choices.text: Tie the knot and leave the talking

effects.log: You tie it, and it is perfect, and Mu Ruoshui runs a thumb along it and says nothing for a long time. It is the best praise you have had.

choices.text: Ask them to teach you the knot by touch

effects.log: You learn it blindfold, a hundred times. The elder is delighted. You will never again tie a knot without thinking of a cup of tea that does not spill.

events.text: Mu Ruoshui is leaving, as the old do, up a stair that has no top. The sect lines the steps, and nobody speaks. At the foot, the elder turns, finds you by the sound of your sleeve, and presses a plain old sword into your hands. It weighs almost nothing. 'It was never very sharp,' Mu Ruoshui says. 'It never needed to be.'

choices.text: Take it, and carry it always

effects.log: You take it. Years later it cuts something that no keener sword could, and you do not understand how, and you do not need to.

choices.text: Hang it on the Wall of Swords

effects.log: You hang it on the Wall. The other swords, which have never agreed on anything, are silent for a day.
You say it, and it is short, and plain, and Mu Ruoshui, climbing, lifts a hand without turning. That is the whole of the farewell.

events.text: At Sword-Washing, one blade will not be rinsed. It is an old plain sword that every year goes to the cloud's edge and is carried back dry, because the one rinsing it holds it a moment and cannot let it go in. This year it is your turn. The sword feels, somehow, like a held breath.

effects.log: You lower it in. Nothing happens, and then the sword exhales, a long cold sigh, and a name goes out across the clouds and is gone.
The Sword-Warden says no one knows, which is not the answer. You hold it in the morning light and a small, old sorrow, not yours, fits itself to your hand.

choices.text: Hand it on to the next

effects.log: The next takes it, goes pale, and passes it on in turn. By evening the sword has been held and handed on forty times, and has still not been rinsed.

events.text: A very old person, in a plain robe, arrives at the sect gate asking to see the Wall of Swords, and is told it is closed. They look at you as you pass, and say the name of the sword you held at Sword-Washing, and ask whether it has been rinsed yet. They are weeping, quietly, as the very old do.

effects.log: You take them to the Wall, past the Sword-Warden, who looks away. They stand before the sword a long time. It does not hum. It seems, if anything, to lean toward them.
They tell you, and it is a long story with a shorter ending, and you realise the sword was the last thing a person made before they gave up making.

choices.text: Tell them it has been rinsed

effects.log: They nod, and thank you, and you are sure they know. They go down the stairs slowly, lighter. You will always wonder about the lie.

events.text: The plain sword is gone from the Wall. In its place, a small cloud-flower grows from the rack, white as jade, which opens at dawn and shuts at dusk. The sect cannot agree what it means. The old person, you are told, has gone, and left nothing but the flower and a small clean mark on the stone.

effects.log: You water it with cloud, each morning. It lives longer than you would have thought, and the Wall seems warmer around it.
You write it, plainly, and leave it in the archive. A hundred years later a young disciple reads it, and weeps, and does not know why.
You leave it be. Sometimes the right thing to do with a miracle is to be quiet around it, and this is one.

events.text: During the Unsheathing, one sword in the Hall stays drawn an inch too long, and nobody puts it back. The whole line of disciples stands with their blades half-out, and nobody moves, because the sword in question belongs to Sword-Warden Lian Shu, who has fallen asleep on their feet.

effects.log: You push it home with a finger. Lian Shu wakes, nods, and says that you have been listening. It is the highest compliment the Warden gives.

choices.text: Stand like the rest, and wait

effects.log: You wait, and so does everyone, for a full hour. The sect remembers it as the Longest Unsheathing, and the one time all agreed.

choices.text: Draw your own blade the extra inch

effects.log: You draw yours another inch. Lian Shu wakes, sees, and says in a thick voice, 'Show-off.' You are, strangely, not offended.

events.text: There is a rule on the white jade stairs: no talking, for the stairs listen and remember. Nobody knows who first proposed it and nobody wishes to ask. A stranger on the stairs, a merchant of low isles, is talking loudly on the thousand-and-first step, quite unaware. The stairs, you notice, have begun to hum.

choices.text: Warn the merchant, silently, with a gesture

effects.log: You wave. The merchant stops mid-word, bewildered, and goes the rest of the way up on tiptoe. The stairs stop humming, and you feel, absurdly, thanked.

choices.text: Let the stairs have their say

effects.log: The stairs repeat the merchant's last remark, in a voice like grinding stone: 'And so I said to him...' It echoes for a month.

choices.text: Speak to the merchant, and take the blame

effects.log: You speak. The stairs remember. For the next century, whenever you climb them, they hum your name, softly, to remind you.

events.text: A merchant of the cloud-ports offers the sect ten thousand spirit stones for any single sword on the Wall. He is not rude about it. He has a small, hopeful smile and a long table, and the Elders find themselves, uncomfortably, discussing it. The swords hum. They do not sound pleased.

effects.log: You refuse. The merchant bows, unoffended, and says he will come again in a century. He does, with a smaller smile and a higher offer.

choices.text: Ask what he wants it for

effects.log: He wants it for his daughter's wedding, as a thing to hang. The Elders look relieved and embarrassed. A plain sword is lent, and returned, and a small bond is made.

choices.text: Name a price no one could pay

effects.log: You name it. He pays it, in full, over thirty years, and the Wall gains a very ugly sword that nobody likes and everybody defends.

events.text: It is Empty Hand Day, when every blade of the sect is locked away and the disciples must fight with nothing. The Elders enjoy it. The disciples do not. You are paired with a very young disciple who cries into their sleeve at the first throw and then, to everyone's surprise, throws you through a door.

effects.log: You bow from the floor. The young one is horrified and delighted. The Hall applauds, which is not usual, and Qin Haoran looks away to hide a smile.
You demand it, and win it, narrowly, with a trick you have kept for six hundred years. The young one watches, learning, with an expression you do not like.

choices.text: Ask them to teach you the throw

effects.log: They are shy, and then proud. In an hour you have a new movement, and they have a new friend.

events.text: Once a century the sect re-braids its sword-cords, a task that takes a decade and the whole sect. The pattern is secret, and each disciple learns only a small part. When it is finished, nobody can say what the whole is. It is, the sect likes to say, the shape of what they do not know.

effects.log: You learn it, and do it, over ten quiet years. It is peaceful work, and when the cords are done, you feel a part of something larger and entirely mysterious.

choices.text: Try to work out the whole pattern

effects.log: You try. By year six you have it half-guessed, and by year nine you realise you have been woven into it.

choices.text: Make a small mistake on purpose

effects.log: You make a tiny error in your portion. It is never found, and it is the only flaw in the pattern, and it is yours.

events.text: A cloud crane has nested on the roof of the Hall of Unsheathing and refuses to leave. It is an enormous white bird, mild-eyed, with a talent for dropping things on the visiting. Sword-Warden Lian Shu has tried firmly, politely, and with a ladder. The crane regards you instead, as if you might have a better idea.

choices.text: Feed it, and let it stay

effects.log: You feed it, daily. The crane lets you stroke its neck, and, in time, takes a particular dislike to people who bring bad news, and warns you of them.

choices.text: Ask it to move, and mean it

effects.log: You ask. The crane thinks it over for a week, and moves to the Nine Clouds Palace. They send a note of thanks.

choices.text: Name it, and say it belongs to the sect

effects.log: You name it Qingshu. It answers to the name, immediately, and the sect has a bird.

events.text: A Demon Realm general sends a polite challenge to the sect: a duel, by the old rules, for no reason at all except respect. It is not a threat. It is, in the manner of the realm, a compliment. Elder Qin Haoran says it is a bad idea. Sword-Warden Lian Shu says it is a good one. Both look at you.

ok.log: You win, narrowly, and the general bows, laughing, and says that is the best fight in a century. Respect, it seems, has been exchanged.

fail.log: You lose, honourably, and the general helps you up. It is oddly friendly. Your pride is a good deal sorer than your ribs.

effects.log: You decline, and send a flask of good tea. The general sends back a bottle of something fiery. Neither is opened for a year.
You propose a duel of poems, in the mountain's style. The general is delighted, and the poems are terrible, and everyone has a lovely evening.

events.text: The oldest Elder of the sect, Mu Ruoshui, has not spoken in six hundred years, and the Hall has grown used to it. This morning, at the Unsheathing, they say, quite clearly, a single word. Nobody agrees what it was. The word is argued over for a decade, and a faction forms around each version.

choices.text: Say you heard it, and say what

effects.log: You say what you think you heard. A third of the Hall agrees. It is not enough, but it is enough to make you a faction.
Mu Ruoshui smiles, and says nothing, and refills your cup. It is, you conclude, the only answer there will ever be.
You say nothing and think about it for a century. You are right, as it happens, and nobody ever finds out.

events.text: The Void Stance is the sect's first great trial: you stand on a ledge of white jade over nothing, with nothing beneath you, for a day. A younger disciple is watching you. You are expected, as an elder, to make it look easy. You have done it a hundred times. Today your knees, for the first time, have opinions.

effects.log: You stand it out, shaking, and the young one, who sees, is oddly comforted. By dusk you have taught more than a lesson.

choices.text: Step back and say you are tired

effects.log: You step back and say so. The young one, who feared you, laughs, and for the first time, relaxes. It is, perhaps, the better lesson.

choices.text: Stand it out in perfect stillness

effects.log: You stand it perfectly. The young one gazes, awed. It costs you a month of aching, and it is the myth that the sect most wishes to keep.

events.text: The Sect Ancestor naps at midday, in a pavilion at the very top of the white mountain, and nobody is allowed to be noisy. A visiting immortal from the Star Sea Pavilion has brought a set of small bells as a gift. Nobody has the courage to tell them. The bells begin, gently, to tinkle in the wind.

effects.log: You take them down, one by one, in a silence that costs three hours. The Ancestor wakes at the end, and says only, 'Thank you,' and you feel ten feet tall.
The bells ring. The Ancestor wakes, listens, and says it is the first sound that they have liked in a thousand years. The bells stay.
You mute them. The Star Sea visitor is a little hurt, and later sends a quiet gift, much more suitable.

events.text: A swordsmith from the cloud-isles asks to repair a blade older than the mountain. It is a plain grey sword with no edge to speak of, and a crack through the middle that has been there since before anyone can remember. The Elders are divided. The swordsmith has brought a very small hammer and a very large tea-set.

effects.log: The repair takes three years, and when it is done the sword is, to everyone's disappointment, exactly the same, except that it is happier.
You forbid it. The swordsmith bows, and leaves, and a crack in the sword, you notice, is very slightly wider the next day.
You ask. It hums, once, in an approving tone. The swordsmith begins, and the whole sect watches, in silence, from a respectful distance.

events.text: The swordsmen of the Jade Void are famous for their bad poetry. Once a year, on the Night of Dull Verses, the entire sect gathers to read their worst work aloud. It is held in great affection. A visiting poet of renown, trapped in the front row, has gone the colour of old paper. You are on after the Elder.

effects.log: You read it. It is so bad that the poet is forced to laugh, and the hall applauds for ten minutes. You are given a prize, a wooden cup with a hole in it.
A good poem slips out, to your horror. The hall falls silent. It is the only unwelcome thing to happen on the Night of Dull Verses in six hundred years.

choices.text: Pass, and ask the poet to read instead

effects.log: The poet reads one line, and the sect is humbled, and then delighted. The Night is a triumph, though not of anyone's making.

events.text: In the high winter, ice forms on the white jade, and the sect walks in sword-cord boots, tied tight, and does not speak of the cold. A young disciple has slipped and clung, with one hand, to the edge of the stair, over nothing, and is being very quiet and brave. You are the nearest.

effects.log: You grab them. They come up, white and silent, and then they say, very formally, 'Thank you,' and are sick on the stair.
The cord goes taut at once, and honest, and holds. They climb. It is, you note, the first time the cord has been used for this, and it is very good at it.
The Elders arrive, with ropes, and a great deal of dignity. The disciple is saved, and a safe rule is made. You are mildly ashamed at how long it took.

events.text: A young prodigy of the sect, Lu Yan, has beaten every Inner Immortal in the Hall and now stands in the courtyard, looking for the next. They are polite about it, and entirely without doubt. The Elders look at their hands. Elder Qin Haoran says, quietly, that they have been waiting a long time for someone to say no.

effects.log: You say no, and fight them, and lose, slowly and gracefully. They are thoughtful, afterwards, and for the first time, uncertain. It is the start of an education.
You say yes, and win, by a hair, using an old trick. Lu Yan is furious, and then fascinated. You acquire a pupil who will not leave.
You offer tea. Lu Yan, who has never been offered tea by an opponent, does not know what to do. It is the first time you see a prodigy confused.

events.text: A contest is held, once a decade, among the swordsmen: whose cut through a cloud closes the slowest. The winner's cut hangs in the sky for years, a scar of light. Your cut is respectable. The present champion's cut, a century old, has not closed at all, and people go out to look at it, and sigh.

choices.text: Cut a cloud and close it fast

effects.log: You cut, and it closes in a breath. The crowd titters. It is the smallest cut in the history of the contest, and you win a prize for modesty.

choices.text: Cut it as deep as you can

effects.log: You cut it deep, and it hangs, white and thin, for a decade. People point, and then, shyly, make wishes on it.

choices.text: Ask the champion how they did it

effects.log: The champion tells you, and it is the most beautiful lesson of your century, and has nothing to do with swords.

events.text: The scabbard of a founder is missing from the Hall. It is not valuable, only old, and its absence is felt more than its presence ever was. Sword-Warden Lian Shu wants it found without a fuss. The only clue is a smear of white powder on the floor, and a faint smell of plum blossom.

effects.log: It leads to the roof, where the cloud crane has made it a bed. You return it, with a bow to the crane, and the crane, with a bow to you.
The Hall, under its dignity, mutters. A very young disciple admits they borrowed it for a game. It is returned, sheepishly, and the game is moved outside.

choices.text: Say it is lost, and let it stay lost

effects.log: You say so. The scabbard is never found, and becomes the most revered object in the sect, simply by being missing.

events.text: The white jade mountain has exactly one tree, a small plum, growing out of a crack in the south terrace. It blossoms once a century, for a day. The sect holds a vigil. A visiting guest from the Nine Clouds Palace begins, to everyone's dismay, to cut a twig for grafting. You are standing next to them, with a sword.

effects.log: You stop them, politely, with the flat of a blade. They are horrified, and apologise, and a quiet friendship is made.
You let them. The graft takes, in the Palace, and bears fruit that tastes of white jade. The sect pretends not to mind, and sends tea.

choices.text: Cut the twig yourself, and give it

effects.log: You cut it, cleanly, and give it with both hands. The Palace remembers, for a thousand years, and the plum on the mountain blooms a day longer.

events.text: One of the white jade stairs sings. It sings a single low note when stepped on, and has done since before anyone was born. This morning it sings a different note, and everyone who passes stops, and tilts their head. A very old Elder says, in a slow voice, that the last time it changed, a mountain fell.

effects.log: You search it, and find nothing but a very small crack, from which something very small and shy is peering out. It is a cloud-mouse. It sings.

choices.text: Test the note against a sword

effects.log: You strike a sword on the stair, and find the note matches it exactly. It is, it seems, a greeting. You return the courtesy, shyly.

choices.text: Keep the sect off the stair

effects.log: You keep them off it for a month. Nothing falls. The stair resumes the old note, with a slightly embarrassed air.

events.text: An old rival of yours, long thought gone from the mountain, has sent back your sword, which they borrowed in a quarrel eight hundred years ago. It arrives in a plain box, with a note that says nothing but your name. The blade has been polished, and re-hilted, and is a little shorter. It still hums, faintly, in your hand.

effects.log: You send a note, only your rival's name. Nothing else. A year later, a package arrives with a pot of plum jam, and you are friends again, or something like it.
You go. It takes three years, and a mountain's worth of stairs, and when you find them, you do not speak for an hour, and it is a lovely hour.

choices.text: Keep the sword, and say nothing

effects.log: You keep it. It cuts better than before, and you will never quite know why, and you pretend that is enough.

events.text: At the start of every century, the disciples of the Jade Void swear the Oath of the Empty Hand: that they will never draw their sword first, and never leave it undrawn when it is needed. It is a short oath and a long wait. You are asked to witness it for forty young ones. Three of them, you suspect, do not mean it.

effects.log: You witness it. Two of the three keep it. The third breaks it in a hundred years, and is forgiven, and you were right all along.
You speak to them. One tells you the truth, one runs, and one laughs. It is a good day's work, and none of it is on the record.
You swear it with them. Your voice is old and theirs are young, and you are, for a moment, the same age as they are.

events.text: A pilgrim has come to the sect gate and asks to be refused. They want to be told, by someone with a sword, that they are not good enough, so that they can go home with a clear conscience to a quiet life. They have walked eleven years to be turned down. The gatekeeper asks you what to do.

effects.log: You refuse them, kindly. They bow, weeping with relief, and go home, to a life that, you hear, goes very well.

choices.text: Accept them, to spite their expectations

effects.log: You accept them. They are appalled, and then furious, and finally, after a decade, a good swordsman who hates you with great affection.

choices.text: Ask them why they really came

effects.log: They tell you, over three nights, and it is not about swords at all. By the end they are crying, and you are making tea.

events.text: Tea in the Jade Void is taken with the swords laid on the table, hilts toward the host, which is an old courtesy and a threat in the same gesture. A new Inner Immortal has put theirs the wrong way round, point toward the host. The hall goes silent, and everybody finds something to look at, and the host, an Elder, goes white.

effects.log: You turn it, with a smile, and the Elder breathes again. The young one is mortified, and thanks you in a whisper, and will remember all their life.
You say it is a joke, and laugh. It is not very convincing, but the Elder, relieved, joins in. The room, slowly, thaws.

choices.text: Let the Elder deal with it

effects.log: The Elder deals with it, with great gravity, and a fortnight's penance for the young one. It is, you suspect, entirely unnecessary, and entirely effective.

events.text: On the Day of Paper Cuts the swordsmen of the sect take a single sheet of paper each and cut a character from it with one stroke of a sword. The characters are hung in the Hall, and are read by the others, and are, by custom, always about something the cutter fears. Yours is one you did not know you would cut.

choices.text: Hang it where all can see

effects.log: You hang it high. The hall reads it, and falls silent, and over the next year, three people come to you, quietly, and say, 'Me too.'

choices.text: Hang it in a dark corner

effects.log: You hang it in a corner, behind a pillar. It is found by a young disciple, in a year, who reads it, and stays for a long time, and goes.
You burn it, in a small brazier, and the smoke goes up as a faint white thread. You feel lighter, and slightly dishonest, and it was, for a moment, enough.

events.text: Apothecary Lu Qing finds, at the back of the Cinnabar Palace's cold store, a pill the colour of dusk, labelled in a hand that is yours. You have never brewed it. Lu Qing holds it with two fingers like a hot coal and asks, very quietly, whether you would like it destroyed.

effects.log: Lu Qing does not know. Nobody does. The label says only 'for when it is needed'. You tell Lu Qing to keep it, and Lu Qing, relieved, locks it away.
It dissolves in the Frost bell's water with a sigh like a person setting down a bag. Lu Qing is sad for a week and cannot say why.
You swallow it. For a day nothing happens, and then the whole Palace smells of the sea. You are quite well. You are also, somehow, owed an apology.

events.text: Ninety years on, a young alchemist of the Palace falls into a fever no pill can touch. Lu Qing's successor remembers the dusk-coloured pill in the cold store and looks at you. The label, they say, now reads 'for this'. They did not write that either.

choices.text: Give it to the young one

effects.log: The fever breaks by dawn. The alchemist wakes, thin and starving, and asks for noodles. The pill's label reads, in your hand, 'done'.

choices.text: Withhold it and try the old cures

effects.log: The old cures work, slowly, at a cost to the young one's strength. The label on the pill goes blank, and you feel obscurely graded.

events.text: A traveller from the Star Sea arrives at the Palace and asks for the pill 'that you made when you were somebody else'. They have read it in the stars. They are polite, and sad, and say it is not for them but for someone not yet born. They will wait.

choices.text: Give them the pill's recipe, written

effects.log: You write what you remember of it, which is more than you thought. The traveller leaves with it folded in a star-chart, and you never learn the rest.

choices.text: Tell them the pill is spent

effects.log: The traveller nods, gentle. 'Then it was needed already,' they say, and go. You sit a long while with the label.

events.text: Steward Tao Mingyi comes to your door at night in his slippers: the Ninefold Furnace has gone out. It has burned since the Palace was founded. The nine palace masters are in the courtyard, each blaming the weather, which on nine clouds that never rain is a special sort of excuse.

effects.log: The hall is cold and the great bronze belly smells of nothing at all. You lay your hand on it and feel, very faintly, a pulse, as of something asleep and not dead.
The nine come, and argue, and by the time they stop it is dawn and the Furnace has been cold for six hours. It is a very long argument and a very tidy one.

events.text: The Ninefold Furnace is still cold, and now the Palace is cold with it: the nine clouds have begun to drift. Palace Master Yun Fei offers a plan to relight it with a flame from the Jade Void's Wall of Swords. It would make the Palace beholden to the sword immortals for a thousand years.

effects.log: The flame is brought down the white stairs in a lantern by an unsmiling swordsman. The Furnace takes it. The Palace is warm and in debt, and a sword hangs in the foyer ever after.

choices.text: Try to relight it from your own qi

effects.log: You spend a year at the bronze belly, feeding it. It stirs. It does not catch. You are changed by it, a little, in the way a hearth changes a house.
The Palace is colder and the nine clouds drift into nine separate weathers. The masters, appalled, begin at last to talk to one another.

events.text: The Furnace is lit again, and it is not the same flame. Its fire is slightly green, and the pills it makes are slightly better, and Palace Master Yun Fei, who is seven hundred, weeps openly in the furnace hall because it smells like her mother's kitchen.

effects.log: You stand with her in the green light, saying nothing. The Palace, by old custom, does not speak of what is seen in the furnace hall.
The new flame gives you three formulas the old one never allowed. They are in the Palace library to this day, under your name and a smudge of green.

events.text: Array-Reader Sima Ruo, who hears formations the way others hear music, stops in the middle of the Third Palace's courtyard and will not go on. The floor, she says, is hollow in a way no one built. She asks you to stand where she points and tell her whether you hear it too.

effects.log: You hear it: a low and patient note, under the stones, like someone holding their breath. Sima Ruo nods and marks the spot with a pinch of chalk.

choices.text: Tell her it is only the cloud

effects.log: She looks at you for a long moment and says nothing, and moves the chalk herself. You are right, probably, and it matters not at all.

events.text: Beneath the Third Palace lies a formation older than the Palace, and it is not dead. Sima Ruo has dug to its edge and refuses to dig further without someone of rank. The formation, she thinks, is a door, and it is waiting for a hand to ask it politely.

effects.log: You knock, as at a neighbour's, and say your name. After a minute the array hums, once, and a seam of pale light opens. Sima Ruo is white to the lips.
The Palace seals it with nine layers of lacquer and a slab. Sima Ruo stands guard at the slab for a month in silent protest, and nobody dares move her.

events.text: Through the door under the Third Palace is a long white room with one table in it. On the table lies a cup of tea, still warm, and a note: 'Take your time. We have kept this for whoever came.' Sima Ruo reads it and laughs and cries, and says it is the first array she has ever loved.

effects.log: It is excellent tea. The room fades politely as you finish, and the door becomes a plain floor again, now with a small round stain in the shape of a cup.

choices.text: Leave the tea for Sima Ruo

effects.log: She drinks it, slowly, and says nothing for an hour. The Palace never learns what the room said to her. She is gentler ever after.

events.text: A tenth cloud has appeared over the Nine Clouds Palace: small, grey, shy, trailing the others like a child at a party. The nine palace masters hold a hasty council on whether it counts. Tao Mingyi consults the founding charter, which says nine, and also, in a margin, 'or as many as come'.

effects.log: You send tea up to the little cloud on a ladder. It rains, for the first time in Palace history, exactly one drop, on the tea. Everyone agrees this is a yes.

choices.text: Rule it a guest, not a palace

effects.log: The cloud is housed as a guest, with a small card on its door. It seems content, in the way of the very polite.

events.text: The tenth cloud has grown. It now drifts at the head of the Palace, and the nine masters have grudgingly started to defer to it, which is not an arrangement the charter foresaw. Something lives in it, small and curious, that watches the furnaces with its whole face.

choices.text: Ask the cloud what it wants

effects.log: It wants to learn. You take it as a pupil, a small grey patient thing, and in a century it is the best array-reader the Palace has ever had.

choices.text: Offer the cloud a palace of its own

effects.log: The Palace builds it a pavilion of pale glass. The cloud moves in, grave and pleased, and rains a single drop of thanks on each of the nine masters.

events.text: The Night of Nine Fires is one fire short: the ninth furnace of the Frost Palace will not light, and the Frost Master, a thin lady with a very formal bow, apologises to the whole assembled order and asks permission to borrow a flame. Eight palace masters stare politely at the ground.

effects.log: You lend a spark from your qi. The ninth furnace lights, blue and shy. The Frost Master bows lower than she has ever bowed to anyone.

choices.text: Offer to light it from the tea-stove

effects.log: The tea-stove's honest orange fire takes. The furnace burns a sensible colour all night, and the Frost Master never lives it down, and loves you for it.

events.text: A pill-seller from the low isles has been selling 'authentic Nine Clouds elixir' for years, and the Palace has finally heard. The Stewards want him ruined. He is a gentle old man who sells what is, in fact, a rather decent honey cordial, and has done good with it. He is waiting at the gate with his basket.

choices.text: Let him sell it, under licence

effects.log: The Palace licenses the cordial as a minor remedy, to the Stewards' disgust. The old man weeps and sends a barrel of it every New Year.
The basket is confiscated. The Palace's honour is satisfied. A story goes round the low isles about the cruelty of the clouds.

events.text: The nine clouds have been drifting a hand's breadth closer every century. Sima Ruo, on a clear night, shows you her calculations: in four thousand years the palaces will touch. The masters agree it is a problem for later, and argue about the date of later.

effects.log: You draft a charter for the Palace's eventual merger, and everyone agrees to forget it. A copy, sealed, is kept for the people of four thousand years on.
You speak to the nearest cloud, courteously. It drifts back a little, offended, and then forward again in the night. Sima Ruo notes it down as a hopeful result.

events.text: At the Palace gate a delegation of the Jade Void demands the return of a sword left behind in a brewing accident three hundred years ago. It is in the Palace pantry. It has been used, since, as a skewer. The sword, summoned, is delighted by the attention and ashamed of the smell.

choices.text: Return it with a cleaning and an apology

effects.log: The swordsmen accept it stiffly. The sword hums happily on the way home, smelling of cardamom. The feud is cooled, at the cost of one skewer.

choices.text: Keep it as a skewer and say it is lost

effects.log: The delegation leaves, suspicious. The sword is a very good skewer. The Palace does not entertain Jade Void guests at dinner for some decades.

events.text: The Palace's annual great brew has been given to you to oversee. It is a hundred-day elixir of nine herbs, and it must be stirred every hour by someone awake. The stirring is dull. The tradition is that the stirrer thinks of one good memory per hour, and that the elixir takes its taste from them.

effects.log: It takes a hundred days, and by the end the elixir tastes of fresh bread, rain on a roof, and someone's laugh. The Palace sells it out by morning.

choices.text: Think of the same one, over and over

effects.log: The elixir tastes of a single afternoon in a mortal year. It is the finest brew in the Palace's history, and it sells to no one, and you keep a jar.

events.text: A cloud-beast, an ancient and soft one, has taken to sleeping across the entrance of the Cinnabar Palace. It is warm and kind and it blocks the door. Nobody has the heart to move it. Palace Master Yun Fei steps over it each morning with the air of a woman performing a small, daily penance.

effects.log: You coax it with a bowl of sweet gruel. It follows, and settles at the foot of the stairs, and you are for a century the only one it comes to when called.

choices.text: Build a small door beside it

effects.log: A little door appears in the wall beside the beast, with a brass plate: 'For the use of the Palace, and the beast.' It is the pride of the order.

events.text: A young alchemist of the Palace has produced the first pill in four hundred years that works exactly as intended. It cures a headache. That is all it does. The Stewards are furious, since it is too simple to be a secret. The young one is shaking, and holds the little pill out to you.

choices.text: Praise it and make it standard

effects.log: The pill becomes the Palace's most-sold remedy and the young alchemist's life work. They say it is the one thing they ever made that did not need an explanation.

choices.text: Ask them to try for something harder

effects.log: They try, and fail, and learn, and ten years later brew a pill of real subtlety. They keep the headache pill in a drawer, with love.

events.text: The Palace is hosting a conference of the five factions on the use of dream-herb. The Star Sea wants it regulated, the Demon Realm taxed, the Jade Void banned, and the Celestial Ministries registered, filed and audited in triplicate. You are asked to chair. The herb, in a small jar, is sprouting gently on the table.

effects.log: It takes three weeks and nine pots of tea. The result is a treaty so tangled it works. The herb, in the jar, flowers on the last day.
In the open air the delegates calm. The herb is declared a gift of the clouds, which no faction may own. It is the shortest treaty in the isles.

events.text: The Palace keeps a rule that no formation may be left unfinished at night, because unfinished formations 'dream'. A junior array-master has left a small ward half-drawn on a classroom floor and gone to bed. The ward is, you see, drawing the rest of itself.

effects.log: The ward completes itself, a pretty little thing that does nothing but hold a candle steady. The junior is mortified, then proud, then asked to train others.
You wipe the chalk. A faint, wounded hum goes up from the floor and fades. The junior, in the morning, asks where their little ward has gone, and you cannot say.

events.text: Tao Mingyi, the Steward, has run the Palace's books for nine hundred years without a single error, and has just made one: a rounding, in a column nobody reads. He has come to you in the dark to confess it. He is shaking, and asks if he should resign.

choices.text: Tell him it is the best news in centuries

effects.log: He laughs, appalled, then weeps. The error is framed and hung above his desk. He is happier ever after, and, strangely, better at his job.

choices.text: Correct the entry and say nothing

effects.log: You fix it quietly. He never learns. You carry the small cool weight of a kindness uncredited, which turns out to be enough.

events.text: A great storm gathers around the Palace, one that has never been on any chart: a rainstorm. The nine clouds that never rain are suddenly dark and heavy. Sima Ruo reads the signs with a face like a held breath. Something is about to be wept.

effects.log: The rain falls, the first in Palace history, and it is warm. The Palace stands in it, hands out, laughing. The furnaces steam. Afterwards the gardens are green past all reason.
The wards hold. The rain falls round the Palace in a ring, and the storm, sulking, goes elsewhere, and the clouds remain dry and, you think, slightly sad.

events.text: Your assigned apprentice in the Palace is a demon youth sent by the Realm to learn pill-craft, on the understanding that they will go home with it. They are charming, brilliant, and have already started telling the other apprentices about the Realm's feasts. Half the Palace has taken to staying up late for stories.

effects.log: You do, over thirty years. They go home a great alchemist and send, ever after, a barrel of fiery wine at the turn of each century.
You teach them half. They notice, at the end, and bow to you with great respect and some reproach. You are not sure which of you was right.

events.text: The Palace's roof gardens grow a single flower that blooms only for a minute every ten years, and only if no one is looking. The botanists have been trying to catch it for six centuries. You are on the roof, alone, with a book, when the corner of your eye notices a petal.

choices.text: Keep reading, and do not look

effects.log: You read on. A scent drifts across the page and is gone. Later, a gardener finds a blossom, and swears, and the Palace never knows it was you.
You look. The flower is gone, but its absence has a shape you will carry. The botanists are very polite about it.

events.text: A famine hits the low isles, and the Palace is asked to open its stores of grain-pills. The Stewards point out that the stores are for the Palace's own long fasts. The Palace Master looks at you. The grain-pills are a hundred years' supply, and the low isles, they say, hold five hundred thousand mouths.

effects.log: The Palace goes hungry for a season, with good grace. The low isles remember. A hundred years on, a whole isle still keeps the Palace's name in its prayers.
The Palace opens half and brews with everything it has. By spring both are fed. The Stewards are exhausted and vindicated, and the furnaces never burned brighter.

events.text: In the library of the Cinnabar Palace you find a book of recipes in the margin of which a past Palace Master has written: 'I do not think this will work, and I am doing it anyway, and if you read this, forgive me.' It is dated nine thousand years ago. The recipe, you think, might work.

effects.log: It works, to a degree that frightens you. You write 'forgiven' in the margin and put the book on the highest shelf.

choices.text: Write a margin note and leave it

effects.log: You write 'not yet'. The book returns to its shelf. In a thousand years someone else will read both notes and wonder about you.

events.text: At the monthly tasting of the Palace's elixirs the judges are blindfolded, and one of them, the oldest, announces that a sample is 'perfect'. The sample is water. It was a test, and the old judge has failed it, and is silent in the dark, unable to remove the blindfold.

effects.log: You say the water is the best you have tasted. The old judge exhales. Over the next century the Palace adds a glass of water to every tasting, and nobody forgets why.

choices.text: Say nothing, and lift the blindfold gently

effects.log: The old judge squints, sees only you, and takes your hand. The tasting resumes without comment. It is the kindest silence of the year.

events.text: The Palace's founding stone is cracked down the middle, and a thin warm light leaks out. The Stewards, to a man, decide to ignore it. Sima Ruo, kneeling at the crack with her ear to it, says something is singing in there, in a language she nearly knows.

effects.log: You listen for an hour. The song is the sound of nine clouds learning to float. At the end, you can almost hum it, and for a decade you do.

choices.text: Seal it with a lacquer of gold

effects.log: The Palace seals it. The light dims to a hair. Sima Ruo is quiet for a year, and then carves the song's melody on a small flute, for herself.

events.text: A famous immortal beauty, tired of her face, comes to the Palace asking for a pill to make her plain. The Stewards refuse; it offends the craft.
