She sits at the gate in the rain, cheerfully refusing tea. She says she has been looked at for eleven hundred years and would like to look at something else.

effects.log: You brew a mild one, and it works, and she vanishes into a crowd of grey cloaks with a delighted laugh. She sends a postcard from a small isle: 'Nobody has looked at me in months.'
You sit with her in the rain for an hour, and she talks, and at the end she goes home as she is, and says she feels, absurdly, seen.

events.text: Two of the nine palace masters have fallen in love, and are far too dignified to say so. The whole Palace knows. A sweepstake of guesses has been running for three hundred years, and a clerk keeps the ledger with a trembling hand. The masters, passing in the corridor, nod stiffly. The guess is due.

effects.log: You arrange for two chairs side by side at the next feast. The masters, after a long pause, sit. The sweepstake is closed and the clerk, weeping, retires.
You guess never, out of mischief. You lose, at last, eleven years later, with delight. The winnings go to a fund for the clerk's retirement tea.

events.text: A formation that heats the Palace baths has begun humming a rude song. The array-readers are mortified, and cannot find the fault. The song is, in fact, a quite accurate summary of the Palace's last council meeting. Sima Ruo, red to the ears, says she cannot silence it without losing the heat.

effects.log: The bath song becomes beloved. By winter the whole Palace knows the verses, and the council meetings, for fear of the baths, grow remarkably brief and polite.

choices.text: Silence it and take a cold bath

effects.log: You silence it. The baths are cold for a week. The array-readers are quiet and grateful, and wonder, a little, where the song learned its tunes.

events.text: The Palace needs a new Palace Master, and Yun Fei, who has held the post for six hundred years, has proposed you. The council finds the idea hilarious and horrifying. Yun Fei insists she is serious. She has packed a small bag and will, if refused, leave anyway.

effects.log: You name a thin, serious young alchemist. Yun Fei approves. She leaves her bag in the hall, unlifted, for another thirty years.

choices.text: Accept the post for a year as a trial

effects.log: You are Palace Master for a year and nine days, and it is the most tiring pleasure of your life. At the end, Yun Fei takes back the chair, grinning, and the council toasts you in the soup.

events.text: The Palace decants a new vintage of cloud-wine every nine hundred years, and tonight is the opening. The cork comes out and the wine is, to everyone's mortification, vinegar. The assembled order stares at their cups. Tao Mingyi, the Steward, announces it is a deliberate choice. Nobody believes him.

effects.log: You praise it with a face of stone. By the third round of toasts the vinegar is a dish, a fashion, and an ancient tradition. The Palace dines on it for centuries.

choices.text: Pour yours into the nearest plant

effects.log: The plant, a spindly Palace shrub, flourishes at once and blooms purple. The vinegar becomes the garden's tonic, and nobody toasts it ever again.

events.text: Sima Ruo's apprentice, a girl of fifteen with a gift for arrays and none for sleeping, has been found asleep on the roof, on top of an unfinished formation, which is humming her lullaby. Sima Ruo, rigid with horror, asks if you could, please, wake her gently. The formation seems to be keeping her warm.

effects.log: She wakes, confused, to a roof of stars and a formation she has completed in her sleep. It is the best she has ever drawn. Sima Ruo does not speak for a day.

choices.text: Let her sleep and draw a blanket over her

effects.log: You put a blanket on her, and a second one on the formation. In the morning both are warm. Sima Ruo puts a third on you, wordlessly.

events.text: A very old and very famous alchemist of the Star Sea comes to the Palace to die. They wish to do it at the Palace, they say, because it has the best tea. The Stewards are appalled. The visitor sits in the garden, calm and enormous, and asks only for company.

effects.log: You sit for nine days. On the ninth they tell you a recipe that has never been written, and go in the evening, with a smile. You write the recipe down, and it is the best tea.
Yun Fei comes, and takes your place. You leave them alone with their tea. It is the right thing, and you carry its shape for years.

events.text: The Ninefold Furnace has one oddity: when someone in the Palace tells a deliberate lie in its hall, the fire flickers. It has been a running joke for millennia, and a deterrent for none. You are asked, now, to testify before the nine masters, in the hall, on a matter of delicacy.

effects.log: The flames stand perfectly still. The masters note this, one by one, with a distinct and ominous respect. You are never questioned in that hall again.

choices.text: Testify with a mild kind lie

effects.log: The fire flickers once, and then, as if forgiving, steadies. The masters pretend not to have seen. Your lie is received as the truth and later turns out to be one.

events.text: On the roof of the Palace a stranger has set up a stall selling little maps of the nine clouds. The maps are accurate. They are also, you realise, accurate about things that have not happened yet. A map marks a small cross on the Cinnabar Palace, with the caption 'where you will stand on Thursday'.

effects.log: On Thursday you stand on the cross, feeling foolish, and the roof gives way slightly, and a pill falls out of a ceiling and into your palm. It is a very good pill.

choices.text: Ask the stranger for the rest

effects.log: The stranger smiles and hands you a blank one. 'Fill it in yourself,' they say. By the next century, it is full of your handwriting.

events.text: Every morning at the third bell of night, the Observatory Terrace holds the Reading of the Hour. {b3_elder} says missing it is noticed and never punished, which everyone knows is worse. Today there is a gap where Reader Maelis Quen's cushion used to be, and a hundred pretend not to look at it.

effects.log: You step into the gap. Nobody speaks of it, and by the end of the day everybody has.
The line shuffles shut over the missing place, and the ritual goes on as though nothing could ever have been absent.
{b3_elder} tells you at length and with rather more feeling than the rite allows. You understand the order a little better.

events.text: Everyone passes the brass armillary, and nobody has ever moved it: eleven rings that have never once agreed with each other. A newcomer asks what it is for, and {b3_elder} gives the answer that it measures the sky. You have a second answer. It is better, and no one in the Observatory Terrace wants to hear it.

effects.log: You give it. {b3_elder} listens, thanks you, and says the first answer will remain the official one. Several people copy yours down.
You nod at the official answer. The newcomer looks at you and decides, correctly, that there is a better one somewhere.

choices.text: Ask the newcomer what they think

effects.log: Their idea is wrong and delightful. You spend the afternoon showing them why, and come away with a better question than you started with.

events.text: {b3_peer} and Reader Orsolo Fen have not spoken for ninety years, and the Observatory Terrace is arranged around the silence: the east stairs are for one and the west stairs for the other. Today you are asked, very politely, to carry one sentence between them.

effects.log: You carry it exactly. Reader Orsolo Fen considers it for an hour and sends back four words. You decide not to be the one who edits those.
You soften one clause and sharpen another. The answer comes back warmer than it ought to, and neither of them ever learns why.
You decline. Both of them are slightly relieved to have someone new to be offended by.

events.text: The kitchens of the Observatory Terrace have served cold starfruit broth for four thousand years. A guest from {b3_foe} calls it something a comet left behind. The hall goes entirely quiet, and every eye turns, for no reason you can name, to you.

effects.log: You eat a second bowl with great ceremony. The guest, who did not expect an argument made of soup, stops speaking for a while.
You answer, and it is a good one. It is quoted at the order for a decade, and the guest is not seen at table again.

choices.text: Change the subject to something terrible

effects.log: You ask the guest about their own order's cooking. The ensuing silence is longer, but it is no longer yours.

events.text: An envoy of {b3_foe} comes to the Observatory Terrace and is received with tea and a very long silence. They want a copy of the Pavilion's reading of the next three centuries, and say it as if asking for the salt. The room waits to see whether you, of all people, will be the one who answers.

effects.log: You answer: not yet, and not like this. It is neither yes nor no, and the envoy bows to it as a proper reply.
You step back. {b3_elder} answers instead, and later remarks that you were right to leave it to someone with a longer memory.

choices.text: Ask the envoy what they are really after

effects.log: You ask. The envoy blinks, and then, very quietly, tells you. You are no longer sure you wanted to know.

events.text: The Observatory Terrace keeps the anniversary of the Night the Sea Went Dark. It is the same speech every year, so the whole Pavilion mouths the ending. This year {b3_elder} falls ill, and the room discovers that you are the only one who has been paying attention.

effects.log: You give it, and add one line. It is not forgiven for a week, and then it is added to the speech for good.

choices.text: Give it exactly as it was

effects.log: You give it without a syllable changed. People say afterwards it was the best it ever was, and you cannot tell if that is praise.
You hand it to the youngest present. They are terrified and magnificent, and the order talks of nothing else.

events.text: You have been {b3_rank} of the Star Sea Pavilion long enough that the Observatory Terrace has a word for it: a Slow Star. It is said with affection and a little worry. {b3_peer} suggests, over tea, that the word may not be only a joke.

effects.log: You make your case, and it is heard in full. It is not granted this year, but you are no longer the one waiting quietly.
You take it as one. The tea tastes better, and the worry lives in somebody else for a season.
You pick one of the young and teach them everything. The word falls off you almost at once, and onto them.

events.text: A rumor goes round the Observatory Terrace: the Pavilion has read its own end and is selling the date. {b3_elder} denies it in a perfectly steady voice, which is how everyone knows. By evening the denial itself is the rumor, and someone has started a list of those who looked surprised.

effects.log: You trace it back three mouths and stop at a person you like. You do not tell anyone, and you do not forget.
You add a better rumor and it travels twice as fast. The first is forgotten, along with your fingerprints.
{b3_elder} looks at you a long moment, then says only, “Ask me again in a century.” It is not a denial. You file it.

events.text: An anonymous client leaves a jar of pressed starlight at your door with no note. The Star Sea Pavilion keeps an exact ledger of such things, and by morning three people have asked, in three different tones, whether you intend to keep it.

effects.log: You say so, plainly. The ledger writes it down, and a surprising number of people respect that.
You hand it over. It is placed in the Observatory Terrace where everyone can see, and you are thanked, with some suspicion.
It takes a month. The sender is a person you offended once, and the gift is the most elaborate apology you have ever received.

events.text: The old saying of the Star Sea Pavilion goes: “Everything is written; the rest is invoicing.” A junior asks you whether it is true. You have lived long enough to have seen it be true, and false, and both in the same afternoon.

effects.log: You say yes. They write it down, and for the first time you wonder how many of the sayings you hold were this kind of yes.

choices.text: Tell them it is mostly true

effects.log: You say mostly. They look relieved to have been told there is a rest of it, and you spend the evening telling them what.
You tell them to go and find out. They go, and they come back a year changed in a way you cannot take credit for.

effects.log: You give it without a syllable changed. People say afterwards it was the best it ever was, and you cannot tell if that is praise.
You hand it to the youngest present. They are terrified and magnificent, and the order talks of nothing else.

events.text: You have been {b3_rank} of the Demon Realm long enough that the Hall of Standing Challenges has a word for it: a Long Siege. It is said with affection and a little worry. {b3_peer} suggests, over tea, that the word may not be only a joke.

effects.log: You make your case, and it is heard in full. It is not granted this year, but you are no longer the one waiting quietly.
You take it as one. The tea tastes better, and the worry lives in somebody else for a season.
You pick one of the young and teach them everything. The word falls off you almost at once, and onto them.

events.text: A rumor goes round the Hall of Standing Challenges: the Demon Emperor means to hold an open challenge this century. {b3_elder} denies it in a laugh that goes on slightly too long. By evening the denial itself is the rumor, and someone has started a list of those who looked surprised.

effects.log: You trace it back three mouths and stop at a person you like. You do not tell anyone, and you do not forget.
You add a better rumor and it travels twice as fast. The first is forgotten, along with your fingerprints.
{b3_elder} looks at you a long moment, then says only, “Ask me again in a century.” It is not a denial. You file it.

events.text: An unknown admirer leaves a horn cup of black wine-smoke at your door with no note. The Demon Realm keeps an exact ledger of such things, and by morning three people have asked, in three different tones, whether you intend to keep it.

effects.log: You say so, plainly. The ledger writes it down, and a surprising number of people respect that.
You hand it over. It is placed in the Hall of Standing Challenges where everyone can see, and you are thanked, with some suspicion.
It takes a month. The sender is a person you offended once, and the gift is the most elaborate apology you have ever received.

events.text: The old saying of the Demon Realm goes: “Strength is law; manners are how we survive it.” A junior asks you whether it is true. You have lived long enough to have seen it be true, and false, and both in the same afternoon.

effects.log: You say yes. They write it down, and for the first time you wonder how many of the sayings you hold were this kind of yes.

choices.text: Tell them it is mostly true

effects.log: You say mostly. They look relieved to have been told there is a rest of it, and you spend the evening telling them what.
You tell them to go and find out. They go, and they come back a year changed in a way you cannot take credit for.

events.text: A lord of the Reed Isles wants his stones back. The Pavilion's reading promised a fat harvest and delivered a plague of moths. The Pavilion's rule: readings are never refunded. Reader Maelis Quen signed it. You are asked to look at the chart, and Quen will not meet your eye.

effects.log: You spend a month with the chart and find it: a figure was altered after Quen signed. The ink is newer than the page. You say nothing yet.
You defend the rule with such polish that the lord leaves almost satisfied. Quen thanks you in a flat voice that stays with you.
You find the lord a small rare thing from the Pavilion store, citing a clerical oversight. Quen learns of it and sends a note with one word: thank you.

events.text: Years on, Reader Maelis Quen finds you on the Observatory Terrace at the third bell and sits down without a word. They have worked out whose hand altered the chart. It is someone you eat supper with. Quen only wants to know whether you are going to be the one who says it aloud.

choices.text: Say it aloud, before the Pavilion

effects.log: You name Orsolo Fen before the assembled readers. The room does not breathe. Fen is not surprised, which is the worst part.
You go to Fen's rooms with the chart. Fen listens to the end, nods, and asks for a week. They take two, and use it.

choices.text: Tell Quen to let it lie

effects.log: Quen nods slowly, folds the chart, and puts it in a sleeve. You both know it is still there, and that it will outlast you.

events.text: A century after the moths, {b3_peer} tells you that Orsolo Fen has left the Pavilion, taking no books and leaving one sealed reading on your cushion. It is a reading of you. It is short, and in a hand that cannot be Fen's, because it is signed by Maelis Quen, years dead.

choices.text: Break the seal and read it

effects.log: You read it. It is an apology and a prediction, in that order. The prediction is small and specific, and you are unnerved that you believe it.

choices.text: Put it in the Pavilion archive unread

effects.log: You file it under your own name, sealed. The archivist says that is the only honest thing anyone has done with a reading in a century.
You burn it in the brass bowl. It burns blue for a long time. Afterwards, nobody asks, and everyone checks the ashes.

events.text: A client in a travelling cloak asks the Pavilion for the one reading it never sells: the date of their own death. They offer a library and an isle. You are the only reader free. The rule is old and clear, and the client's hands are shaking.

effects.log: You refuse and give them tea instead. They leave without the reading and without the library, and you are never sure which you took from them.

choices.text: Sell them the year, not the day

effects.log: You tell them the year. It is a partial truth and a breach of a rule, and you carry the breach like a small stone in a shoe.

choices.text: Refer them to the Pavilion Master

effects.log: You pass it up. The Master refuses in four words, and the client is gone before you can follow.

events.text: The traveller comes back sixty years later, very old for an immortal and altogether calm. They have read their own star themselves, at last, from a mountain with no name. They bring you a gift: a star chart of the Pavilion's own founding, which the Pavilion lost.

effects.log: You accept. The chart is correct and is not flattering to the founders. The Pavilion argues about it for ten years and you are blamed for most of it.
They tell you, and it is not a date. It is a sentence of five words. You write it on the inside of your sleeve, where you will see it every day.

choices.text: Decline: it was not honestly come by

effects.log: You decline. They smile, take it back, and leave it, anyway, with the gatekeeper, who does not ask you.

events.text: Word comes down the Terrace that the traveller is gone. The Pavilion wants to know whether the lost founding chart should be read to all, or locked. {b3_elder} says lock it. A reader of the new generation says read it. You are asked, because you were there.

effects.log: You read it in the great hall at the third bell. Half the Pavilion weeps and half writes. The founders' portraits are, after some debate, left up.
You lock it. It sits in the vault for a thousand years more, and every new reader is told there is a secret, and none of them ever finds out how true it is.

choices.text: Read it only to those who ask

effects.log: You post a notice that the chart is available to the curious. Fewer than twenty come, and they are exactly the twenty who should have.

events.text: Keeper Tiv Arasel brings you a new apprentice who cannot read a single chart. The apprentice hears the stars instead, a faint humming, different for each. Tiv wants them kept. The Pavilion's rule: a reader reads. Tiv looks at you as one who might know how to bend a rule without breaking it.

effects.log: You stand surety. For a year the Terrace is full of a boy or girl humming along with the heavens, and the readers learn to ignore it, and then to depend on it.

choices.text: Send them to the observatory kitchens

effects.log: The kitchens take them in kindly. Tiv thanks you stiffly and is not seen on the Terrace for a month.

choices.text: Test them on a hard sky

effects.log: You test them. They hum the right note against three wrong charts, all in one night. The Pavilion is fairly silent for a while after that.

events.text: Twenty years on, the humming apprentice is the best reader the Pavilion has never officially had, and two senior readers have noticed that the apprentice's readings contradict theirs and are right. A petition is brought against the apprentice. Keeper Tiv looks very old.

choices.text: Speak for the apprentice before the assembly

effects.log: You speak for them. Some readers walk out, and the apprentice receives their first formal title that evening in a half-empty hall.
You propose a test, three nights, open sky. The apprentice wins by one star, and the senior readers go quiet and sullen, and then a little curious.
You stay out of it. The petition is withdrawn after the apprentice walks out on their own. You find you minded more than you expected.

events.text: The apprentice, a Reader now, hears something on the Terrace that none of the instruments show: a star humming wrong, low and sour. They ask you to come and listen. You hear nothing. You also know better by now than to say so.

choices.text: Take it seriously and tell the Master

effects.log: You tell the Master. A month of argument, and then every instrument is turned toward the sour star. It is one of the Pavilion's oldest, and it is dying.

choices.text: Sit with the Reader through the night

effects.log: You sit through the night. By morning you do hear something, very faint, and it is worse than hearing nothing.

choices.text: Ask the Reader to write it down first

effects.log: The Reader writes it all down. It is a better record than yours. They hand it to you with a small, unreadable smile.

events.text: The sour star goes out in the autumn of a century nobody can name afterwards. The Pavilion holds a vigil on the Observatory Terrace, and the Reader who heard it first is asked to say the last words. They say them, and then they look at you, and you understand that you are being given the Terrace.

effects.log: You accept. The Reader's hum goes on for ever in the walls of the Pavilion. Visitors ask what the noise is, and are told it is a custom.
You share the honour. It is a very small gesture, and the Pavilion remembers it for a very long time.

choices.text: Decline, and keep your own rooms

effects.log: You decline. The Reader takes the Terrace, and you take your rooms, and somewhere in between you are both exactly where you belong.

events.text: A chart arrives at the Pavilion gate with no client, no seal and no payment: a star at a position where there is no star. The Terrace argues for a week. {b3_elder} says it is a joke. {b3_peer} says it is a threat. The chart is addressed, in very small writing, to you.

effects.log: You look. It is not a joke. The star is exactly where the chart says, if the sea of clouds is where it is in some other age.

choices.text: Return it to the gate unopened

effects.log: You send it back. It returns on the next tide. The gatekeeper, who has to carry it, is not pleased.

choices.text: Put it in the archive and wait

effects.log: You file it, labelled, and wait. For years the archive smells faintly of mint, and nobody can find the source.

events.text: The star on the chart rises. It is small, low and unmistakable, over an isle that is not on any map. The Pavilion goes out onto the Terrace in the middle of the night and stands looking. Nobody says anything clever. At last {b3_elder} says: “Well. Somebody ordered it.”

choices.text: Take a team to the isle

effects.log: You lead a small party. The isle is empty and warm, and on its one hill stands a lectern with a book of your own handwriting that you have no memory of writing.
You record the star for three hundred nights. It does not move, which in itself is the strangest thing anyone has ever recorded.

choices.text: Sell the reading to the highest bidder

effects.log: You sell it. The buyer is a lord of the clouds who never says what he reads. The Pavilion is richer, and uneasy.

events.text: The book on the lectern is a reading of the Pavilion's end, in your own hand, with the date left blank and a margin note: choose. The star over the isle is brighter tonight. Maelis Quen's old cushion has been placed beside the lectern by someone, for no reason anyone will admit.

effects.log: You write a number so large the page will not hold it. The star dims to a steady candle. The Pavilion, which never knew, sleeps well for ages.
You leave it blank, because a blank is the only honest answer. The star holds, and the Pavilion keeps doing what it does, which is exactly what you hoped.

choices.text: Write the true date, if you can read it

effects.log: You write the true date, small and level. It is not as soon as you feared. It is not as late as you hoped. You tell nobody.

events.text: The Pavilion's price list is a state secret and also posted on the gate. The two facts do not trouble anybody. A new client, a very polite young cloud-lord, asks you to explain how this works. You find that you can, in one sentence, and that the sentence is rather damning.

effects.log: You say it plainly. He laughs, then stops laughing, then pays in full. It is, you reflect, a perfect demonstration.

choices.text: Say that readings are priced by their weight

effects.log: Your answer is as satisfying as it is meaningless. He departs thoughtfully and tells his friends the Pavilion is wise.

events.text: A reader who is very sure of themselves announces a reading that the isle of Little Orris will sink by the end of the month. The isle has a fair few permanent residents who know nothing about it. The Pavilion's rule: sell the reading, not the warning. {b3_peer} looks at you.

effects.log: You send a quiet warning. The isle is moved in a week. The reader is cross for a decade and then grateful for a century.
You keep to the rule. The isle is fine, as it turns out. The reader says that was the point. You are not sure they are right.
You check it. The reader was off by a digit. The isle floats on, and the reader cannot meet anyone's eye for a year.

events.text: The Pavilion has a custom of sealed readings: each reader's yearly reading of their own year is locked in a drawer and opened only at the year's end. This year you have read something in yours that you would very much like not to find out is true.

effects.log: You seal it. At the year's end you open it with fingers that are not quite steady, and you find it is only half true, which you take as a mercy.
You rewrite it kinder. The drawer, which has seen this kind of thing before, makes no comment.

choices.text: Act on it before it closes

effects.log: You act on it at once. The year goes differently, and you never learn if the original was right.

events.text: A cloud merchant asks the Pavilion for a reading of whether a ship will arrive. You read it, and the ship will arrive, and so will the thing in its hold that the merchant has not mentioned. The reading is paid for already.

choices.text: Tell them what is in the hold

effects.log: You tell them. The merchant goes pale and then asks, very quietly, whether you also read how to unload it.
You sell the reading as written. The merchant leaves content. It will turn out to be the most expensive satisfaction they ever bought.
You add a small footnote in the margin, no larger than a thumbprint. The merchant reads it, and is the one who decides.

events.text: The sea of stars is generous tonight and the Terrace is full of readers lying on their backs in rows, murmuring numbers. It is not at all a ritual. It is simply the most pleasant working hour the Pavilion has. {b3_peer} makes room for you on a cushion with no comment.

effects.log: You lie down and read. By dawn you have a good reading and a stiff neck, and the best sleep in a decade.

choices.text: Hold the lamp for the others

effects.log: You hold the lamp until the cold seeps in. Nobody thanks you. Two readers remember you next year when it matters.

events.text: Someone has stolen the Pavilion's Second Best Star Chart. It was never meant to be a secret and was never meant to be locked up. The thief has left a better copy in its place, and a note: Yours had errors. The Terrace is divided between fury and professional interest.

effects.log: You compare them for a month. The thief is right about eleven errors and wrong about two. It is the most useful theft in the Pavilion's history.
You find them: a student from a lesser isle with a good eye and no money. You take them on as an assistant, to everyone's alarm.

choices.text: Publish the corrections as the Pavilion's own

effects.log: You publish them without comment. Nobody ever finds out, and you wonder if you did the right thing.

events.text: A client has paid for a reading of her love life. The Pavilion is reading a great many of these this season and the Observatory Terrace is full of embarrassed readers trying to be neutral. The client's star is a bright, difficult one that has been in the sky for ages.

effects.log: You read it honestly. The client takes it in stoically, pays twice, and sends a card the following year saying you were right.
You read it generously, and it comes true because they believe it. The Pavilion calls this good practice and does not look at it too hard.
You pass it on. The colleague, who is fond of love, does it far better, and the two of you split the credit.

events.text: The Pavilion Master calls an assembly and announces a new rule: readings of the Jade Court are to be sold at triple the usual price, because the Court has been paying late. The Terrace is cheered, and slightly afraid. {b3_elder} makes no sound at all.

effects.log: You support it. The Court pays on time, and with an air of weary dignity, for centuries.
You argue for a gentler one: late fees, not triple. It is adopted with minor changes and everybody claims they thought of it.
You watch. The Court, it turns out, was never going to pay anyway, and the whole thing is forgotten by spring.

events.text: A reader from the Pavilion's southern watch returns after eighty years with a theory that the stars are not fixed but are, in fact, slowly moving apart, all of them, always. The Terrace has not had a theory like this in three thousand years and does not know how to behave.

effects.log: You work with them for ten years. The theory is eventually accepted, and the reader is given your cushion, which you did not offer.

choices.text: Test it against the old records

effects.log: The old records agree, a little, in a way that makes your stomach turn. You write a careful paper and hand it to the Master.

choices.text: Remind them of the first rule: sell nothing unproven

effects.log: You remind them. They bow, and go away and prove it. Ten years later, they send you a rude and grateful letter.

events.text: The Pavilion kitchen has run out of starfruit for the first time in four thousand years. The cooks are in tears. The chief reader has fainted. {b3_peer} points out, reasonably, that a Pavilion of seers ought to have foreseen this.

effects.log: You admit no one did. The Terrace has a quiet, somewhat chastened supper, and the readers are noticeably kinder to the cooks for a decade.
You read it that very night. There will be starfruit by spring. The cooks name a dish after you which you never taste.

choices.text: Open a trade route to another isle

effects.log: You open a trade with a neighbour. It is not as good as home and it is not as bad as feared. The soup, surprisingly, improves.

events.text: The Pavilion's oldest Reader, who is said to have read the stars before they were named, asks to see you. They say only: “Do not sell the comet.” Then they close their eyes and are asleep for a decade. You are not aware of any comet.

effects.log: You look. One is on its way, a small bright thing three hundred years off. You record it and say nothing, and it is a rule you are still keeping.
The others laugh, and then stop laughing. Nobody else has been told anything. You are more careful about who you speak to afterwards.

choices.text: Do as asked, and sell nothing

effects.log: You add a line to the price list: no comets. The clerks are baffled, and for ever afterwards there is a small cold spot in the sale ledger.

events.text: The Pavilion holds a Night of Contradictions every century, when all the readers read the same sky and the results are compared. This century, for the first time, every reader agrees. The silence on the Terrace is complete. Nobody wants to be the first to say it is worrying.

effects.log: You say it. The relief is audible. By dawn there are eleven more readings, all disagreeing, and the Pavilion is itself again.
You look. Nobody is. That is the worst answer, and you hold it quietly for a month before you tell the Master.
You propose a toast. Nobody joins. You raise it alone on the Terrace with a view of the very agreeable sky.

events.text: A client has come to the gate with a reading from another order and asks you to say whether it is right. This is, strictly, forbidden: the Pavilion does not review the work of others. You have read it already over their shoulder, and it is wrong.

effects.log: You say nothing. The client leaves content. You wonder, later, if silence counts when it is sold to you by the rules.
You tell them. They are grateful and furious in equal measure, and later you receive a minor, anonymous apology from the other order.

choices.text: Offer them a Pavilion reading instead

effects.log: You offer one at a price that makes them wince. They pay it, and it is, to your own relief, correct.

events.text: The Pavilion's habit of never saying 'I don't know' has finally cost it a client. A cloud-lord asked what the stars say of his mother's illness, and the reader, trained not to hesitate, said something that sounded definite. It was a guess. The lord is on his way to see you.

effects.log: You tell him the reading was a guess, and that the Pavilion is sorry. He sits down heavily and says no one has ever told him that before.
You re-read it and it is hopeful. He leaves with something to hold, and you stay up the rest of the night hoping you were right.
You send word that you are unavailable. It is the rule, but it sits badly, and the lord does not return.

events.text: {b3_peer} has been reading the same sky for forty years and has never once written the result down. When you ask why, they say it is because the stars are not a book. A year later, the stars do something nobody has ever seen, and the only person who is not surprised is {b3_peer}.

effects.log: {b3_peer} says, quite sincerely, that they do not know anything. They simply looked. It is the best explanation you have heard in a century.
You spend a year looking without writing anything down. It is the longest and most difficult year of your life, and it changes how you read.

events.text: A young cloud-lord buys a reading, hears the answer, and demands a different one. The Pavilion has a rule for this: nothing is refunded and nothing is rewritten. He draws his sword in the hall, which is also against several rules. {b3_peer} has already left the room.

effects.log: You stand your ground and say the reading again, word for word. He sheathes the sword, red-faced, and pays the required fee for damage.
You read his sword arm aloud: the stance, the weight, the next move. He stops mid-stroke. It is the kind of trick the Pavilion is good at.

choices.text: Step aside and call the guard

effects.log: You step aside. The guards are sufficiently Pavilion to ask him politely to leave, and he does, mortified.

events.text: The Pavilion's brass armillary has stopped. All eleven rings, for the first time in six thousand years, are still. Readers gather round it in a hush. {b3_elder} says it is the sky that has stopped. A very young reader says it is the armillary. Nobody can prove either.

effects.log: You oil the rings, one by one. They start again with a faint squeal. The Pavilion decides, collectively, never to speak of this.

choices.text: Watch the sky for a night

effects.log: You watch the sky. It moves, and the armillary does not. The very young reader was right, and is given a small ceremonial promotion.
You leave it. The armillary is a monument now, and the Pavilion has a new kind of silence, one that visitors find very reassuring.

events.text: A student asks you the oldest question in the Pavilion: if the stars decide, why read them? You have been asked this a hundred times and have always had the neat answer. Tonight, for the first time, the neat answer sounds like something someone said to you once.

effects.log: You give it. The student is satisfied. You are not, and you think about it for a decade.
You say so. The student looks at you with such relief that you laugh, and then spend the evening trying to find a better answer together.

choices.text: Tell them to ask the stars

effects.log: You send them up to the Terrace. They come back at dawn with a very odd look and no answer, which is exactly right.

events.text: The Pavilion has an annual contest for the most useless accurate reading. This year's winner is a precise account of how many grains of sand are on the beach at the edge of the Isle of Pelm at this moment. The prize is a cushion. The loser is asked to carry the winner round the hall.

effects.log: You enter. Your reading, of the number of dust motes in the archive, comes second, and you are carried round the hall on a stretcher of cushions.
You judge. It is a hard office; everyone is a friend and all the entries are, in their way, beautiful.

choices.text: Complain that it is a waste of the stars

effects.log: You complain. You are made chair of next year's committee, as a punishment, and you are surprisingly good at it.

events.text: A reader of the Pavilion has fallen in love with a client. The rule is clear: never read for those you love. The reader comes to you quite white in the face and asks you to read the client's future, for them. They want to know whether it is wise.

effects.log: You read it. It is happy, and uncertain, and ordinary. You tell them to go, and they go, and the Pavilion is short a reader and glad of it.
You refuse, on the grounds of the rule. The reader nods and goes, and finds out for themselves, which is, as it turns out, how it is done.
You read it, and it is not happy, and you say it is. The reader goes, and for years afterwards you check the sky for news.

events.text: A star the Pavilion has watched for four thousand years goes out in the middle of your shift. You are the one who has to write it up. The entry is a single line in the oldest ledger, between a minor comet and a lost key. You hold the pen over it for a long time.

effects.log: You write: Star of the Eastern Watch, out. The ink dries. It is oddly dignified. Others add notes in the margin over the years.
You ring the old bell, which has not been rung since the Dark Sea. The whole Pavilion comes out onto the Terrace to stand in silence.
You leave the line blank for a year. When you finally write it, the star has become the thing the Pavilion does not mention, and that is its own kind of record.

events.text: The Star Sea Pavilion's dinner is a long table where everyone must sit in the order of their readings from the previous year, best to worst. You are, by an unlucky margin, in the middle. The one beside you, a new Star Keeper, whispers that they have never enjoyed anything so much.

effects.log: You do. It turns into the most pleasant dinner in years, and your next reading is, to everyone's surprise, a good one.

choices.text: Explain the politics of the seating

effects.log: You explain. They become, within the hour, the most nervous Star Keeper in the isles, and it is entirely your fault.
You swap, quietly. It is a minor kindness to the one who ends up beside you, who says nothing and looks very happy.

events.text: {b3_elder} asks you to read a sky for them privately. It is their own, and they are older than the Pavilion's oldest record. They do not want a date. They want to know whether it was worth it. You have nothing in the books for that.

choices.text: Read honestly, and say it was

effects.log: You say it was. It is not a reading. It is only that you have watched them for years and can see it. They nod, and ask for tea.

choices.text: Say there is no such reading

effects.log: You say there is not. They smile, because that is exactly the answer they were hoping you would not give.

choices.text: Ask them to tell you instead

effects.log: They tell you. It takes all night. You are changed, and you do not tell anyone how.

events.text: The Pavilion is hosting a visit from the Jade Court's own astronomers, who have come to see how readings are made. They are shocked by the sealed drawers, the cushions and the unfinished tea. You are asked to show them the real work, which is mostly waiting.

effects.log: You show them a night of waiting. They are bored and then, by morning, quietly moved. They send their thanks in the form of a better telescope.
You put on a good show, and it is entirely false. They leave impressed. You feel a bit unclean and a bit proud.

choices.text: Let a young reader show them

effects.log: The youngest reader shows them, with total sincerity and slightly wrong facts. They are charmed. The Court sends flowers.

events.text: A seer from the Pavilion has gone mad, in the quiet way: reading the same sky aloud for nine days and nights without stopping. {b3_peer} asks you to sit with them, because you are the only one the seer does not frighten. The sky they read is, for the most part, a good one.

effects.log: You sit. On the ninth night they reach the end of the reading, and stop, and look at you, and say: thank you. You never learn what they saw.
You turn their chair away from the sky. They fall silent, then cry, then sleep. It is the first healing you have done in a long time.
You write it all. It is, for the most part, correct. The Pavilion adds it to its archive with a note: the author was unwell.

events.text: The Pavilion is to be audited by the Celestial Ministries, who suspect it of reading their private ledgers. It does. Everyone at the Pavilion knows it does. The Pavilion Master asks each reader, in turn, whether they have ever read a Ministry ledger. You are third.

effects.log: You admit it, and note that the Ministry ledgers are the most beautifully accurate documents in the isles. The auditor, to your surprise, agrees.
You deny it. The auditor writes it down. There is a long pause in which both of you appreciate the craft.
You cite the old privilege of silence. The auditor does not know it exists, and neither, strictly, do you.

events.text: An invitation arrives, written in what is very probably ash: the Iron Duchess invites you to supper. Nobody refuses. Nobody has been seen eating much there either. Captain Brakka tells you the only rule of the table: whatever you do, do not be the strongest person present, or the funniest.

effects.log: You go and are comprehensively dull. The Duchess gives you a long, level look and seats you at the quiet end. It is the safest seat in the hall.
You go and watch. Four people try to impress the Duchess, and three of them are gone by morning, in the sense of being given postings abroad.
You go and are yourself. The Duchess laughs at one thing you say and says nothing else all evening. By dawn the whole realm knows.
You decline. The silence in the gallery the following day is the loudest thing you have ever heard, and you are not invited again for a century.

events.text: The Iron Duchess sends for you in the dark hours. The supper, she says, was a trial and you have passed it, in some way, and she wants a favour that is not an order. A rare thing. A Duke of the court has been carrying a stolen name for a thousand years, and she wants to know whose.

effects.log: You take it. For a year you read the old court rolls and ask very careful questions. At the end you find the name, and it is nobody anyone would have guessed.
You ask. The Duchess laughs, deep and brief, and says a favour from her is a very specific thing. You take it, and it is enough.

choices.text: Decline, and keep out of the Court

effects.log: You decline. She is not offended, which is more worrying than if she were. The realm rearranges itself around your refusal.

events.text: The stolen name belongs to a Duke who is, in point of fact, rather good at the job. The Duchess waits for your report in the dark, and the Duke waits in the hall outside, drumming one clawed hand on his thigh. You are the only one in the realm who knows both halves of the story.

effects.log: You tell her everything. She is quiet for a long time, then summons the Duke, and the two of them talk with the door shut until morning. Nobody dies.
You warn the Duke. He takes the news like a man hearing the weather, thanks you with two small bows, and by morning he has a plan.
You burn your notes. It is the only sensible thing in the realm to do, and for a century you are known as the one who knows nothing, which is a great compliment.

events.text: A very young demon with enormous horns and a very small sword stands at the gate of the Realm and challenges you by name. They have walked eleven years to do it. The guards, who are fond of this sort of thing, have pulled up stools. Strength is law, and the law is, tonight, standing in the rain.

effects.log: You accept, and win in three moves, and then spend an hour teaching the young one the fourth. The guards applaud, and it is remembered.
You lose, carefully and with some drama. The young one is stunned. You are a hero of a very particular kind, and nobody ever tells them.
You send them home with a list. They glare, then bow, then are gone into the rain, and you hear nothing for a long time.

events.text: A century on, the young demon is back at the gate, a good deal broader and entirely unrecognisable but for the horns and a certain quality of hope. They challenge you again. The guards have brought the same stools, and some of them are their own children.

effects.log: You fight in earnest, because the first time was a lesson, and this is the exam. It is a close, lovely thing. You win, narrowly, and the challenger weeps and laughs.
You yield. It is the right thing, and there are tears in the guards' eyes. The challenger, stunned by their own victory, asks you what to do next.
You propose to each cook a meal for the other. It is the closest thing the Realm has had to a peace treaty in years.

events.text: A third century. The challenger, now a Captain of the Realm, comes not to the gate but to your door. They do not draw a sword. They bring a small, scarred wooden one, the size of a child's. It is the one from the first night. They want you to have it back.

effects.log: You take it. It goes on a shelf in your rooms, and for ever afterwards, in the evenings, you find yourself looking at the notches.
You tell them to keep it, and to give it to the next. They nod gravely. A Realm needs a gate that someone will walk eleven years to knock at.

choices.text: Challenge them to a last friendly bout

effects.log: You fight one last bout, in the yard, for nothing but pleasure. It lasts the whole afternoon. At the end, nobody counts who won.

events.text: The best tavern in the Realm is called the Broken Teeth, and it is run by Madame Orruk, a retired General with a ladle. Rule one: nobody fights inside. Rule two: the ladle is not for stirring. You are taken there by Captain Brakka and told to be on your best behaviour. You are, for once, very good.

effects.log: You buy a round of the fire-tea. The tavern goes quiet, and then roars, and by evening you are a regular, with a stool and a name.

choices.text: Sit in a corner and listen

effects.log: You listen to a night of the Realm talking to itself. It is the most useful education you have had, and the tea is excellent.
You challenge Madame Orruk. The ladle is used once, with great precision. You are tipped gently into the street and the tavern applauds.

events.text: Madame Orruk is dying, or says she is, which in the Realm is an excellent way to find out who your friends are. She has called the whole tavern together and is being unusually kind to people, which frightens them. She asks you to take the Broken Teeth when she goes.

effects.log: You accept. The ladle is ceremonially handed over, and so is the cat, which is in charge of everything but admits it to no one.

choices.text: Say you cannot, and offer to help find someone

effects.log: You say no, with real regret. You spend a year finding the right person, and the tavern is the better for it.

choices.text: Challenge her to a duel for it

effects.log: You challenge. She laughs till she coughs, which is a good sign, and agrees, and wins, and is entirely well again by the new moon.

events.text: A very senior general comes into the Broken Teeth in plain armour, orders one cup of fire-tea and sits in the corner. The whole tavern realises, in the way a crowd does, that they are being watched. The general is gathering names for a purge. Madame Orruk looks at you.

choices.text: Stand between the general and the room

effects.log: You stand. The general lifts one eyebrow, finishes the tea, and says: “I have enjoyed this tavern.” Then leaves. Nobody breathes for ten minutes.
You buy it. The general, a little thrown, drinks it, and the conversation, which lasts three hours, becomes the quietest peace of the century.

choices.text: Slip out the back and warn the regulars

effects.log: You warn them. By the time the general stands, there is nobody left worth the name, and the tavern is, for once, very quiet and very tidy.

events.text: Ten thousand years after your first visit, the Broken Teeth has a plaque by the door. It says only: Nobody fights inside. Under it, someone has scratched in smaller letters: except once. The tavern is full, loud and exactly the same, and the cat's descendant glares at you from your stool.

effects.log: You sit. The cat's descendant, outraged, climbs onto your shoulder and stays. It is the most honoured seat in the Realm.

choices.text: Add a line under the plaque

effects.log: You scratch a line of your own. In a thousand years it will be the plaque's official third line, and nobody will remember who wrote it.

choices.text: Buy the whole tavern one last round

effects.log: You buy the whole tavern a round and a song. It is the best one the Realm has ever heard, and it is entirely about a ladle.

events.text: General Ushar Tol, who has held the northern marches for four thousand years, asks to see you. They are tired, and they say so, which in the Realm is a confession. They want to retire. By the law of the Realm that means one last duel, with someone who might actually win.

effects.log: You accept. Ushar Tol bows, the first bow in a thousand years, and names a date. The Realm starts laying odds, loudly, and is told to stop.
You name a Duke who owes you a favour. Ushar Tol nods slowly. It is a small, correct, painful kindness.

choices.text: Tell them the law is stupid

effects.log: You say it, plainly. Ushar Tol roars with laughter, which is a good sound and nobody has heard in years, and says: yes, but it is ours.

events.text: The last duel of General Ushar Tol is held at dawn on the northern wall, before a crowd of thousands who all pretend not to have come. Ushar Tol fights as they have always fought: simply, without a wasted motion. You find, with some alarm, that you are enjoying it enormously.

effects.log: You fight to win, and you do, by a hair, on the last stroke. The wall is silent, and then the general's own soldiers lift both of you onto their shoulders.
You fight to give the crowd a duel to remember. It is a draw, a long one, and a ruling is made that the law is satisfied.

choices.text: Yield at the last, and say why

effects.log: You yield, with one clear sentence of respect. The law has no provision for this, and for once the Realm is delighted.

events.text: A century later, General Ushar Tol is a retired old demon in a small house by the north wall, growing something unspeakable in a pot. You visit. They are happy, and they are bored, and they ask whether you would like to hear the real story of the duel. They have been dying to tell someone.

effects.log: It takes an afternoon. The real story is shorter, sadder and funnier than the legend, and you are one of three living people who will ever know it.

choices.text: Bring them back to the wall as an adviser

effects.log: You bring them back as an honorary adviser. They are impossible, correct, and happier than they have been in a thousand years.

choices.text: Just sit with them and look at the pot

effects.log: You sit and look at the pot. It is an ugly and astonishing plant. You both say nothing, and it is the best part of the year.

events.text: The Demon Realm has one law: the strong rule. It has also, over time, developed seventeen customs about how they may do it, each older and stricter than the last. A new captain asks which to follow. You realise you have been following all of them without knowing.

effects.log: You teach them, one by one, with examples. By the end they know the Realm better than most of its nobility, and are quite nervous about it.

choices.text: Tell them to follow the strongest

effects.log: You tell them to follow the strongest, as the law says. They nod, and then look slightly puzzled about who that might be.

choices.text: Tell them the customs are mostly manners

effects.log: You tell them the customs are mostly manners, which a strong person can afford. They laugh, and spend the next year being unusually polite.

events.text: A demon of the Realm called Grubba the Quiet has beaten nine champions in a row without saying a word, and the Hall of Challenges has taken to laying odds on how long they will keep it up. {b3_peer} has staked their name on the silence. You are asked to guess.

effects.log: You guess it will break. It breaks that week, and the first thing Grubba says is: “I was only thinking.” Everyone is faintly disappointed.
You refuse. {b3_peer} calls you a coward and then, a week later, a sage, when Grubba turns out to be mute.
You challenge. Grubba bows, and fights, and loses, and says: “Good.” It is the only word you ever hear them say.

events.text: The Realm keeps a Gallery of Dents, where the marks of famous duels are preserved in the stone floor. Today the Gallery is closed for repairs, because someone has been fighting in it. The fight was the most enjoyable of the century. Everyone knows who, and nobody will say.

effects.log: You admit it, and pay for the repairs with an apology. The Gallery reopens, and your dent is added to the collection, in the corner, labelled.
You say nothing. The mystery stays unsolved, and for centuries, in odd moods, you will walk the Gallery and look at your own dent.

choices.text: Blame a friend who will not mind

effects.log: You blame an old rogue who is delighted to be credited. It is not quite honest, and not quite a crime.

events.text: The Realm's cooks, the most feared cadre in the demon armies, have gone on strike. A fortnight without ember ribs and every captain in the Realm is short-tempered and slightly faint. {b3_elder} asks you to speak with them, since you are, for some reason, trusted by the kitchens.

effects.log: You hear them out. They want a day of rest, a thicker apron and for nobody to say the word medium. You win all three.
You order them back. They go, one by one, in a terrible silence, and the ribs that evening taste of nothing but contempt.
You cook for a night. It is a legend of its own, in a distinctly negative sense, but it ends the strike in an hour, out of pure professional pride.

events.text: A demon prince has arrived to petition the Realm for a place in its ranks. They have the strength, the lineage and a certain sneer. {b3_elder} would like you to run the entrance trial, and to lose, if you can manage it. It would be better for the Realm's sense of fair play.

effects.log: You lose, with panache. The prince is admitted, and is quite insufferable for a century, and then mellows into a good captain.
You win and say so. The prince, humbled, takes a lowly post and works up honestly. It is the better outcome, and {b3_elder} is not speaking to you.

choices.text: Make the trial a team event

effects.log: You make it a team trial. The prince finds, to their horror, that they cannot win alone. It is the best lesson of their life.

events.text: A small demon with a ledger arrives to audit the Realm's duel records. Every duel ever fought must be recorded, with its winner, its cause and its dent. The auditor has been working from the first page for six hundred years and has reached last Tuesday. You are in last Tuesday.

effects.log: You help them. The auditor is moved to tears, and your entry is the most accurate in the book.

choices.text: Correct the record, in your favour

effects.log: You correct the record, in your favour, by a small amount. The auditor writes it down, gravely, and puts a faint mark beside it.

choices.text: Ask to see your first duel

effects.log: The auditor finds it, after an hour. It is a draw, with a beggar. You read it with a very strange expression.

events.text: The Realm holds a festival of the Breaking of Bad Habits, in which each demon publicly names one and then breaks a plank to mark giving it up. The planks are heavy; the habits more so. You have your plank. {b3_peer} has already broken two, and is on a third.

choices.text: Name an honest habit and break it

effects.log: You name one, and break the plank in a single stroke. The crowd cheers, and you, privately, do not get rid of the habit, but try.
You name a joke habit, a fondness for slippers, and are cheered even more. Over the century the habit, unaccountably, vanishes.
You refuse. The Realm admires it, in an unspoken, slightly nervous way. A demon with no named habit is a demon one must watch.

events.text: A scholar from the Nine Clouds Palace has come to study the Demon Realm, and has been asked to leave three times, and is still here, sitting calmly in the Hall of Challenges with a notebook. The guards are baffled. {b3_elder} says: you deal with this, you are the diplomatic one.

effects.log: You show them the Realm, its kitchens, its stairs, its silences. At the end, the scholar is in tears of admiration, and sends a paper that mocks you gently and honestly.

choices.text: Challenge them to a duel of ideas

effects.log: You hold a debate, with rules of your own. The scholar wins on points, and loses on style, and both are pleased.

choices.text: Let the guards deal with it

effects.log: The guards, who are nicer than their reputation, carry the scholar out on a chair. The scholar waves, gratefully, all the way to the gate.

events.text: The Demon Realm's rule of precedence says that the one who strikes first is the stronger. It has caused a hundred thousand duels, and one very long argument about whether a bow counts as a strike. The matter has come to you, as a tiebreaker, since you have no friends who will be offended.

choices.text: Rule that a bow is a strike

effects.log: You rule that a bow is a strike. For a century everyone bows with great force and alarming speed, and the Realm has never been so polite.
You rule that it is not. The Realm shrugs, and goes on, and only the two most formal Dukes are secretly disappointed.

choices.text: Rule that the law needs rewriting

effects.log: You say so. A committee is formed and takes eleven hundred years, and eventually proposes a ruling that a bow is a bow.

events.text: A very old demon, a Duke, dozes in the Hall of Standing Challenges for forty years and then wakes up and challenges the first person he sees. It is you. He has forgotten, entirely, what the quarrel was about. He is perfectly cheerful, and wants to fight anyway.

effects.log: You fight, and let him win. He is overjoyed, and goes back to sleep at once, and a blessed quiet falls on the Hall.
You fight, and win, and he congratulates you warmly, and challenges you again the moment he wakes up.

choices.text: Remind him what it was about

effects.log: You make up a quarrel. He is deeply moved, and apologises, and you both feel much better, which is not how a duel is meant to go.

events.text: A debt of eleven jars of black wine-smoke is owed to you by a Captain, and everyone in the Hall knows it. The Captain has been avoiding you for three weeks, and is now hiding behind a pillar in an unconvincing way. The pillar is not nearly broad enough.

choices.text: Call in the debt in public

effects.log: You call it in, loudly. The Captain pays with a bow and all eleven jars, and your reputation for fairness rises, at the cost of a friend.
You walk up to the pillar and say it is forgiven. The Captain weeps with shame and relief, and is yours for ever.

choices.text: Make the Captain work it off

effects.log: You set the Captain a task in the kitchens. They cook for a month, and turn out, to everyone's astonishment, to be very good.

events.text: The Demon Emperor is said to be out of the Realm for a century, and to have taken their throne chair with them. The Dukes are discreetly, loudly, not admitting it. A guest from outside asks, innocently, where the Emperor is. The Hall goes quiet, and every head turns toward you.

choices.text: Say the Emperor is on a long progress

effects.log: You say so, with perfect gravity. The Hall relaxes, and the guest is shown to the finest room, and nobody ever speaks of it.
You say you do not know, which is true. The Hall is scandalised, and also faintly relieved that someone has said it.

choices.text: Change the subject to the weather

effects.log: You say the weather is fine for demons. The guest accepts it, in the way of people who know exactly what they have been told.

events.text: The Realm's duels have a rule: no killing in the daytime. It dates from a very dull war. A bored young demon asks you why, and you realise, reluctantly, that you do not know, and that no one in the Realm does either. The rule has simply held, which is the hardest kind to break.

choices.text: Find out where it came from

effects.log: You search the old records and find a very short entry: someone asked. You are a little moved, and a little amused.
You tell a good story about it. It becomes the official origin by lunch, and by supper there is a ballad.

choices.text: Say rules are for the weak

effects.log: You say it. A hush falls, and then three captains start laughing, because it is the sort of thing that is only said by the most careful.

events.text: Someone has stolen the Iron Chair. It is eleven tons of iron, and is in the Hall of Challenges, and nobody saw anything. The Dukes accuse each other, politely. {b3_peer} accuses you, less politely. In the morning, the chair is found in the kitchens, covered in flour.

effects.log: The cooks say they are making the Realm a very large pie. It is, in fact, a pie, and the chair is the lid. You eat a slice.

choices.text: Put the chair back with ceremony

effects.log: You return the chair with full ceremony, flour and all. The Realm decides it is more dignified than it was, and nobody washes it.
You say the Realm has done without a chair for a day and thrived. The Dukes object. The cooks cheer. It is moved back at midnight, secretly.

events.text: A very young demon, newly arrived, asks to be taught the secret to being feared. You have been feared, and respected, and now are mostly both. The truth is dull: you keep your word, small and large, and let the rest fall away. It sounds, said aloud, too simple to be true.

effects.log: You tell them. They write it down, and look at you with great suspicion, and in forty years they are the most feared demon in the Realm, with a ledger of kept promises.
You give them a long, dramatic answer. They are satisfied. The simple one would have worked better, and you know it.
You take them through a day of your own, unedited. By the end they are tired, a little shocked, and a good deal wiser.

events.text: A bridge-troll of the Realm tolls you for crossing, though you are of the Realm, and the bridge is of the Realm, and so is the troll. The toll is small, and the principle large. The queue behind you is getting longer and is mostly quiet in a very expectant way.

effects.log: You pay. The queue relaxes. The troll, grudgingly, hands back a copper, and says you looked like you needed it.

choices.text: Argue the law of the Realm

effects.log: You argue it, with citations. The troll agrees with every point and still takes the toll. It is, on reflection, a perfect piece of Realm logic.
You challenge. The troll, who is eight feet of old stone, steps aside, with a bow, and says: no toll for the brave. Everybody behind you cheers.

events.text: The Realm's winter is a long, grey, sulking affair. The demons are bad-tempered with it, and fights multiply. {b3_elder} proposes a Warm Week, in which duels are replaced with a competition for the best soup. It is a very odd idea. It might, you think, just work.

effects.log: You back it, and cook a soup that makes a captain cry. The Realm has never been so mild, and the idea is made permanent after three weeks of grumbling.

choices.text: Say it will ruin the Realm's edge

effects.log: You say so. {b3_elder} nods, thoughtful, and the idea is quietly shelved, and the Realm goes on being beastly all winter.
You enter a soup under a false name. It comes second, and you spend the rest of the winter outraged at the winner.

events.text: A young demon arrives at the Hall with a grievance against a Duke and the courage of someone who has not been told what happens to those who bring such things. The Hall is not unkind: it merely waits, with interest, for the Duke's response. {b3_peer} asks if you will stand beside the young one.

effects.log: You stand. The Duke arrives, sees the two of you, and decides on the spot to be reasonable. The grievance is settled in an afternoon.
You advise caution and a better lawyer. The young one takes both, and eventually wins, quietly, years later.
You stay out of it. The young one is not seen again, which you try not to think about, and fail.

events.text: A parade is held to mark the Realm's three-thousandth year of not losing a single war. The Captain of the Parade has made it very loud and has hired four brass bands, none of which are playing the same piece. {b3_peer} leans over and asks, with great sincerity, whether the Realm has ever won one either.

choices.text: Say it has never needed to

effects.log: You say it, with a straight face. {b3_peer} chokes on a pastry and the parade proceeds, magnificently out of tune.

choices.text: Say it has won many, quietly

effects.log: You say so. It is true. {b3_peer} looks at you, half in alarm, half in respect, and offers you the pastry.
You join the loudest band and play an enormous drum badly. It is, by popular acclaim, the highlight of the parade.

events.text: A scribe of the Realm is writing the history of its great duels and has asked you to check the account of yours. It is accurate in every detail except that you are, on the page, very slightly taller, and the duel is a good deal more graceful than it was. The scribe is quite proud.

effects.log: You let it stand. Over the centuries your legend has grown, and for a time you try to live up to it, which is exhausting.
You correct the height and leave the grace. The scribe nods, makes a very serious note, and the history is the better for your vanity.

choices.text: Ask for the truth to be written, warts and all

effects.log: You ask for the truth. The scribe is stunned, and then thrilled, and writes a far better chapter than the first.

events.text: A great demon lord, a Duke, wants an heir, and the Realm has no marriage customs, only challenges, and the Duke has put out the call for a challenger worthy to father their children. The Hall is in a peculiar mood. {b3_elder} asks you, with great delicacy, to supervise the ceremony.

effects.log: You supervise. The ceremony turns out to be mostly an elaborate dinner with a great deal of staring, and ends in an engagement and a good deal of applause.
You suggest it. The Duke is horrified, and then, tentatively, relieved, and the first conversation in four hundred years is held over a very long soup.
You decline. {b3_elder} nods, quite understanding, and finds someone else with less to lose, and a much louder laugh.

events.text: You are halfway across the Hall of Standing Challenges when you realise that the entire room has stopped fighting at once and is looking at the floor. A small, plain demon child has wandered in from nowhere and is drawing on the flagstones with a stick. Nobody knows whose they are.

choices.text: Kneel down and ask what they are drawing

effects.log: You kneel. It is a duel, a very exciting one, with the child as the winner. You admire it at length, and the Hall, by degrees, forgets itself and starts fighting again, more gently.

choices.text: Pick them up and carry them out

effects.log: You pick them up and carry them to the kitchens. They are given a pie. Somebody, eventually, turns up and claims them with an air of mild guilt.
You leave them to it. The Hall, in its own time, sorts itself out, and the drawing is preserved, years later, in the Gallery of Dents.

events.text: A great and terrible demon general asks for your advice, privately, on how to be less terrible. They are exhausted by it. People flinch when they sit down, and they have not been touched, kindly, in two thousand years. You, of all people, have been chosen as the confidant. It is a hard post.

effects.log: You give them a list: say good morning, ask a name, return a thing borrowed. It takes a century. By the end, the general is quite popular, and slightly bewildered.

choices.text: Tell them terror is a gift

effects.log: You tell them that being terrible is a service. They are comforted, in a strange way, and the Realm stays as it was.

choices.text: Take them to the Broken Teeth

effects.log: You take them to the tavern. Madame Orruk, who is not afraid of anyone, treats them like a nuisance. It is the best thing anyone has done for them.

events.text: The Realm has a day each century when everyone must swap rank for a day, so the lowest captain commands the highest general. It is a rule of the old Emperor, who is thought to have found it funny. This year the lowest captain is a very small, dutiful demon, and the highest general is you.

choices.text: Obey the captain with good grace

effects.log: You obey, for the entire day, with a straight face. The small captain issues the most sensible orders the Realm has ever received, and you are quietly impressed.

choices.text: Obey, and sulk with great style

effects.log: You obey, and sulk with panache. It is the entertainment of the day. The captain, who is nobody's fool, plays along beautifully.

choices.text: Suggest that the captain keep the post

effects.log: You suggest it. The captain faints. In the end it is a three-week arrangement, and the captain is made a general, to nobody's regret.

events.text: The Realm's strongest demon of the age announces that they intend to retire to a small farm and grow turnips. The Hall is aghast. The strongest has been undefeated for nine hundred years and is, by law, the most important thing in the Realm. They look at you, shyly, and ask for some advice on soil.

effects.log: You advise them. For ages the Realm's greatest warrior grows turnips with a tenderness that causes questions to be asked in the Hall, which are not answered.

choices.text: Tell them the Realm needs them

effects.log: You tell them so. They are sad, and stay, and are slightly less good at fighting from then on, and slightly more good at everything else.

choices.text: Offer to take over the turnip farm

effects.log: You offer. They are touched and appalled. You compromise on a joint farm, and the Realm has a new, secret hobby.

events.text: The Hall is quiet this morning. It is the sort of quiet that comes from an old and terrible demon having just been publicly beaten in a duel by an unknown. You were there. The unknown looks no older than a hundred, and is shaking, and is holding the winner's pennant like a bird.

effects.log: You congratulate them, loudly, before anyone else. It shifts the whole mood of the Hall, and they are, at once, a person and not a rumour.

choices.text: Ask the loser how they are

effects.log: You ask the old demon how they are. They look up, surprised, and say, honestly: relieved. It is a very good answer.

choices.text: Offer the winner your own challenge

effects.log: You offer a challenge. The winner, terrified, declines, which is a wise answer, and a few weeks later asks you for lessons.

events.text: A merchant from the clouds has brought a very rare thing to the Demon Realm: an apology. It is addressed to an old general for an ancient slight, and has been written, rewritten and burnished by a great many hands over a thousand years. The merchant would like to deliver it to you, since you are the general's neighbour.

effects.log: You deliver it. The general reads it, long and slow, and says nothing, and then asks if the merchant would care for tea.
You read it. It is moving, and a little dishonest, in the way a thousand years of drafts can be. You deliver it anyway.
You refuse. The merchant sighs, and leaves, and the apology waits another thousand years, in a drawer, getting better.

events.text: Someone has been sitting outside your door in the morning for a week, with a scroll and a flask of tea and no appointment. The gatekeepers of {b3_order} will not move them: it is the oldest right of the order, to petition the seat. They are very polite and very persistent, and very, very old.

effects.log: You receive them. The scroll is a grievance against a decision of your predecessor, {b3_oldhead}, four thousand years old and exactly as fresh as the day it was made.
You make them wait. They are there every morning, with the tea. By the end of the month you have started to feel guilty, which is probably the point.

choices.text: Send an elder in your place

effects.log: You send {b3_elder}. The petitioner is courteous and unmoved and asks, again, for you.

events.text: The old grievance is real. {b3_oldhead} made a ruling that destroyed a small family of {b3_order}, in the name of peace, and never took it back. The petitioner is the last of that family. They do not want money or restoration. They want the ruling read aloud, once, in the great hall, and a line added.

choices.text: Read it aloud, and add the line

effects.log: You read it before the whole of {b3_order}, and add: this was wrong. The hall is entirely silent. The petitioner bows, and weeps without any sound.

choices.text: Read it, but do not add a line

effects.log: You read it in the hall, flat. It is half of what was asked, and the petitioner accepts it as a thing begun.

choices.text: Refuse: the seat does not apologise for the seat

effects.log: You refuse, with reasons. The petitioner takes it without anger, and departs, and the order is divided for a generation on whether you were right.

events.text: A century on, a stranger lays a single scroll on your desk and goes away before you can speak to them. It is the line you added: this was wrong, copied out in a beautiful hand, and below it a reply from the family, in nine words, that you will not forget. It is on your wall now.

effects.log: You hang it where you work. Visitors read it, and say nothing, and it does more for the order than any of your decrees.

choices.text: Have it carved over the great hall door

effects.log: You have it carved. It is the first thing every disciple of {b3_order} reads, and it changes the order for the better, slowly.
You keep it in a drawer, and take it out on the worst days. It helps more than it should, and you tell no one.

events.text: The order of {b3_order} has a custom you have never liked: the seat must name an heir within a thousand years. You are nine hundred and ninety and counting. The candidates are one brilliant and unbearable, one dull and good, and one nobody mentions. {b3_elder} wants it done; so, plainly, does everyone else.

effects.log: You name them. The order cheers, a little too loudly. The brilliant heir is exactly as unbearable as feared, and exactly as good.

choices.text: Name the dull and good one

effects.log: You name them. The order is stunned, and then, over a decade, rather pleased. The dull heir is the best listener you have ever met.
You name them. The order's gasp is audible. The third candidate stares at you in horror, which is, you think, a good sign.

events.text: Ten years on, the heir comes to you in the night, and says it plainly: I do not want it. They have seen the seat, and your face, and everything the seat has cost, and they would like to be released. It is a rare honesty, and very disrespectful of the order's customs.

effects.log: You release them, and name another. The old heir goes off, grateful, to become the finest teacher of {b3_order}, and the order calls it a scandal for decades.
You insist. They look at you, understanding it all, and say: very well. You are not sure which of you has lost.

choices.text: Give them a year to decide again

effects.log: You give them a year to travel. They come back changed, and still unwilling, and the order, watching, begins to learn something about the weight of seats.

events.text: The seat of {b3_order} has been handed on. You stand at the edge of the great hall on the day of the ceremony, an elder among elders. Someone puts a cup in your hand. It is the old cup of the seat, and you are, rather suddenly, no longer the one it belongs to. It is the lightest thing you have held in ages.

choices.text: Drink, and bow to the new seat

effects.log: You drink, and bow. The new seat bows back, a good deal lower. It is a small, true moment, and the hall remembers it.
You make a short, bad speech. It is warmly applauded for being short. You sit down feeling, for the first time in centuries, entirely like yourself.
You leave before the feast, and take the long way home. It is a beautiful, ordinary evening, and nobody calls on you for a century.

events.text: The first sound in your rooms every morning is the sound of petitions. Not the people, the paper: it is stacked outside the door on a trolley and creaks. Today the trolley has two new things on it: a jar of pickled plums, and a note that says: from someone who loves you, and has a request.

effects.log: You read it. It is the smallest petition of the year, and you grant it at once. The plums are excellent.

choices.text: Eat the plums, then read it

effects.log: You eat the plums. The request, when you reach it, is a good deal bigger than the jar, and is also not quite refusable.
You send them back. You are immediately lonely, for no good reason, and you have your own cook make plums by evening.
