events.text: {b3_elder} has had one piece of advice for you since the day you took the seat, repeated every season with unfailing grace: be more like {b3_oldhead}. This season you have decided to tell them, finally, what it was like to be that kind of seat, and why you are not.

effects.log: You tell them kindly. They go quiet, and later say they had never thought of it. The advice, for a century, is replaced by tea.
You tell them sharply. They bow, and withdraw, and the advice comes back changed, and much worse, in the form of silence.

choices.text: Ask what they are really asking

effects.log: You ask. It turns out they are afraid. It is a long, difficult conversation, and the best you have had in years.

events.text: Every day, someone from {b3_order} comes to ask whether the seat will do something. Today there are fourteen. Most of them are inaudible beyond the door. You can tell by the shuffling which are the real ones: the shuffle of those who have prepared a speech and forgotten it.

effects.log: You receive the shufflers first. Each says one honest sentence, and you decide four things before noon. It is a very efficient day.

choices.text: Receive them in order of arrival

effects.log: You receive them in order. It is fair and dull, and takes until dark. At the end, you are exhausted and entirely correct.

choices.text: Hold open court in the garden

effects.log: You hold court under the old tree. The shufflers relax, and the order has a better afternoon than it has had in a long time.

events.text: You ask a very young disciple of {b3_order} what the order is like from the bottom. They are terrified, and say, very fast: it is like a tree where the leaves are not allowed to know about the roots. Then they apologise, with feeling. You find you cannot stop thinking about it.

effects.log: You change a small rule, the right one. The disciple is told only that the seat listened. It is, in the long view, the best thing you do that year.

choices.text: Ask them to speak to the elders

effects.log: You ask. They do. The elders are, to their credit, more shaken than angry, and a reform follows, slowly.
You tell them to hush, gently. The look they give you, then, is the only criticism you are never able to answer.

events.text: A letter arrives from {b3_oldhead}, who has been silent since the seat changed hands. It is a single sheet, and says only: you have probably already noticed the roof leaks in the east hall; do not fix it; it is the only thing in the order that is honest. You go and look at the roof.

effects.log: You leave it. The east hall becomes a place where disciples sit and think, listening to the drip, and it is the quietest hall in {b3_order}.
You fix it. The east hall is dry and unremarkable, and {b3_oldhead} sends a one-word note: well.
You write back, and a correspondence begins that lasts a very long time. It is, in its way, the finest thing the seat ever gave you.

events.text: It is the day of the Reckoning, when the seat of {b3_order} must account to the whole order, in person, for what has been done since the last. The speech is long. The order is patient and has brought cushions. In the third hour, a very small voice at the back asks: but what is it all for?

effects.log: You answer honestly. It takes a long time, and nobody moves. At the end, the hall is quiet in a way you have not heard before.
You deflect with a joke. The hall laughs, with relief, and the small voice does not speak again. You feel, for a week, slightly sick.

choices.text: Say you will think about it, and mean it

effects.log: You say it. And you do. By the following Reckoning, you have an answer, and it has changed three things.

events.text: The seat of {b3_order} has a private bath. It is old, deep and very hot, and the wall behind it is covered in the names of every previous seat, scratched in over thousands of years by the bored and thoughtful. There is room for exactly one more. You do not yet know what you will write.

effects.log: You write your name. It looks small among the others. It looks, also, quite certain, and you leave it at that.
You write: be kind to the next one. It is the only advice on the wall, and in the end it is the only part anyone reads.
You leave it blank. The wall has an empty space, for a long while, that makes the order a little nervous.

events.text: {b3_peer} comes into your rooms without knocking, which nobody has done in centuries, and sits down on your best chair. They say: I have come to tell you that you are no longer funny. It was, they admit, a very good thing about you, once. They would like it back.

effects.log: You tell them a story about the seat. It is quite funny. They laugh, and you laugh, and for a while the seat is a person again.
You admit it. It is a quiet, true moment. They nod, and suggest a walk, and you take it, and you tell no one you needed it.
You have them removed. It is, immediately, the worst joke of your tenure, and you spend a century apologising for it.

events.text: A great honour is offered to the seat of {b3_order}: a vast and ancient jade tablet, made by the first builders of the isles, to be hung in the hall. It is beautiful. It is also covered in orders and insults to the order, most of them true. The giver, a polite old rival, waits.

effects.log: You hang it. The hall is the better for it, and the order sees itself clearly for the first time, and is, after a while, proud.

choices.text: Accept it and keep it in the vault

effects.log: You accept it, and file it. The rival bows, knowing exactly what you have done, and is, for once, quite complimentary.
You refuse. The rival smiles and says that was the answer they expected, and that it is a pity. They hang it in their own hall instead.

events.text: You have just realised that you have not been out of the hall of the seat for eleven years. It happened by degrees, and nobody remarked on it. The order has arranged itself around you, like water around a stone. You are, by any measure, doing very well. You would like to see a hill.

choices.text: Walk out, and see a hill

effects.log: You walk out and see a hill. It is a very ordinary hill, and it is the best afternoon of the century. The order, startled, manages without you.

choices.text: Order the hill brought to you

effects.log: You order a small hill brought to the garden. It arrives, and is so charmingly absurd that the order starts a new custom.

choices.text: Stay, and send a disciple to see the hill for you

effects.log: You send a disciple. They return and describe it, and you listen with great care. It is nearly as good, you tell yourself.

events.text: The oldest rule of {b3_order} is that the seat may be challenged by any elder, at any time, in the open. It has not been used for a thousand years. Today, a small, tidy elder asks for an audience and says, with real apology, that they intend to use it. It is nothing personal.

effects.log: You accept, and the duel is held in the open yard. It is a close and remarkably decent affair, and you win, and the elder bows and says: thank you for the lesson.
You ask. They have a list, and it is a good one, and you adopt six of the eleven. The challenge is withdrawn, with honour on both sides.
You offer them the seat. They are appalled, and decline. You have both learned a lot about each other, and the order has, again, a seat.

events.text: Something is wrong with the order's tea. It is a matter of the first importance: the seat of {b3_order} receives, by tradition, a pot of the old green at dawn. It tastes, lately, very slightly of something else. You look into it and find that a young servant has been sweetening it in secret, out of love.

effects.log: You leave it. The tea is better, and everyone knows it is, and the servant, who has been terrified for a year, is promoted to cook.

choices.text: Scold gently, and drink it anyway

effects.log: You scold, and drink. The servant is frozen with relief and embarrassment, and the tea stays sweet.
You order it. The servant, grey with sorrow, obeys. The tea is correct, and nobody enjoys it, and you drink it with great ceremony.

events.text: At a feast, a disciple of {b3_order} raises a cup and toasts the seat as the wisest being in the isles. The order cheers. You know exactly how unwise you have been this very week, in ways that would make the cheering stop. You raise your own cup, and the hall waits to see what you will say.

choices.text: Accept the toast with a joke at your own expense

effects.log: You tell a story of your worst decision this week. The hall laughs, and the toasting disciple blushes, and you are, for a moment, both honest and loved.
You raise it and do not drink. The order sees only the seat, and you, for a moment, see only the cup. It is a very lonely little silence.
You refuse the toast and ask for a different one: to the ones who tell the seat the truth. It is drunk with real feeling.

events.text: In the quiet hours you add up what the seat has cost you: the friends who are now petitioners, the walks you no longer take, the words you must weigh. It is a heavy sum. It is not, strangely, a bitter one. You are not sure whether this means you have been wise, or only used to it.

choices.text: Keep the seat, and keep the sum

effects.log: You keep the seat. The sum is a quiet companion, and it makes you a better one.

choices.text: Resolve to spend an evening a week as nobody

effects.log: You do. For ages, every seventh evening, the seat of {b3_order} is simply gone, and no one knows where, and the order prospers.

choices.text: Write it down, and burn it

effects.log: You write the sum, and burn it, and watch the smoke go out over the isles. You feel lighter by exactly the weight of a page.

events.text: Two isles have been in debt to each other for ten thousand years, and nobody remembers what for. The League has been called in because the debt is, at last, coming due: both isles have started to build walls. The Arbiter hands you the file, which is a single stone tablet and a very long list of footnotes.
events.arc: The Debt of Ten Thousand Years

effects.log: You read them all. The debt is a loan of a single cup of rice, and a gift of one pot of tea, and each isle believes it is owed the other. It is exquisite.

choices.text: Ask both isles to tell you their version

effects.log: You listen to both. They are the same story, from two sides, with only the villain swapped. It is hard not to laugh.

choices.text: Tell them the debt is void

effects.log: You declare it void. Both isles are outraged, in the same words, at the same moment, and temporarily united in their dislike of you.

events.text: The two isles, having learned about the cup of rice, have each prepared an enormous banquet to repay it, and each insists on delivering it first. Both arrive at the border ford at the same hour. Both have brought two hundred porters. Nobody has brought a plan. You are the League's only representative.
events.arc: The Debt of Ten Thousand Years

choices.text: Hold a joint banquet on the ford

effects.log: You make a banquet on the ford itself. The two isles, appalled and delighted, eat together in the shallows, and the debt becomes a holiday.

choices.text: Have each isle receive the other

effects.log: You swap the banquets: each isle eats the other's. It is a quarrel of such grace that it is remembered as the Peace of the Cup.
You send them both home. The banquets rot, and the ford is quiet, and the debt remains, in the way of old things, perfectly safe.

events.text: A thousand years on, the two isles hold an annual Feast of the Cup. It is the most popular festival in the League's territory, and the only one where both sides have a stage. The Arbiter's seat has your name carved on it, in small letters. You are, at last, asked to give the toast.
events.arc: The Debt of Ten Thousand Years

effects.log: You give it: to the cup, and to forgetting why. The two isles roar. The cup, a small pewter thing, is passed from hand to hand for an hour.

choices.text: Tell the story of the first quarrel

effects.log: You tell it, as accurately as you can. It is long, funny and far too honest, and both isles love it more than they should.

choices.text: Pass the toast to the youngest present

effects.log: You pass it. The youngest, a small, solemn child of one of the isles, says one sentence. It is the best toast ever given.

events.text: A Warden of a Ford has stopped answering the League's letters. The Ford at Three Cranes has been quiet for a century, and the League's rules are that a silent Warden must be visited. You are sent, with a small bundle and a worse map. The ford, when you reach it, is full of cranes and of nothing else.

effects.log: You search. The Warden is there, very old and very well, and has been teaching the cranes to carry messages, which they do badly and with great dignity.

choices.text: Wait on the bank for a day

effects.log: You wait. The cranes look at you for a long time and then one of them steps forward and drops a very small scroll at your feet.
You report it. The League sends a bigger party, which finds the Warden and the cranes, and is much amused, and you are mildly blamed.

events.text: The Warden of the Ford at Three Cranes, who has been alone for a hundred years, has decided to retire. There is a difficulty: nobody wants the ford. It is too quiet, too cranelike and too far from anything. The League's seat has asked you to take it, for one year, as a favour.

choices.text: Take the ford for a year

effects.log: You take it. The year is peaceful, strange and entirely unproductive. The cranes learn your name. You leave in autumn, a little lighter.
You search the isles for a successor. After a year, you find one: a retired duellist who has always wanted a quiet place and a bird.

choices.text: Decline, and propose shutting the ford

effects.log: You propose shutting it. The cranes, informed, are pointedly silent. The League turns down the proposal, with some embarrassment.

events.text: Seven hundred years after your year at the Ford at Three Cranes, a message arrives: carried, with perfect efficiency, by a crane. It is from the successor, and it says: the cranes ask after you. A smaller line is added: so do I. There is a bird at your window, and it is waiting, formally, for a reply.

effects.log: You write, and go. The ford is the same. The cranes are the same. You have changed, and the ford, in its way, has been waiting to see how.
You write a long, warm letter. The crane carries it with unusual speed. It is the best correspondence of the century.

choices.text: Send the crane back with a joke

effects.log: You send a joke, a bad one. The reply, a week later, is worse, and nicer, and you laugh for a day.

events.text: The Isle Peacekeepers' League has a rule: before a duel is stopped, both duellists must be offered tea. It is intended to cool tempers. Today you offer tea to two ancient swordsmen, both mid-lunge, both furious. One accepts, and the other, seeing this, does too, rather sulkily.

effects.log: You pour. The two swordsmen sit down, and glare, and drink, and by the end of the pot they are old friends who have not quite noticed.

choices.text: Ask what the quarrel is about

effects.log: It is a matter of a lost fan. They have forgotten the fan, and remember the principle. You make a note to keep the principle out of the report.

choices.text: Propose they settle it with a game of stones

effects.log: You offer a board. The game lasts three weeks, and the quarrel never returns.

events.text: A messenger comes running to the League's ford post: a duel is about to begin on the Isle of Pale Orchards, and it will be a bad one: a Core Immortal against a younger sword who has been drinking. You are the closest Watcher. The Isle is a day away. You have a fast cloud and a slow horse.

effects.log: You take the cloud, and arrive at dawn, breathless, in time to stand between them. The younger sword is mortified, and the duel is replaced by a very awkward breakfast.
You send word. By the time you arrive, a third party has stopped it, and everyone looks at you with a faint, polite disappointment.
You arrive in time to see a good, clean duel, which ends harmlessly. You write a report that is entirely true and entirely unhelpful.

events.text: A League notice goes up on the board of the ford post: Missing, one border stone. The stone in question is a boundary marker between the Isle of Greys and the Isle of Silent Fields, and is eleven feet high. It is not at all easy to lose. Both isles have accused each other. The stone is not found.

effects.log: You search for a week. The stone is on a cloud, a mile up, with a small, smug cloud-fox sitting on it. The fox will not discuss terms.
The records show that the stone was moved a hundred years ago, in the dark, by both isles at once, in opposite directions. You write up a very careful report.
You raise a new stone. Both isles claim it favours the other, and are united in their suspicion. It is a small success.

events.text: At the League's ford post a Peace Envoy comes in from a very long mission, and is so tired that they fall asleep sitting up at the table. The Watchers, who are young, look to you for what to do. They have heard about the Envoy. Nobody dares to move them.

effects.log: You cover them with a cloak, and the Watchers tiptoe out. The Envoy wakes at dusk, and says only: thank you, and pays for supper for the whole post.

choices.text: Wake them gently for the report

effects.log: You wake them. They give an excellent, slurred report. It is later found to contain three secrets, and you are blamed for none of them.
You sit watch. It is the quietest night of your service. In the morning, the Envoy tells you something that stays with you.

events.text: A League Warden of a Ford has been bribed. It is a small bribe, a single pot of honey, offered by a smuggler of cloud-pears. The Warden, a decent immortal, took it, and has been wretched since. They come to you to confess and to ask for the rule. The rule is dismissal.

effects.log: You apply the rule. The Warden goes, grey and dignified. The ford is the poorer for it, and the League is, for a time, the cleaner.
You search the old charter and find a lesser rule: a year on the ford at the worst post. The Warden accepts with tears.

choices.text: Say you did not hear it

effects.log: You say you did not hear. The Warden stares. It is the sort of thing that is either a great kindness or a great mistake, and you hope for the former.

events.text: A great lord of the Nine Clouds has sent the League a gift: a case of fine tea, a sword of white jade, and a note asking that a certain duel against his rival be quietly overlooked. The League's rule is plain. The tea is very good. The sword is lovely. You are the one who has to say.

effects.log: You return it all with a note of thanks. The lord is displeased, and his rival is, in time, impressed, and you earn a reputation.

choices.text: Keep the tea, return the rest

effects.log: You keep the tea, and return the rest. It is not quite honest, and not quite a crime. The tea is delicious.

choices.text: Stop the duel, and keep nothing

effects.log: You stop the duel, and the lord is furious. In ten years he becomes a quiet patron of the League, which no one can explain.

events.text: The League's oath includes the line: I will keep the peace even against my own friends. Today, for the first time in nine hundred years, you are asked to. A friend of yours is about to start a feud over a small slight, and everyone, including your friend, knows you are the one who can stop it.

effects.log: You go, and talk. It is a very hard evening and a very good one, and the friend, at the end, says: all right, you stubborn mule.
You go in your robes, and give the order. The friend obeys, and is cold with you for a century. The feud, however, does not start.
You warn them, and step aside. The feud starts anyway, and you are, in the end, the one who stops it, much later, at greater cost.

events.text: A very small isle, hardly more than a rock with a house on it, has declared itself independent of everyone, and has sent the League a formal note announcing the fact. It is signed by a single immortal, who is the entire population. The note is polite and requests a postal service.

effects.log: You recognise it. The League writes a very serious charter. The isle receives a postal service, and a flag, and is, for ages, the happiest country in the isles.
You visit. The immortal, who is lonely, gives you a small, strange cake. You sit and talk until midnight, and the matter is settled, with no paper.
You send back a mild, amused letter. The isle replies with a very stern one, and you realise, with a pang, that it was in earnest.

events.text: A League patrol has found a stray sword on the ford road: a very good one, alone, humming faintly. It seems to be looking for someone. The Watchers are alarmed. It will not leave the patrol, and keeps pointing, very gently, in your direction.

effects.log: You take it. It is an old friend of a previous owner, and it is an odd, comfortable weight. You learn its history over a very pleasant century.

choices.text: Ask the sword who it wants

effects.log: You ask. It turns toward the ford, then toward a far peak. You follow its direction for a month and find a grave, and a very small cairn.
You hand it up. The Arbiter turns it over, says nothing, and sets it on a shelf. It hums, there, for a thousand years.

events.text: The League holds a day each century when every Warden of a Ford swaps posts with another, to prevent anyone growing too attached to a stretch of water. This year you have been sent to the one ford where, famously, there is no ferry, no bridge and no sense. The previous Warden has left a note: good luck.

effects.log: You build a small ferry. It is a delightful nuisance, and the whole ford turns up on the first day to ride it, and fall in.

choices.text: Learn to swim it, like the locals

effects.log: You learn. It is cold, difficult and strangely joyful, and you cross the ford, by the year's end, forty times.

choices.text: Petition the League for a bridge

effects.log: You petition. The League refuses on grounds of tradition. The ford, you gather, is a minor sacred thing, and you are quietly proud to have asked.

events.text: A young Watcher asks you what the League is for. You say: peace. They look unconvinced, and ask: whose? It is a very good question, and you are not at all sure how to answer. The Watcher has put down their sword, which is a sign, in the League, that a real question has been asked.

effects.log: You say it, and it is not entirely true, and not entirely false. The Watcher picks the sword up again, and says: all right, I can do that.

choices.text: Say you will find out together

effects.log: You say so, and you do, and it takes a century, and the Watcher is a Warden of Wardens by the end.

choices.text: Say it is above their rank

effects.log: You say it. The Watcher bows, and goes away, and for a time is a great deal more careful, and sad.

events.text: The oldest rule of the League is that no duel is stopped by force until three attempts at words have failed. Today you are on the third. The two duellists are a pair of immortals as old as the isles, who have been fighting on and off for six thousand years and are, you suspect, rather enjoying it.

effects.log: You say, simply: you are both very good, and it is very late. They look at each other, and sheathe, and go to dinner. It is the best thing you ever say.
You stop it by force, with great care and some difficulty. They are both quite impressed, and furious, and invite you to dinner as an apology.
You let them finish. It is a draw. They go off arm in arm, and you write the best report of your career.

events.text: A League Envoy reports from the Isle of Lanterns: the isle has had no quarrel for three hundred years, and the Envoy is worried. They have not seen so much agreeableness in anyone. The Envoy is convinced that something is being hidden. You are sent to find out, and you find a very contented isle.

effects.log: The elder says: we simply decided. You look for the catch for a year and there is none. You write a report that says: they are happy. It is very badly received.
You search. There is a secret quarrel, a tiny, loving one, about a shared garden. It keeps the peace, you realise, by being nothing at all.

choices.text: Stay a season, and enjoy it

effects.log: You stay a season. The isle, which is not trying, wins you over completely. Your report, when you finally write it, is a love letter.

events.text: A duel is arranged on the day of the League's autumn banquet, between two Peace Envoys, over a point of procedure. You are the host. The tables are laid, the lanterns lit, and the guests are in a state of delicious alarm. The Envoys, standing in the garden, ask whether the banquet can wait.

effects.log: You make them eat first. Well fed, and mellowed, they settle the point of procedure with a handshake and a pun. The banquet is a triumph.
You postpone the banquet. The duel is a short and decent one. The guests, annoyed at the delay, are consoled with the best cake of the century.

choices.text: Stage the duel as the entertainment

effects.log: You make the duel part of the evening, with rules. It is applauded, and nobody is hurt, and the point of procedure is forgotten.

events.text: In the League's records there is a debt of the Watchers to a small orphaned isle that lost its last harvest to a flood, three thousand years ago. It was never paid. Nobody now knows who owed it. The isle, now a flourishing little place, has sent a polite reminder, with interest, in the form of a fruit basket.

effects.log: You pay it, from the League's own coffers, in stones. The isle sends a second fruit basket, with a card that simply says: well done.
You pay half, and apologise in person. The isle, touched, forgives the rest, and the League is, ever after, an honoured guest.
You contest it, with citations. The isle replies with better ones. The League pays, grumbling, a year later, and you are quietly relieved.

events.text: A Lord Peacekeeper comes to inspect your ford post. It is the first inspection in four hundred years. You have cleaned everything, and the Watchers have been told to look alert. The Lord, a tall, slow immortal, walks the whole post in silence, and stops, at last, at a small jar of pickled plums on the sill.

effects.log: You offer one. The Lord eats it, gravely, and says: very good. It is the only comment of the inspection, and the post is rated excellent.
You admit it. The Lord says that every good post has something that is not in the rules, and writes it down, kindly, as a virtue.
You say a Watcher made them. The Watcher, summoned, is mortified and delighted, and promoted a rank on the spot.

events.text: A new League standard is to be presented at the autumn assembly, and the design is decided by a vote of all the Wardens. The two finalists are a single white crane on a field of blue, and a very detailed picture of a ford at dawn. Each has a passionate faction. You are, inconveniently, the swing vote.

effects.log: You vote crane. The crane wins by one vote. The Wardens who lost, sulking, put a small ford in the corner, and the standard is the better for it.
You vote ford. It wins by one, and the crane faction is outraged, and somebody, in the dead of night, adds a crane. Nobody confesses.
You propose both. It is a very busy flag. It is adopted by acclamation, and flown, for ages, with great pride and some embarrassment.

events.text: A long-retired Lord Peacekeeper, the oldest living member of the League, dies in her sleep, and leaves the League only one possession: a small notebook. It is filled, in a spidery hand, with every quarrel she ever stopped, and under each, one word: worth it, or not. The League asks you to decide what to do with it.

effects.log: You publish it. It is the most honest book in the League's history, and the Watchers read it, and are changed. Many of the 'not's are very instructive.

choices.text: Keep it for the Lords alone

effects.log: You keep it for the Lords. It is passed, from one to the next, a private inheritance, and each adds a line of their own.
You burn it, with honours. The Watchers are puzzled, and then understand: the ones who stopped quarrels did not do it for the book.

events.text: A very junior Star Reader has made a mistake in a reading that is, as it happens, of no consequence at all: a client's lucky colour is wrong. They are inconsolable. The Pavilion's rule is that no error, however small, goes unrecorded. You are the one who must write the correction in the great ledger.

effects.log: You write: a small error, found early, by someone who cares. The Reader, reading it later, sits very quietly for a minute, and then goes back to work.
You write it exactly, in the plainest hand. It is a fair and unhelpful entry, and the Reader learns, thereby, how the ledger works.

choices.text: Write nothing, and tell them to watch it next time

effects.log: You write nothing. The Reader watches it for ever after, and is, a century later, the most scrupulous reader the Pavilion has had.

events.text: At the top of the White Stairs a clerk the age of a mountain hands you a cup of water and a brush. "Sign the ledger of those who climbed," they say. The page is nine thousand years of names. Yours goes at the bottom, in wet ink, next to a smudge that used to be somebody famous.

effects.log: You sign with your best hand. The clerk blots it and says nothing, which at this height is praise.

choices.text: Read the names above yours first

effects.log: Half of them you have heard of in songs. One is crossed out with a very angry line. You sign under it, thoughtfully.

events.text: Climbers say the White Stairs have three thousand steps. The last thousand, you notice, were never counted by anyone who came back. A young examiner confides this over tea and then asks, rather anxiously, whether you counted. You did. You were off by about nine hundred.

effects.log: The examiner writes down your answer with relief and pretends not to notice you are lying beautifully.

choices.text: Say you lost count at the second cloud

effects.log: The examiner laughs and tells the table. By evening a story about you is already two thousand steps longer than the stairs.

events.text: The faction envoys wait at the summit in a row, each with a banner and an offer. They have been polite for an hour, which on the isles is a fierce form of competition. One has brought a folding stool for you to sit on while you decide. It is a very good stool.

choices.text: Take the stool and hear everyone

effects.log: Five speeches, one stool. By the end you know who flatters, who lies, and who forgot the speech and is eating plums.

choices.text: Refuse the stool and choose quickly

effects.log: Standing, you are done in a quarter hour. The envoys resent you a little, and respect you more than they let on.

events.text: The test of the third landing is a door that opens only to those who are no longer afraid of it. You went through with a very ordinary fear, and it opened anyway. The door-keeper, a spirit in a wicker hat, peers at you. "Most are unafraid because they stopped thinking," it says. "You thought, and went."

effects.log: It bows, creaking. For the next hundred years a wicker-hatted spirit tells climbers about someone who said thank you.

choices.text: Ask what it makes of the ones who ran

effects.log: It says they are welcome back, and that it keeps a seat warm for them. The seat is in fact warm. It is the most human thing on the isles.

events.text: Your result is announced from a balcony by a herald whose voice is a gong nobody has taught to be quiet. The whole stair-yard hears. Some applaud. A rival you never knew you had begins, with some effort, to applaud as well. Both of you will remember this.

effects.log: The yard likes it. A rumour starts that you are gracious, which is the cheapest way to be called great.

choices.text: Find the rival in the crowd and nod

effects.log: The rival stiffens, nods back, and goes off to practise. You have become a long project in somebody else.

events.text: The old examiners keep a custom: after a pass, one of them walks you down by the hidden spiral and tells you one true thing. Yours stops at a landing, looks over the edge at the sea of clouds, and says, "Nobody up here is as sure as they sound." Then they go back up.

effects.log: You carry the sentence all the way down. In later centuries it will rescue you from three bad meetings.

choices.text: Ask for a second true thing

effects.log: A pause, then a dry laugh. "The tea is really quite poor." You like them enormously.

events.text: After the Trial the stair-sellers press their wares on the newly passed: ribbons, talismans, a vial of "authentic summit air". You have become a customer. A very small spirit sells you a ribbon and says it is for luck. The price on it is written in a script you can read, and it is honest.

effects.log: It is a decent ribbon. By the next morning it has caught on three doors and saved you from one bad bargain.

choices.text: Teach the small seller a trick of bargaining

effects.log: You spend an hour on it. The seller doubles prices by dusk, and sends a small bow in your direction as thanks.

events.text: Someone from a faction you did not choose catches you on the terrace and says, quite kindly, that the examiners were split on your result. Two wished to pass you, one wished to keep you a year as a secretary, and one wished to publish your answers as a warning. Which, they ask, was which?

effects.log: You guess right. "Dangerous," they murmur, and go to tell everyone you read people well.

choices.text: Say you would rather not know

effects.log: They are charmed. It is the most disciplined answer they have heard in a century.

events.text: On the last landing there is a bench, and on the bench a very old swordsman asleep with a bowl of congee in his lap. A passing clerk whispers that he has been there since the Stairs were built. Past him lies the summit. Passing the Trial apparently includes not waking him.

effects.log: The swordsman murmurs a name you do not know as you pass. Nobody has ever asked what the name was.

choices.text: Cover the congee against the wind

effects.log: He does not wake, but the bowl is empty the next morning, and the clerk swears it was always so.

events.text: You were expecting a hall of examiners. What you got was a long table of old immortals eating noodles, who put five questions to you between mouthfuls. The fourth was whether you had ever lied for the right reason. You said yes. Several noodles stopped halfway.

effects.log: You give the story in three sentences. A noodle-eater nods slowly and writes a note that says only "again".

choices.text: Say no one should have to explain that

effects.log: The table goes quiet, then someone says "hm" in a tone that decides it.

events.text: One examiner voted twice to pass you, loudly, and was overruled twice, quietly. Afterward they find you at the foot of the Stairs with a small wrapped parcel. "Take it. Do not open it before you have been somewhere you hate." They are gone before you can refuse.

effects.log: It is surprisingly heavy for its size. You carry it into the next stretch of your life like a held breath.
The clerk at the desk says there is nobody of that description. You are left holding an apology for nobody.

events.text: Years on, you are in a place you hate: a long, stale meeting in a hall with bad light. You remember the parcel. Inside is a very small bell and a note: "Ring it when you want to leave and cannot." Everyone in the room is looking at you for an answer.

effects.log: A clear note sounds. For one breath everyone remembers they could be elsewhere, and the meeting ends well before it should.

choices.text: Leave it in the bag and endure

effects.log: You endure it, and answer well. The bell weighs rather more afterward.

events.text: The examiner is gone now, and you are summoned to a funeral for a name you did not know until it was read. One line of the eulogy: "who voted twice for the ones that others doubted." The bell, in your sleeve, rings once on its own.

effects.log: You stand at the back. A young clerk asks if you knew the dead. You say, truthfully, for a single afternoon.

choices.text: Pass the bell to the clerk

effects.log: The clerk takes it as though it were a coal. "I will ring it for the right one," they say. You believe them.

events.text: The Stairs reward the humble and the stubborn about equally, and nobody has ever worked out what the difference is. At the top, an examiner asks which you were. You are honest and say you cannot tell. "Good," they say. "That is the first time today."

effects.log: They tell you, with relish. Most of them were certain, and half of those were wrong.
The examiner is startled, and then very pleased. The tea is, for once, good.

events.text: You pass in the presence of two witnesses: a grand elder of one faction and a clerk of another. They disagree about which of them gets to claim you, politely, at length, while you stand holding your robes. A third voice from behind says, "Perhaps the climber should be asked."

effects.log: The room approves. Everyone wanted to be the one who waited, and now everyone is.

choices.text: Name the faction you like best and why

effects.log: You do so in two sentences. The loser claps first, and loudest, in a manner that suggests they will be a problem later.

events.text: At the second landing of the White Stairs the Stairs simply stop letting you climb, politely, like a door deciding. A servant spirit brings a cushion and a cup of tea. You sit for an hour and watch others go past. One of them is carrying a cat.

effects.log: They say the cat knows the stairs. You ask to borrow the cat. The cat declines. You go down, and the cat looks back, kindly.

choices.text: Stay for the full hour and learn the pace

effects.log: By the end you can see where the Stairs lean on a climber. It is a lesson you did not pay for.

events.text: Failure on the Stairs is not announced. The herald reads the list and your name is simply not on it, and nobody turns around. You stand there, a little cold, reading a list you are not on. A passing immortal says gently, "It is hard to see from here. Try again in three years."

effects.log: You go down quickly and without a word. The sky is wide below the Stairs, and entirely unbothered.

choices.text: Ask what they saw in the climb

effects.log: They think, then say you rushed the sixth bend. It is the most useful sentence you will hear all decade.

events.text: A young examiner finds you in the stair-yard after your failure and offers, low and nervous, to tell you the question you missed. It is forbidden. They have plainly been rehearsing the offer for some time.

effects.log: They whisper it. It was easier than you feared and harder than you hoped. You owe the examiner something now.
They exhale like someone surfacing. "Good," they say. "I would have hated myself." You both feel better.

events.text: You fell at the Trial. Down in the stair-yard a food-seller has put up a sign: "Consolation Buns, for the Not Yet." The trade is thriving. You buy two. The first is the most honest thing you have eaten in months, and the second is better.

choices.text: Sit among the Not Yet and eat

effects.log: Four other failures and a very cheerful baker. You trade stories until dusk, and one of them will matter in a thousand years.

choices.text: Ask the baker how long the stall has stood

effects.log: Eleven centuries, and not one bun wasted. There is a kind of promotion in that.

events.text: On the way down, a landing spirit sets a stool in your path and says that most who fail come back stronger, and most who fail do not come back at all, and it has never been able to tell in advance which kind it is talking to. It asks, with real interest, which kind you are.

effects.log: The spirit puts a tick on the wall of the landing. You see how many ticks there are, and how few are in the second row.

choices.text: Say you do not know yet

effects.log: It nods as though that were the best answer, and moves the stool out of your way.

events.text: Your friends have organised a surprise feast for your pass. Now it must be a feast for your failure, and nobody has had time to rewrite the banner. It reads "To Our Dear Climber, Who Rose". Everyone is mortified. You look at the banner and begin, to your own surprise, to laugh.

effects.log: The feast is a great success. The banner is kept, and used for the next five failures, which is a tradition now.

choices.text: Take the banner down yourself and fold it

effects.log: The silence is heavy, and then somebody sniffs, and then everyone is kind at once. It is almost worse.

events.text: Losing at the White Stairs costs you something small and specific: your name goes into the book of those who fell, and stays three years. The scribe is apologetic. "It is cleaned off, after. The ink is only slow." The scribe offers to leave a margin for a note.

effects.log: The note stays. By the time you return the scribe has underlined it twice, and a stranger has added "good luck" beside it.
Every page after yours has notes; yours is the one clean margin, and people read it.

events.text: Some failures happen with grace. Yours happens as a wobble on a cloud-step, a loud echo, and a long, public slide of eleven stairs on your back. A watching cloud spirit applauds the way spirits do, by raining a little. The examiners wait politely for you to get up.

choices.text: Get up and bow to the cloud

effects.log: The spirit rains harder, delighted. A rumour of the one who bowed to the weather runs the Stairs for a decade.

choices.text: Lie there and watch the clouds

effects.log: It is, in truth, a good view. The examiners, after a decent interval, decide you may as well rest until the next sitting.

events.text: A faction envoy, seeing you fail, sends a servant down with a quiet card: if you would care to join their house without passing, there is a back door. They would of course say nothing. The card is expensive paper. The back door comes with a lower first rank and a lifelong silence.

choices.text: Take the card, and keep it unused

effects.log: The card sits in your sleeve for years like a small warm coal. You never use it. You never throw it away.

choices.text: Send it back, thanking the envoy

effects.log: The envoy sends a courteous reply. They remember you, and will be glad when you climb for real.

events.text: The climber who passed beside you on the Stairs, a thin, anxious immortal called Lin Yuhe, finds you at the foot afterwards and offers, awkwardly, to carry your pack to the road. "I was lucky," they say. "It could as well have been you." They are not lying, which is the unbearable part.
events.arc: The One Who Passed Beside You

effects.log: Lin Yuhe walks with you to the road and talks about nothing for an hour. At the fork they say "next time". You believe them for some reason.
Lin Yuhe nods, stung, and goes. It was not cruel; you only wished to be left alone.

events.text: Three years later you are back at the Stairs, and Lin Yuhe is on the landing in the robes of a faction, trying very hard not to look as though they have been waiting. "I hoped it would be today," they say. They have brought tea. It is still bad, and still wonderful.
events.arc: The One Who Passed Beside You

choices.text: Take the tea and the news

effects.log: Lin Yuhe tells you which examiner is kind this season and which one naps. You take the next landing with the fastest step of your life.

choices.text: Say you would rather climb alone this time

effects.log: They nod, and walk down the stair beside you for one landing, silent, in case.

events.text: Years after, a messenger brings a red-paper invitation: Lin Yuhe, now of high rank, asks for you by name for a council seat. "You were the one who did not take the back door," the note says. "I thought of it often." You have not thought of it in decades.
events.arc: The One Who Passed Beside You

effects.log: You go. The council, you find, is mostly old friends of Lin Yuhe, and they treat you like a long-awaited letter.
Lin Yuhe understands. Your gift hangs in their gate hall, the plainest thing there, and the one people ask about.

events.text: Each faction keeps a small watching-pavilion at the foot of the Stairs where its members sit and judge the failures. The Star Sea is in professional pity, the Jade Void in the polite silence of swordsmen, and the Demon Realm lounge is plainly laughing, and says so, cheerfully. One of them waves you over.

choices.text: Go over and take the joke

effects.log: They give you a cup of tea and a dreadful toast to the Failed. Two of them quietly tell you how to climb the bend you fell on.
They laugh again, not unkindly. One throws you a plum as you go.

events.text: Sometimes the Stairs refuse because of something you carry rather than something you lack. The examiner, stooped, says your step is heavy with a small old grief. "It is not a flaw. It is only weight. Put it down somewhere before the next climb, or the Stairs will keep counting it."

choices.text: Ask where to put it down

effects.log: They draw a small map on a leaf with a cross at a stream. You go, and put something down, and come home lighter in an odd, quiet way.
The examiner bows, as to someone who has chosen a very long road. You climb again in three years, and the Stairs count it, and let you through.

events.text: You fail by the narrowest margin. The examiner makes a very small gesture with thumb and forefinger. "That much," they say. "A hair." They look pained. Behind them the other examiners look as though a hair is a hair and always will be.

effects.log: They laugh in spite of themselves. For the rest of the year they tell people about the climber who asked for the hair back.
You take the lesson with the hair. Next time you will be a hand ahead.

events.text: A cloud-sweeper finds you sitting on the last good step, looking at the summit. In four thousand years of sweeping, the sweeper says, the Stairs have been kinder to those who sit and look than to those who run. The broom is held out, mildly, as one hands over a baby. "Do the next five steps with me."

effects.log: It takes an hour. At the fifth step you notice you have been breathing correctly for the first time in the climb.
The broom is taken back without offence. The Stairs are patient, the sweeper says. So is the sweeper.

events.text: The Scripture Vault of {b3_order} is shelved by the order in which things were forgotten, not written. A vault-keeper explains this with great pride and no further help. You find the scroll you want in the end because a mouse is sitting on it.

effects.log: The mouse accepts a crumb and a long look. The scroll is a treatise on patience, and it is better than it has any right to be.

choices.text: Ask the keeper whether the mouse is staff

effects.log: It is, in fact, on the pay-roll. The keeper writes you a small note of introduction to it.

events.text: Deep in the Vault of {b3_order} there is a reading room where the scrolls whisper. Not words: only the sound of being read. You learn that if you sit quietly the scrolls grow shy and begin, one by one, to offer themselves. The keeper warns that this ends in an hour, when they all want attention at once.

effects.log: Three scrolls, three ideas, and a headache that tastes of ink. All three prove useful over the next century.
Forty scrolls unroll over you like cats. You read none well, and come out knowing what each is about, which turns out to be the better wisdom.

events.text: A margin note in an old text of {b3_order} reads, in a hand you almost recognise: "This is wrong. See page 400." Page 400 says the opposite and also says, in the margin, "This is wrong. See page 12." You are on your third circuit before you notice the notes are in your handwriting.

effects.log: On the fifth pass you find the real answer, hidden in a corner both notes pointed away from. You laugh aloud in the Vault, and are shushed by a statue.

choices.text: Add a note of your own

effects.log: You write "Both right. Eat something." You leave it there. Later readers swear it is the only useful line in the book.

events.text: The vault-keeper of {b3_order} permits one scroll out of the room per century. You may borrow it and carry it to your own rooms, provided you promise to read it in the dark. The keeper does not say why. The keeper has also, you notice, closed the shutters.

choices.text: Promise, and read in the dark

effects.log: Words glow faintly in the dark, written in something that only lives there. It is a map, of a place that is mostly about listening.

choices.text: Decline the loan; read it in the light of the Vault

effects.log: In the light it is only a blank scroll. The keeper nods, as if you had passed some small test that the keeper had been curious about.

events.text: Someone else is reading in the Vault of {b3_order}: a very young immortal, not yet five hundred, who is plainly out of their depth and refusing to notice. They are holding a text upside down. The keeper looks at you over their spectacles and then, very deliberately, at the ceiling.

choices.text: Turn the book right way up, quietly

effects.log: The young one gives you a look of mortified gratitude. They will say your name warmly for a thousand years, and you will not remember theirs.
They get the book the right way up in the end, by themselves, which seems to matter to them more than you might have guessed.

events.text: A scroll of {b3_order} turns out to be a recipe. A bad one, for a soup nobody has made in four thousand years, and attached with great solemnity to a note that reads, "Preserve at any cost." The cost has evidently been the rest of the shelf. You have been reading for six hours.

effects.log: It is terrible. It is also strangely moving. The order serves it at one festival a century now, with great ceremony and a spoon each.
You copy it out carefully. Behind you, the soup shelf settles with a small, grateful creak.

events.text: The Vault of {b3_order} keeps a Forbidden Shelf behind a very small door. The door is unlocked. It is always unlocked: the point is that nobody opens it. On the shelf, you gather, there is only a note that says "Well done." The keeper has never seen it.

effects.log: A single scroll, a single line: "Curiosity is rewarded here. Well done." Underneath, a very small drawing of someone shrugging.
You never learn. For the rest of your life you carry a small, interesting hole where the answer would be, and the hole is useful.

events.text: The Scripture Vault of {b3_order} is rearranging itself. The keeper explains, a little tired, that it does this about once a century, and that the scrolls take offence if they are looked at during. You may wait three days. You may also look, and be dealt with.

effects.log: You wait, drinking tea in the yard. When you go in, the Vault has put the scroll you needed in the first row, with a small bow.

ok.log: The scrolls, caught, shuffle sheepishly and make room for you. You read among them like a thief who was welcomed.

fail.log: A scroll rolls itself into a tube and cracks you on the head. Everyone is very kind about it afterward.

events.text: You are given a reading assignment by the Vault of {b3_order}: one scroll, no commentary. After a week you realise it is the accounts of an isle that went down in a storm four thousand years ago, and the accountant kept accounting right up to the last day. Every entry is calm. It is a very long scroll.

effects.log: The last line reads "Provisions adequate. Weather unusual." You close it, and the Vault is very quiet around you.

choices.text: Skim and ask the keeper what it is for

effects.log: The keeper says it is for seeing what steadiness looks like when it has nowhere to go. You decide you will be more careful about where you point yours.

events.text: A page of a tutorial text in the Vault of {b3_order} has been torn out. Not recently. A faint note in the gutter says "Taken for safekeeping by the third head." The third head has been dead nine thousand years. The page, if it exists, is somewhere in the buildings. There is a rumour.

effects.log: You find it behind a loose beam, wrapped in oilcloth and a dead sparrow. It describes a way of breathing that you have been doing wrong.

choices.text: Report it to the keeper and let them seek

effects.log: The keeper is moved to tears, and then to action. It is found in a month. You receive a copy and the credit.

events.text: On the reading desk of {b3_order} there is a scroll with a hole burned through the middle, the exact size of a thumb. The keeper says it was done by a famous immortal who, reading a particularly good line, gripped it too hard with their sword-fire. It is the most-read scroll in the Vault.

effects.log: It is only half there. You supply the other half from your own life, and are surprised how well it fits.

choices.text: Press your thumb into the hole

effects.log: It fits. The keeper laughs and takes a note. You are the fourth this century.

events.text: The Vault of {b3_order} has a visiting scholar from another faction, and there are rules for this: they sit at the far end, speak to nobody, and the keeper inspects their sleeves on the way out. Yours, you note, are inspected on the way in. The scholar glances at you with something like sympathy.

choices.text: Trade a nod with the scholar

effects.log: Over the afternoon you trade ten pages of notes, across forty feet of Vault, via a very bored mouse. Both orders are improved.
Silence is the Vault in its natural state. You read three scrolls, and finish one idea you had not known you had begun.

events.text: You find a scroll in the Vault of {b3_order} written by someone who plainly hated {b3_order}, preserved with all its insults, and annotated in the margins by generations of the order replying. The thread goes back six thousand years. Some of the replies are now older than the order thought it was.

effects.log: You write a short, civil, devastating line. By the next century it will be one of the replies they teach the new.
It is a long argument that turns out to be a love letter, mostly, to the thing it hates. You come out thoughtful.

events.text: At the end of a year in the Vault of {b3_order} the keeper gives each reader a task: say, in one sentence, what you learned. Yours is waiting. The keeper listens with their eyes shut, as if tasting.

effects.log: The keeper opens one eye. "Humble, and true. Rarer than you think." They stamp your reader-slip with a very small star.
The keeper opens both eyes and sighs. "Yes, that will do for the others." You are given a second, smaller task, which is harder.

events.text: The reading lamps of {b3_order} run on a pale flame fed with the pages of rejected manuscripts. You find a lamp burning a very good poem. The poet is long dead. The keeper explains: the poem was good, and the lamp was cold.

choices.text: Copy the poem before it goes

effects.log: You write it down in the last light. The lamp dims, as if with thanks. The poem is the best thing in your copy-book.
You watch it go, and the light is very good. There is something right about a poem warming a reader who does not know it.

events.text: In the Vault of {b3_order} a master of the old copying art is teaching a class of three how to reproduce a scroll exactly, down to the stains. You are asked to judge the results. Two copies are perfect. The third is subtly better than the original, and the copyist is sweating.

effects.log: The master flinches, then nods. The copyist begins a very long career of improving things that nobody has asked to be improved.
The master looks relieved. "A copyist who improves is a poet who lies." The third copyist weeps, privately, with relief or something close.

events.text: The Scripture Vault of {b3_order} contains one scroll that cannot be read, because every reader sees something different. The keeper offers to take you through it in the presence of a witness. The witness is a very old, very quiet monk. "What you see will tell you what you want," says the keeper. "Please do not say it aloud."

effects.log: You read three lines. They hurt, a little, in a way that clarifies. You keep silent, as asked. The monk nods once.
The keeper says this is also an answer. The monk, at the door, says only, "Good." You walk home through a calm, strangely lonely afternoon.

events.text: A reader of {b3_order} before you left a set of notes in the margins of a hundred scrolls. They are signed only with a small drawing of a crane. The notes get better the longer you follow them, and you find yourself reading the scrolls only for the crane. The keeper will not say who it was.

effects.log: You follow the crane through twenty scrolls. It is leading you somewhere, and the keeper, you realise, knows.

choices.text: Read the scrolls and ignore the notes

effects.log: The scrolls are fine. You feel, nevertheless, that you have declined an invitation.

events.text: At the end of the crane notes you find a locked small drawer in the reading desk, and a key hung in the Vault's own rafters, which takes the afternoon to reach. Inside the drawer is a half-finished note: "If you are reading this, you are the one I was writing to." The rest is blank.

effects.log: You write what you think the crane would have wished you to. It takes a long time, and you do not read it back.

choices.text: Close the drawer, leave it for the next reader

effects.log: The drawer is, you think, a gift that is only a gift if it is left. You tip the keeper's mouse a crumb in thanks.

events.text: Eight years on, a young reader of {b3_order} asks the keeper about the crane notes. The keeper brings them to you. "Tell them," says the keeper. "You are the last who followed it." The young reader has the look of someone who is about to inherit a very odd house.

effects.log: You tell it plainly, down to the drawer. The young reader writes it down. By the next century, the crane has a small shrine in the Vault.

choices.text: Give them the key and say nothing

effects.log: They look at the key as at a new, strange animal. You walk away, and hear them begin, very quietly, to follow.

events.text: The third cellar of the Vault of {b3_order} has a locked door, and from behind it, rather faintly, comes the sound of someone turning pages. The keeper says this has been so since before the keeper. Tonight, the pages stop. The silence is the sort that asks a question.
events.arc: The Thing in the Third Cellar

effects.log: Three small knocks answer you. Then, under the door, a slip of paper: "Not yet. Thank you for asking." Your hands are very cold.
You leave it. Somewhere below, the pages begin again. You find you are relieved, and a little ashamed to be.

events.text: You come back to the third cellar. The door is ajar, an inch. A small note is wedged in the gap: "If you wish. Come in alone. Bring a lamp." The keeper is nowhere to be found, and the Vault is, for once, entirely quiet.
events.arc: The Thing in the Third Cellar

effects.log: Inside there is a very old reader, at a desk, wearing the robes of a long-extinct rank. They look up and say "Ah. You have been long." You sit.

choices.text: Shut the door and report it

effects.log: The keeper, hearing, goes quite pale, and then thanks you, and locks the cellar with a new lock. The pages never turn again.

events.text: The old reader of the third cellar has finished the book at last. They ask you to carry it up and place it, unread, on the highest shelf of the Vault. "It was only ever for being finished," they say. They fade, courteously, like a lamp left to burn out. You carry the book up the cellar stairs.
events.arc: The Thing in the Third Cellar

effects.log: The book goes on the high shelf. The Vault creaks, once, and a long-held tension in it lets go. The keeper weeps and does not say why.
It says only: "Thank you for staying." You close it. It is the best thing anyone has ever said to you, and you tell nobody.

events.text: The reading year ends with a feast of the vault-readers of {b3_order}, held in the stacks, among the scrolls, with no food allowed near them, so the feast is held in the corridor and the guests stand in the doorway gazing in. A toast is proposed to "the Dead who Wrote". It is drunk in tea.

choices.text: Give the second toast, to the Living who Read

effects.log: The corridor laughs, and the stacks, you could swear, rustle in approval. You are asked back every century.

choices.text: Drink the toast in tea and say nothing

effects.log: The tea is hot and a little bitter, and the feast is the most gently happy evening you spend all year.

events.text: You go into {b3_foe} wearing a plain face and an invented family. The first thing they do is feed you. This is not what you were warned about. You are given a seat, a bowl, and a gruff old porter who calls you "the new boy" regardless of what you are, and means it kindly.

effects.log: The porter talks the entire meal, and by the end you know three secrets and the name of the porter's dog, which is, naturally, the most dangerous of them.
The porter approves of the silence. "A quiet one. Good." It is a recommendation you will use later.

events.text: Inside {b3_foe}, you are given a job in the archive. It is the correct job. It is the exact job a spy would have asked for, and they gave it without being asked. You spend a week trying to work out whether this is a trap, and a second week realising it is simply that nobody else wanted it.

choices.text: Read the archive for what you came for

effects.log: It takes three weeks, and the files are mostly complaints about plumbing. Buried in the plumbing is a very plain account of a plan.

choices.text: Do the job well, and wait

effects.log: You become, in a year, the only person who knows where anything is. They would be devastated to learn what else you know.

events.text: You make a friend in {b3_foe}. It was not in the plan. It is a thin, funny immortal who shares their lunch and gives you a nickname. They tell you, one evening, a secret that is entirely personal and entirely useless to your order. You realise it is the only true thing anyone has told you all year.

choices.text: Keep it, and keep the friend

effects.log: You guard the secret more tightly than any you took from the archive. In return the friend never asks your real name.

choices.text: Report it, as your orders say

effects.log: It is of no use to anyone, and you know it, and report it anyway. The friend, later, looks at you in a way that does not fade.

events.text: The cover story you were given in {b3_foe} includes a dead mother, a lost isle, and a fondness for pickled plums. You have used the pickled plums three times now. Someone has begun leaving pickled plums on your desk. It is a kindness. It is also a test. You cannot tell which, and the plums are very good.

choices.text: Eat the plums and say nothing

effects.log: Nobody speaks of it. At the end of the year a small jar is left on your desk with a note: "For the road." Whether they knew, you will never know.

choices.text: Ask who has been leaving them

effects.log: A cook, it turns out, who simply likes you. The plums are, after all, just plums.

events.text: A deadline arrives inside {b3_foe}: a council vote you were sent to sway. You have cultivated two councillors and a clerk. The clerk is the one who really matters, and the one you have been neglecting because the clerk is the dullest of the three. You find, standing outside the hall, that you have no idea what the clerk wants.

choices.text: Ask the clerk what they want

effects.log: The clerk, startled, says they would like to be asked more often. The vote goes your way, on the strength of a very large and sincere cup of tea.

ok.log: The councillors fold, and the vote carries. You feel, rather, that you have won against the wrong people.

fail.log: The councillors, sensing a hand on their back, close ranks. The vote goes against you, and the clerk smiles slightly into their sleeve.

events.text: You come out of {b3_foe} at year's end with their plan in your head and a faint but unmistakable fondness for the place. At the gate, the porter hands you a small bundle: bread, a plum, a note. "In case you are not coming back," it says. "You never said." You never had.

choices.text: Take the bundle, and say thank you

effects.log: You carry it all the way home. Eating the bread, you feel like a traitor in two directions, and rather more accurately than you would like.
The porter nods and puts it away. "The new boy is always the first to leave," says the porter, to nobody, as you go.

events.text: A senior of {b3_foe} takes you aside in the second month and says, kindly, that you are a spy. They are not angry. They tell you the other three spies are in the kitchen and the library, and that you are all so obvious they have begun to keep score on which of you is the best. You are currently third.

effects.log: The senior tells you. It is someone you know. You decide that this is a conversation the world will hear nothing about, ever.
The senior listens, and nods, and says "good", and gives you a very slightly better desk. You are now second.

events.text: The rival order is holding its founders' festival while you are inside it, and the rule is that everyone sings. You do not know the founders' hymn. You have a day to learn it. A very small apprentice offers to coach you, at the price of a solemn promise that you will not laugh. The hymn has a verse about turnips.

effects.log: You sing it with the whole hall, straight-faced, turnips and all. By the last verse you are, to your horror, moved.
You sing a confident, wrong hymn. The apprentice, next to you, quietly changes their own words to match yours, and the hall is none the wiser.

events.text: Inside {b3_foe} there is a door that is always closed, and a guard who is always asleep outside it. You have been told to find out what is behind it. The guard is, you slowly realise, awake. The guard has been awake the entire time. They simply decided, long ago, to look asleep, because it is easier.

choices.text: Share the guard's secret and sit with them

effects.log: You sit with the guard on the cold step for an hour. They tell you what is behind the door. It is an empty room, and it has been one for centuries.
You report that the door guards nothing. This is true, and nobody believes it.

events.text: The tea-room of {b3_foe} is where information moves. You spend your first month there learning to be unremarkable. It is surprisingly hard. People keep remembering you for being so very pleasant. A man selling brushes tells you that nobody forgets a face that nice, and that you would make a poor thief.

effects.log: You work on a face like a closed shutter. Within weeks you pass three people you were sent to watch, and each looks straight through you.
You become the nice one. Doors open, and a great many things are said in front of you, because nobody suspects the nice one.

events.text: Your handler from home sends a message into {b3_foe} by the usual channel, a hollow plum-stone, and it says only: "Come out now." You have not finished. There are two more weeks of work, a friend, and a vote. The order is, for once, not unreasonable. You could go.

effects.log: You leave at dawn. The work you did not finish never gets finished, and the friend you did not tell never forgives it.
You do the work. At home they are cross, and then very pleased, and then they stop speaking of it entirely.

events.text: You are caught copying a ledger in {b3_foe} by a very small, elderly scribe who holds up the lamp and looks at you for a long time. "I should call the guard," says the scribe. "I have not copied anything in two hundred years. Would you show me how you do it so fast?"

effects.log: It takes an evening. The scribe is overjoyed. In the morning the ledger you wanted is on your desk, copied, with a small note: "From an admirer."
You are out of the window with the ledger, and you carry the feeling of the scribe's lamp for a good deal longer than the ledger.

events.text: The rival order has an old custom of the Honest Hour, once a month, when all of them tell one true thing about themselves. You are expected to join. You have, you reflect, a whole life of true things, and none of them can be said. You sit in the circle with your mouth slightly open.

choices.text: Tell a true thing that is not about your mission

effects.log: You tell them about the isle you grew up on, and the way the light was on the water. Nobody mentions that it is not the isle in your papers.

choices.text: Make one up with a true feeling in it

effects.log: You tell a lie in which every emotion is real. They nod, and one of them squeezes your shoulder. It is the worst thing you have done all year.

events.text: In the last month inside {b3_foe} you are given a small job: carry a message to another isle. It is, you suspect, a test, and the message is perhaps a trap, and the isle is a day away through bad weather. You are told you may refuse. Everyone says so. Everyone watches.

effects.log: You carry it. At the other end it is a simple thank-you for a debt. Both sides are entirely innocent, and you are very tired.
You open it with a thin blade and a lie. It is, in fact, a recipe. The test, you realise, was whether you would read it.

events.text: A janitor of {b3_foe} knows exactly who you are. It becomes clear over a series of increasingly meaningful mop-strokes. At the end of the year the janitor says, "I will not say. I want something small." The small thing is a seat at your order's next banquet.

effects.log: The janitor attends the banquet in a very good robe, sits in the corner, and weeps with happiness at the dessert. You will never be able to explain this to anyone.
The janitor shrugs. "Fair." Nothing is said. The year ends and the janitor, at the gate, simply waves, and means it.

events.text: You were sent into {b3_foe} to steal a technique. You have been given the technique, freely, as part of ordinary lessons, in the first month. It is a good technique. You are now unsure what you are supposed to steal. You write to your handler to say so. The reply says: "Steal harder."

effects.log: You learn the whole thing in plain sight. It is returned to you at the gate as a gift and a warning: nothing is ever stolen that is really given.

choices.text: Invent a heist to justify the year

effects.log: You manufacture a theft so that your report will look good. It is a very good theft. You feel, increasingly, like someone robbing their own pockets.

events.text: Inside {b3_foe} you work next to a cook called Ouyang Mei who, over a season of onions, learns your every habit. You are meant to be learning hers. One day she says, without turning: "Your hand does not shake when you chop. A real kitchen hand's would." She continues to chop, and says nothing else.

choices.text: Say nothing, and shake your hand a little

effects.log: Mei laughs, once, into the pot. "Better." You are not caught. You are, in an odd way, taught.
She tells you some of it, in an even voice, over a pot. Then she says, "Do not ask again." You do not.

events.text: Ouyang Mei, it turns out, has been feeding the rival order's secrets to its own enemies for years, in tiny pinches, in the soup. She asks you, calmly, whether your people want any. She is offering to be your mole inside the mole. It is the oddest pitch you have ever heard.

effects.log: It becomes the most productive arrangement you will ever have. You do not know who she really serves. She does not know who you do.
She nods, and goes back to the onions. The next day the soup is a little better than usual, and you do not know why.

events.text: Years later your order summons you: a cook of {b3_foe} named Ouyang Mei has been taken. They want you to say whether she is worth saving. You have, in your sleeve, a small pickled onion she gave you at the gate. It has not rotted in all these years.

effects.log: Your order negotiates her out. She thanks nobody, and one morning a pot of soup arrives at your door. It is the best you have ever tasted.

choices.text: Say it is not your concern

effects.log: She is not saved. The onion, a week later, finally spoils, and you find you cannot eat for a day.

events.text: The false name you used in {b3_foe} has stuck to you. A trader who passed through a month after you left recognises the name and asks for you. You have, in your absence, become a legend there. They say you were generous and impossibly modest. You wonder who you were pretending to be.

effects.log: You answer to it. The trader beams. A very small piece of you begins to live a second life as that person, who is better than you in several ways.
The trader shrugs and goes, puzzled. The name, however, continues to be better regarded than yours.

events.text: A letter in the false name arrives from {b3_foe}: the order invites you to give a lecture on your most famous feat of generosity. It is a feat you never performed. The audience will be several hundred. The order, you realise, has no idea that it is addressing a stranger, and that it is delighted.

effects.log: You tell the story of the true thing the false name did, and leave out the rest. It goes beautifully. For a night you are the person they loved.
The excuse is accepted with the deepest sympathy. A second letter arrives, with condolences for an illness you did not have.

events.text: The false name outlives you in {b3_foe}. A shrine, small, is raised to the generous stranger of that year. A pilgrim of the order says it is a quiet place of peace. You visit, in disguise, to see it. Beneath the offerings there is a note in your own handwriting that you never wrote.

choices.text: Add your real name beneath it

effects.log: You write it very small. A short while later, you hear that a new pilgrim has noticed it, and has decided, in kindness, to say nothing.

choices.text: Leave it, and let the stranger be loved

effects.log: You leave. The name is better kept by those who needed it. You carry the lightness of a very odd, quiet forgiveness.

events.text: The most dangerous thing in {b3_foe} turns out to be its hospitality. You are put up in a room with a view, given a map to the baths, and asked, on the second night, whether you are lonely. You are. The fact that they noticed, and that it is an interrogation technique, and that it is also genuinely kind, is deeply uncomfortable.

effects.log: The host nods. "Then do not be, for a few days." You are not. You hold back only the thing you came to hide, and the host respects the edge of it.
The host says "of course", and sends you a second blanket anyway. It is the most disarming lie you have been told in years, and it is hospitable.

events.text: You return from {b3_foe} to {b3_order} and are told to report to a closed room. There are three elders. One of them asks what you saw, one asks what you did, and one, in a quiet voice, asks whether you still belong. The room is very still.

choices.text: Say you still belong, and mean it

effects.log: The third elder nods, slowly. "Then you may keep what you learned, and we will not ask you to forget the friends." It is a mercy in a very quiet voice.

choices.text: Say you are no longer sure

effects.log: The room stays silent for a long time. Then the elder says, "Then you are more use to us than before." You are not certain it is a compliment.

events.text: The agent who ran you in {b3_foe} has retired, and sends you a small package: a brush, an ink-stick, and a note: "I only ever wished to know what you were thinking." The brush is very good. The ink-stick is the sort that is only made for those whose letters are never meant to be read.

effects.log: You write for an hour. When it is done you do not send it. You keep the page folded in the brush-case, and take it with you for a century.

choices.text: Use the ink and brush for your next report

effects.log: The report is a masterpiece. It is also, you will realise much later, a little more honest than you intended.

events.text: On your last night in {b3_foe} you are asked to attend an ordinary meeting, as one of the order. It is about rebuilding a bridge. The vote is split. They ask you, as a trusted outsider who has seen every side, to cast the deciding voice. You cannot, and everyone knows you cannot, and nobody says so.

effects.log: The bridge is built anyway, two weeks late, a very good bridge. You are thanked for a silence that, you are told, was the wisest voice at the table.

choices.text: Cast the vote for the better plan

effects.log: The vote carries, and the bridge is built. You are, strictly, a spy who has just done a rival order a kindness. It has been the best moment of the year.

events.text: {b3_oldhead} yields the seat of {b3_order} to you in front of the assembly, and does it well. Then, in the quiet after, the old head hands you a heavy ring of keys and says, "Eleven of these open nothing. I would not tell anyone which." A small, dry smile. The ring clinks all the way to your rooms.

choices.text: Try the keys, one a week

effects.log: It takes nearly a year. Eleven open nothing, and a twelfth opens a cupboard of excellent tea that the old head has been guarding for two thousand years.

choices.text: Hang the ring on the wall and leave it

effects.log: It hangs there, an ornament and an accusation. Visitors are shown it, and the story, which improves with age.

events.text: The first morning as head of {b3_order} you wake to find three hundred petitions on your desk, each folded to the same size, each with a small ribbon in the colour of the petitioner's hall. The oldest clerk of the order stands by with a tray of tea, ready, and says nothing at all, as long as you wish.

effects.log: It takes three weeks. Two hundred and ninety are small, nine are serious, and one is a love poem to the previous head. You answer every one.

choices.text: Ask the clerk which nine to read

effects.log: The clerk points out nine without looking. You read them first, and then the poem, which is very good.

events.text: There is a custom in {b3_order} that the new head, on the first night, must sleep in the Head's Chamber, which has been left unused since {b3_oldhead} moved out. The chamber is cold. The bed is narrow. On the pillow lies a note in a firm hand: "Everyone sleeps badly here the first year. It passes."

effects.log: You sleep badly and wake to a clear view across the sea of clouds. It is, you decide, a fair exchange.

choices.text: Move the bed to the window

effects.log: The chamber is transformed. The next head, a thousand years on, will keep the bed where you put it, and will not know why.

events.text: The head of a neighbouring order, a stooped immortal with a face like a closed fan, arrives to congratulate you in person. It is the longest courtesy visit in memory. Midway through the second hour they say: "I wished to see whether you would still be polite to me when you did not have to be." They seem satisfied.

effects.log: The neighbour leaves with a bow that is almost warm. Across the clouds a message goes: the new head of {b3_order} can be trusted with a courtesy.

choices.text: Tell them frankly that you were tired of it

effects.log: A long, surprised silence. Then the neighbour laughs, once, like a crack in lacquer. "Good," they say. "I may be able to do business with you."
