events.text: The seat of {b3_order} carries a duty nobody told you of: you must keep the order's oldest secret. It is told to you in a bare room by an elder, who then falls asleep. When you wake the elder the elder says, "Which secret?" and cannot be persuaded they told you anything. You have, you realise, a secret and no idea what it is.

choices.text: Search the order's records for it

effects.log: You search for a year. What you find is nothing, and a faint, steady certainty that nothing was the secret all along, and that it is meant to be kept.

choices.text: Decide it was about tea, and carry on

effects.log: You choose a secret and guard it with solemn dignity. By the time anyone asks, you have, in effect, made it true.

events.text: {b3_oldhead} remains in the order as a quiet adviser and, for a few weeks, as a haunting. They come to every meeting. They sit at the back with a brush and a very small notebook. You find yourself making decisions in the voice of someone who is being graded.

choices.text: Ask the old head to the front

effects.log: The old head sits beside you, and offers only one comment all year, when you need it most. By spring you need it far less.

choices.text: Ask them kindly to take a long journey

effects.log: {b3_oldhead} goes, with a very small, wounded dignity, to see the far isles. The letters are cheerful. They are also, you suspect, a little sad.

events.text: Your first act as head of {b3_order} is to sign a new seal. The old seal is cracked and has been for nine hundred years; everyone has learned to read the crack as part of the name. The carvers wish to know whether to keep the crack. The faction is, on this, divided, loudly and in the old style, in verse.

effects.log: The carvers cut a new seal with a careful new crack in the same place. It is, a clerk observes, the most expensive flaw in the isles.
The first document with the whole seal is regarded with suspicion for a decade. Then it becomes the order's mark of trust.

events.text: An old rival of {b3_order} sends a gift of congratulation: a perfectly ordinary teapot. Everyone in the hall is waiting to be told what it means. Is it an insult? A threat? A thaw? A scholar, searching, finds that there is no hidden meaning. It is a teapot. It is, however, an excellent one.

effects.log: The tea is spectacular. The rival, hearing, sends a second pot of leaf. You have, by accident, begun a truce.

choices.text: Send a plain, perfect teacup back

effects.log: It is a message in a single object. The rival replies, in kind. Between you the entire shelf of courtesy now stands.

events.text: {b3_oldhead} comes to you with a single request, the only one in a thousand years: to be allowed to see the sun rise from the highest eave of {b3_order}, once, with you, and to say nothing. It is a long, cold climb. The old head moves slowly, with a stick that has been in their hand for centuries.

effects.log: You climb, in no hurry, and watch the dawn arrive over a sea of white cloud. The old head says nothing. At the end they put a hand on your sleeve.
The attendant does it well. The old head, returning, is polite, and a little diminished, and does not ask again.

events.text: Five years on, {b3_oldhead} sends a note: they are failing, and would like to see the eave once more. This time they ask for a different thing too: that you read, aloud, a verse they wrote as a young disciple. It is a terrible verse. They love it dearly.

choices.text: Read the verse with a straight face

effects.log: You read it very well. The old head listens with closed eyes. Afterwards they say it has never been read so kindly.

choices.text: Offer to read a better verse

effects.log: The old head laughs until their stick falls. "No," they say. "That one, only." You read it.

events.text: {b3_oldhead} is gone. Among their things is a sealed letter for you, with a small rule at the top: "Open on the dawn". You take it to the eave, in the cold, and wait for the sun. When it clears the clouds you open it. It says: "Thank you for the climb. It was the best day."

choices.text: Hang the letter in the head's chamber

effects.log: It stays there for the head after you, and the head after that. None of them ever remove it, and none of them know why.

choices.text: Keep it, and climb the eave once a year

effects.log: You climb each year, on that dawn, and say nothing. Some years there is a second shadow on the eave beside yours.

events.text: Your first full council as head of {b3_order} opens with a prayer that has not been changed in four thousand years and includes a line about the speaker being unworthy. All the elders say it. You, now the head, are asked to say it first. The line sticks a little in your throat.

effects.log: The council murmurs. It is the sort of thing that is not forgotten, and it makes you, a little, unworthy in a way that does you good.
You say "tireless" for "unworthy". The council hesitates, and then, in a ripple, a few of the elders repeat it your way. A custom is bending.

events.text: A line of petitioners waits outside the new head's door: those who want a favour, a post, a blessing, or a grudge forgiven. Their spokesman, a small, practised, charming immortal, has prepared a speech of welcome of nineteen verses. You have six minutes before the next meeting.

effects.log: They are, to your surprise, quite good. The speaker is very touched. You are late, and entirely unrepentant.

choices.text: Cut in at the ninth with a warm "thank you"

effects.log: The speaker beams. "He has heard enough," they murmur to the next. They are right, and you wonder how they knew.

events.text: There is a portrait of every head of {b3_order} in the Long Gallery, and they are all in the same pose, and the painters are all the same family. They arrive with their brushes the week you become head. The eldest asks, with great delicacy, which of three poses you would care to be shown in: stern, serene, or, they add, "something of your own".

effects.log: You sit as you sit. The portrait that results is the only one in the gallery in which anyone appears to be about to speak.
The portrait is a success in the way a mountain is. For centuries it will be the one that visitors say they find restful.

events.text: You take the seat, and the order's oldest apprentice, who has never spoken to a head, asks a question in the corridor: "Is it true you can end my apprenticeship any time you like?" It is. You can. The apprentice is not asking for it. The apprentice wants to know, in an even, brave way, what it feels like to hold a thing like that.

effects.log: You say it feels like carrying a full cup through a crowd. The apprentice nods. They will remember this answer for the rest of their life and grow up a little better for it.

choices.text: Promise never to use it carelessly

effects.log: The apprentice bows, deeply, and takes a long time to straighten. You will keep that promise a good deal longer than you thought you could.

events.text: You hold the seat of {b3_order} for nine days before the first assassination attempt, which is delivered by a courteous junior in the form of a poisoned pastry and a very long apology. You are, it turns out, not their target. The pastry was meant for {b3_oldhead}, and the junior simply forgot who had changed.

choices.text: Accept the apology and burn the pastry

effects.log: The junior weeps with relief. The plot, whoever planned it, is quietly dropped. You are credited with mercy and a good nose.
It takes a month. The trail leads to a disgruntled kitchen, a mislaid recipe, and, at the very end, a quarrel that is easily settled.

events.text: A quarrel in {b3_order} over precedence: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} each claim the right to enter the great hall first at the autumn rite. The matter has gone back four thousand years and involves a ceremonial umbrella. Both are polite. Both have, quietly, been avoiding each other's doors for a decade.

effects.log: They go in side by side, a little stiff, each privately sure of having won. The hall approves. You are remembered.
The elder enters first with a small, grave nod. {b3_peer} bows to cover a flinch. Precedence is a very exact kind of memory.
The quarrel runs on, with the umbrella, for another century. You are neither thanked nor blamed.

events.text: {b3_peer} brings you a complaint: {b3_elder} has been quietly moving the order's array stones one hand-breadth to the left each decade, "to see if anyone notices". After two thousand years the whole protective array stands a foot askew. {b3_elder} says it is a test of vigilance. It is also, undeniably, working.

effects.log: The elder agrees, with immense dignity, and spends a decade doing it, one hand-breadth at a time, to see if you notice.
The array holds. {b3_peer} is not pleased, and writes a stiff, correct memorandum for the file.
The order is delighted to have a scandal. {b3_elder} takes it with a wry smile and sends you a very small, very sharp stone.

events.text: The great quarrel of this century in {b3_order}: whether the east hall may be rebuilt in the new style, with windows. {b3_elder} favours windows. {b3_peer} holds that a hall without windows is a hall without distractions. The meeting has lasted six days. It has not yet reached the question of the doors.

effects.log: It is accepted, to general discontent and some relief. The east hall has, to this day, one window, and everyone argues about it.
The hall is rebuilt with windows. {b3_peer} sits in the new light and, to everyone's surprise, begins to write verse.
The hall stays dark. {b3_elder} grumbles for a hundred years and then, secretly, paints a window on the wall.

events.text: {b3_elder} has accused {b3_peer} of stealing a technique. {b3_peer} says they invented it independently. Both have, it turns out, got the same technique from the same dead master, who taught both in confidence and swore each to secrecy. Both are telling the truth. The master left no note.

effects.log: The room is silent. Then, to your great surprise, they both laugh. The quarrel dissolves into a long, stunned dinner.

choices.text: Let the dispute run and benefit from the rivalry

effects.log: Two rivals spend a century refining the technique to spite each other. The order has never been so formidable. Nobody is happy.
Both complain, then both quietly go off and reinvent it in secret. It is the order's most productive decade.

events.text: Over the budget of spirit stones for the new peak, {b3_elder} wants a library and {b3_peer} wants a training ground. There is stone enough for one. Each has a following, a speech, and a string of precedents. The accounts clerk, who is the only person who actually knows the sums, has asked to be excused from the discussion and gone to lie down.

effects.log: {b3_peer} accepts it, stiffly, and files a note. The library is a triumph. The training ground is built by volunteers in a year.
The ground is built, and the library sulks in a corner of the sky for twenty years until somebody quietly donates the shelves.
Half a library and half a ground. Both are useless for a decade and then, strangely, are used together, and are very fine.

events.text: A question of tea. The order's ceremonial tea is made by {b3_elder}'s method, which takes eleven hours, or by {b3_peer}'s, which takes forty minutes and is, frankly, better. The old way is a tradition. The new way is a scandal. Guests have been polite about the eleven-hour tea for centuries and have lately begun to refuse.

effects.log: You drink both, one after the other, and pronounce them equal. The hall is outraged by the diplomacy. Everyone, in private, is relieved.
The old way survives. {b3_elder} is vindicated, and brings you a small cup of the good stuff in a private moment, with a conspiratorial wink.

choices.text: Quietly switch to the forty minutes

effects.log: Nobody notices for two years. Then the elder notices, and says nothing, and drinks it every day with a face of perfect stone.

events.text: {b3_peer} and {b3_elder} each want to take the same promising young disciple. The young disciple, hearing of it, has fled to the roof and will not come down until the matter is settled. A small, thin, determined figure in the rain. Two elders stand below, calling in dueling voices.

choices.text: Go up and ask what the disciple wants

effects.log: The disciple wants to learn from both, a little, and neither, entirely. You arrange it. The disciple comes down, damp, with a very faint smile.

choices.text: Order the disciple down and assign them

effects.log: It is done by authority and the disciple resents it for ten years. The disciple is also, in time, extraordinary.

choices.text: Leave them all in the rain

effects.log: It ends by the evening, unsettled, when someone brings an umbrella. Nobody remembers who.

events.text: An old feud in {b3_order} reaches your desk: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have not spoken since a banquet nine hundred years ago, when one of them sat on the other's hat. Nobody remembers whose hat. Both insist on a formal apology from the other. Neither, it turns out, has been the offender, and the hat is still in a drawer in the archive.

choices.text: Bring the hat to them, together

effects.log: It is a very small, very old, flattened hat. They look at it. The silence is heavy and then someone laughs, and then they cannot stop.
The feud lingers, without its evidence, for a century. It becomes lore, which is worse and also more fun.

choices.text: Hold it over them for later

effects.log: You keep the hat as leverage. It is never used, and you feel, whenever you open the drawer, slightly dishonourable.

events.text: {b3_elder} proposes that {b3_order} should open its gates to disciples of low birth: rogues, wanderers, the unbacked. {b3_peer} is appalled. It is an old question, and one that has divided the order for three thousand years. Both come to you, separately, in the night, with candles, and each swears the other is the danger.

effects.log: You admit a handful of the unbacked each decade. Within a century two of them are among the order's best.

choices.text: Keep the gates as they are

effects.log: Nothing changes. {b3_peer} is relieved. {b3_elder} writes, with cold fury, a very good essay on the subject.
The order floods with strays. Half leave, half stay, all are noisy. Old halls hum with new quarrels, and it is, finally, alive.

events.text: The sword-hall of {b3_order} and its alchemy-hall have a long, dignified war over the use of the shared courtyard on the fourth day of the month. {b3_elder} brings a duel schedule. {b3_peer} brings a cauldron. By midday the courtyard contains both a duel and a small, tasteful explosion.

effects.log: A schedule is drawn. It is violated within a week, and thereafter honoured in the breach, which is, you are told, the best way for an order to be at peace.

choices.text: Give the courtyard to the swords

effects.log: The alchemists take their cauldrons to the roof. The roof, after a decade, is the best-appointed laboratory in the isles.
The swordsmen take their duels to the sky, where, for reasons of gravity, they get on much better.

events.text: {b3_peer} brings word that {b3_elder} has taken on, in secret, an apprentice from a rival order. {b3_elder}, summoned, admits it. "I needed someone to argue with," they say. "You people all agree with me." It is the most disarming answer you have heard. The order, is, however, still bound to rule.

effects.log: The apprentice stays, quietly spies for nobody, and ends the century as the best friend of everyone in the hall.
The apprentice goes with great dignity. {b3_elder} is silent for a year, and then, quietly, takes another.
The order is scandalised, and then charmed. The rival order sends a very stiff letter, and then a gift.

events.text: There is a dispute over a signature. A scroll of the order is signed by a head who died long ago, in ink that is, impossibly, fresh. {b3_elder} says it is a forgery. {b3_peer} says it is a sign. The scroll, when examined, appears to be correct. It simply disagrees with {b3_elder} on a point of law.

effects.log: The order rearranges itself around the dead head's new opinion. It is the most peaceful reform of the century. Nobody knows who benefited.
{b3_elder} is vindicated. The scroll, locked in a case, continues to dry with the slow sound of a patient fingernail.
The scroll sits on a table in the hall, and everyone reads it, and nobody acts on it. It is now a monument.

events.text: {b3_peer} wants to send a delegation to the Isle League's great council. {b3_elder} thinks it is beneath the dignity of the order. Both submit written memorials. {b3_elder}'s is eleven scrolls, bound in silk. {b3_peer}'s is a single sheet with a drawing of a sad-looking duck. It is, on the whole, more persuasive.

effects.log: The order is represented, fairly well. At the council the duck is mentioned, and is received with respectful chuckles.
{b3_elder} is gratified. The delegation does not go. The duck, framed, hangs in the hall of memorials.
They go. They return a month later, exhausted, on terms of grudging, almost warm, respect.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} disagree about the age of the founding hall. One says nine thousand years, the other eleven. They have been conducting competing excavations under the foundation, each digging toward the other, and they will meet, unless stopped, in about a week, beneath the chair of the head.

effects.log: They break through at a quarter past noon. Each looks at the other through a ragged hole. Both burst out laughing. The hall is declared a hundred years older than either claimed.
The proper measure gives ten thousand years. Neither is happy. Both are, secretly, a little relieved.
The foundations are restored. The question remains open. It is, in a way, kinder.

events.text: Two cooks of {b3_order}, followers of {b3_elder} and {b3_peer}, have each declared the other's dumplings an insult to the founders. A faction has formed around each. They sit at opposite ends of the refectory and refuse to pass one another the vinegar. The refectory is dead silent at mealtimes, and the vinegar sits in the middle, unmoved.

choices.text: Eat the dumplings of both, publicly

effects.log: You eat a dozen of each and pronounce them perfect. The refectory gasps, then laughs. The vinegar is passed, with solemn ceremony.
The order, deprived, is united for the first time in a century in resentment of you. Then it has a feast, and forgives.
The standoff continues. The vinegar is eventually, secretly, moved by an apprentice at midnight, and no one admits it.

events.text: A new law is proposed in {b3_order}: no immortal shall cultivate for more than a century without a year of rest. {b3_elder} thinks it a gentle wisdom. {b3_peer} thinks it a threat to the order's greatness. Both have a case. Both are, you notice, quietly exhausted, and arguing from it.

choices.text: Pass it, for a trial period

effects.log: The first rest-year is chaos. By the second, the order is better rested than it has been in a thousand years. {b3_peer} sends a small, graceful concession.
The order works on. {b3_elder}, tired and sad, takes an unofficial year anyway and is not asked about it.
A third of the order rests the first year, a third the second, and the rest never. All three groups are equally sure they are right.

events.text: The order's ancient enemy is dead, and the order has, for the first time in a thousand years, nothing to be angry at. {b3_elder} wants to commemorate the end of the enmity. {b3_peer} wants to find a new enemy. The hall is split. Someone suggests, tentatively, that perhaps the enemy is not dead at all, only quiet.

effects.log: A small, plain ceremony. The order does not know what to do with its hands. By the next season, it has found a hobby.
The order gets a new rival. It is a good one. It is also, you suspect, an excuse.
The silence of the order is oddly loud. It is slowly filled by garden-planting and extremely bad poetry.

events.text: The old and the young of {b3_order} are in open dispute about the morning exercises. {b3_elder} says they should begin at the fourth bell, as always. {b3_peer} says nobody under three hundred can be expected to rise at the fourth bell and the young are all half asleep. The young, consulted, have drawn up a petition in the form of a very long yawn.

choices.text: Move it to the fifth bell

effects.log: The old grumble. The young wake. At the fifth bell the whole hall is, to everyone's surprise, pleasantly alive.
The old are pleased. The young learn, over a decade, to sleep earlier, and grow insufferably virtuous about it.
Chaos for a year. By the second year, the halls have self-sorted into early birds and late ones, who regard each other with great suspicion.

events.text: {b3_elder} makes a formal motion to strike {b3_peer}'s name from the register of the order's heroes, citing "an unfortunate remark", made eight hundred years ago. {b3_peer} makes a formal motion to strike {b3_elder}'s name for "the same remark, repeated, for eight hundred years". The scribe in charge of the register has hidden behind a screen.

effects.log: Both are outraged. Both, privately, are grateful. The scribe emerges, trembling, and is given tea.
The register is lighter by two names. After a century both are quietly put back by different scribes, in different inks, without comment.
It is tabled. The table, a venerable one, acquires a small brass plaque saying "The Remark".

events.text: There is a rumour that {b3_elder} has been selling the order's old tailoring patterns to another faction. {b3_peer} insists on an inquiry. The inquiry finds that the elder has done no such thing and has, instead, been giving them away to everyone, free, with a note, out of sheer love of the patterns. It is, still, technically a breach.

effects.log: The order, a little embarrassed, passes a vote of thanks. {b3_peer} abstains, with a face like a pickled plum.
The elder is told, kindly, to keep to the order. The patterns, however, go on quietly circulating, which is the whole point.
The order sends patterns to all comers, with a seal. Within a century it is the most beloved order of the isles.

events.text: The treasurer of {b3_order} reports a discrepancy: three thousand spirit stones, missing for four hundred years. {b3_elder} accuses {b3_peer}. {b3_peer} accuses the climate. A search of the accounts finds the stones were spent on a wall that was never built, and the wall is found, standing quietly in a valley the order had forgotten it owned.

effects.log: It is, in a way. Visitors come to wonder at it. The accounts balance, and everyone feels slightly foolish and very relieved.

choices.text: Pull the wall down for its stone

effects.log: The stones are recovered, rather smaller. The valley is, thereafter, a good deal bleaker.
Nobody knows. A very old record says "by the grace of the first head." The first head, you are told, simply liked walls.

events.text: {b3_peer} has been given a very good post that {b3_elder} believed should have been theirs. A shy, bitter silence has settled between them. At the next council, {b3_elder} votes against everything {b3_peer} proposes, including a motion to raise the elder's own stipend. It is the most expensive grudge of the year.

effects.log: It is a long, quiet talk. By the end the elder has, grudgingly, begun to be human again. The stipend passes unanimously.
It cools, eventually, over some years. {b3_elder} is left with a rather permanent dryness.
The elder takes it as a confirmation of every dark suspicion. The order's council is, for a time, a very quiet room.

events.text: A quarrel over a bird. {b3_elder} keeps a crane in the order's garden. {b3_peer} has complained, formally and repeatedly, that it screams. It does scream. The crane is eight thousand years old, a founder's gift, and has never been known to like anyone. It likes you.

choices.text: Take the crane for a week

effects.log: The crane follows you through the order like a very tall, very sarcastic shadow. By the end, both elders have forgiven everything.

choices.text: Declare the crane exempt from complaint

effects.log: The crane screams on. The order learns to love it, in the manner of a cracked bell.

choices.text: Move the crane to a distant garden

effects.log: The crane, hurt, stops screaming and begins to stare. The staring is worse.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have each written the official history of the order's greatest battle. The two accounts disagree on who won, who fled, and the colour of the sky. The order is to adopt one. A third scribe, mournful, offers a third version, in which nobody was there and it was all a misunderstanding.

effects.log: It is adopted with great solemnity. It is, historically, the most accurate. Nobody likes it, and everybody uses it.
The order reads a glorious past. {b3_peer} writes another version, in the margins, and calls it a commentary.
The order issues a volume with two columns. It becomes a classic of the genre, and is cited in lawsuits.

events.text: The question of the new hall's name has reached its tenth year. {b3_elder} proposes "Hall of Distant Light". {b3_peer} proposes "Hall of the Southern Door". The mason, who has been waiting a decade to carve the lintel, has quietly started carving "Hall" and has been told to wait.

effects.log: The mason weeps with gratitude. The Hall is a very fine one, and has, for a thousand years, no more name than that, and is the better for it.
The Hall of Distant Light is cut. The south door is never forgiven, and gets a small plaque of its own in the end.
You wait. In time a name arises among the apprentices, rude and perfect. It is carved in small letters under the real one.

events.text: The order is quarrelling about a visiting immortal. {b3_peer} thinks the visitor a spy. {b3_elder} thinks the visitor a saint. The visitor, who has been listening from behind a screen for an hour, emerges and says, mildly, that they are neither, they are merely lost, and could someone tell them the way to the baths.

effects.log: The visitor is a lost scholar of the Silent Dao, and, in return, leaves a very good proof in the guest book. The elders look sheepish.
The visitor is watched for a week and does nothing except bathe, read and, on the last day, thank everyone, very formally. Everyone feels foolish.
The visitor leaves, politely baffled. {b3_peer} is satisfied. A month later a very sharp letter arrives from a distinguished isle.

events.text: One of the order's old treasures, a lamp that never goes out, has gone out. {b3_elder} blames {b3_peer}'s apprentices. {b3_peer} blames {b3_elder}'s oil. An investigation finds that the lamp went out because someone, kindly, filled it with ordinary oil, thinking it had run dry. The lamp was running on something else entirely.

effects.log: The old recipe is found in a forgotten scroll. It requires, among other things, a night's patience and a very small joke. The lamp relights, to a cheer.
A new lamp is bought. It is a fine lamp, and goes out in a decade. The old one is placed in the museum, still dark.
The hall learns to see by other light. It is, strangely, a calmer place.

events.text: At the order's great banquet, {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} give competing toasts. Each is magnificent. Each is longer than the last. Neither will yield the floor. The food is cold. The guests, who have been standing for three hours, have begun, quietly, to sit on the floor and eat the decorations.

effects.log: The hall roars. Both elders sit, laughing, and the banquet resumes with great speed. You are toasted in turn, for ten seconds, by everybody.
The toasts stop. Both elders are insulted. The decorations are, nonetheless, eaten, and are generally agreed to be quite good.
The hall, seeing the head on the floor, decides it is wise. The toasts end in a general muddle, and everyone is happy.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} each hold half of a debt note between {b3_order} and a small isle that lent it stones before either of them was born. Each half is worth nothing alone. Each refuses to give theirs to the other. The isle, meanwhile, is starving politely, and has not asked.

choices.text: Press them to join the halves

effects.log: It takes a month of dinners. At the end they join the halves, grumbling. The note is whole, and nearly comic with the weight of everything it has carried.

choices.text: Pay the isle from your own store

effects.log: The isle is relieved and a little humiliated. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} are both a little ashamed, which is a start.

choices.text: Leave the halves where they are

effects.log: The isle goes on being polite. The notes sit in two drawers, and nobody sleeps well.

events.text: The joined note is read at last: it demands that {b3_order} return not stones but a visit, once a century, by the head, bearing news. The isle has been waiting five thousand years for a visitor. A very small, very old delegation arrives with a dish of dried fish and a rolled-up banner that says WELCOME BACK.

effects.log: You spend a day on the isle. They hang on every word. By dusk you have promised to come again. You will, it turns out, every century for the rest of your life.
The two go, and are treated as ancient friends. They return in an odd, subdued, happier silence, and neither will say anything about it.

events.text: A century later the little isle sends a gift to {b3_order}: a plain, old, smooth stone, and a note: "From those who were listened to." It is set at the entrance of the hall, and visitors are told the story, not as a boast, but as a form of directions.

choices.text: Set the stone at the gate and keep the story

effects.log: The stone becomes the order's oldest custom. New disciples touch it as they enter, and none of them understand why it feels like being forgiven.

choices.text: Write to the isle and say thank you

effects.log: It takes three weeks to write. The letter is plain and warm, and a small, pleased reply returns with a second dish of dried fish.

events.text: {b3_elder} wants the order's great sword, a relic, taken down from its wall and used. {b3_peer} wants it left, as it has always been. The sword has not been drawn in three thousand years. It has, the sword-keeper whispers, started to hum.

effects.log: The sword comes out with a sound like a held note, and shines. {b3_elder} holds it a moment, and puts it back with trembling hands. Nobody speaks.
{b3_peer} is relieved. The sword hums more softly, as if consoled. It keeps humming, quietly, for years.

events.text: The sword of {b3_order} has begun to sing aloud, a little, at night. The order is divided about what it wants. {b3_elder} thinks it wants a wielder. {b3_peer} thinks it wants silence. The sword-keeper, hollow-eyed, sleeps in the hall with a pillow over their head.

choices.text: Offer it to someone who asks

effects.log: A very young disciple, unprompted, asks to hold it. The sword goes quiet at once, as if somebody had come home. The elders watch, stunned.

choices.text: Place it in the vault, wrapped in cloth

effects.log: The singing dulls to a mutter. The order, rather unhappily, goes back to sleep. It is a very bad omen and everyone knows it.

events.text: Years on, the young disciple who held the sword of {b3_order} stands in the great hall to be named bearer. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} are both present and, for once, agree. The sword is placed in a plain scabbard. It hums, softly, a note the whole hall recognises as a welcome.

choices.text: Name the disciple bearer, with full honour

effects.log: The hall rises. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} shake hands at last, over the sword, and everyone pretends not to see.

choices.text: Name the disciple bearer, and say little

effects.log: It is done plainly. The sword approves. The disciple, trembling, says only "thank you", which is exactly right.

events.text: A rumour has gone through {b3_order} that {b3_elder} is preparing to challenge for the seat, and that {b3_peer} is preparing to support the challenge. No one knows who began it. Both deny it with identical coolness. Both, you notice, have recently started eating breakfast together.

effects.log: They are polite, evasive, and say that it is entirely untrue. It is, you will learn, nine parts true. You have, at least, said it aloud.
You watch. It is a long, quiet, careful year. The air in the hall is like the air before a tea ceremony.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} request a private audience with you, on the night of the new moon. They come together, in plain robes, with no retinue. They do not mention the seat. They want, they say, to ask your advice on how to be a good elder. It is the oddest challenge you have ever received.

effects.log: You tell them what you wish someone had told you. It takes an hour. They listen. They leave, thoughtful, with the manner of those who have been disarmed on purpose.

choices.text: Suspect a trap and say little

effects.log: You answer in two sentences. They thank you with the faint courtesy of people who expected it. The air stays tight.

events.text: The rumour of succession in {b3_order} comes to its natural end: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} announce, at a gathering, that they intend to retire together to a small isle and write a very long book on the proper manner of tea. They hope you will not take it amiss.

choices.text: Bless the plan with all your heart

effects.log: You laugh, and weep, a very little. They leave on a plain, small skiff, waving. The book is begun that night.

choices.text: Ask them to stay on a little longer

effects.log: They agree. They write the book in the margins of council minutes, and it is, in the end, the best thing the order ever published.

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have been writing each other furious letters for a hundred years, by courier, though they live in adjacent halls. The couriers have grown old and are due to retire. The letters, it emerges, are the only reason the two still talk. Nobody in the order has told them.

effects.log: You carry three letters in a week. Each is a masterpiece of ferocity and an unmistakable love-letter to being understood.
The letters stop. After a month both elders are visibly lost. A new, shy courier is hired in the nick of time.

events.text: The letters between {b3_elder} and {b3_peer}, carried by you, have changed in tone. They are still furious, but now, between the insults, there are small enquiries after each other's health. Neither seems to have noticed. You find yourself holding your breath at the doors.

effects.log: The letters continue, warming by degrees. You are the quiet witness of a very odd friendship, and it is the best thing you do all decade.
They are mortified, and for a month stop writing. Then they begin again, with great care, and the letters are, if anything, better.

events.text: {b3_elder} has died, or gone away beyond writing, and {b3_peer} comes to you with a last, unsent letter, and asks you to deliver it to a hall that is no longer anybody's. You walk to the empty hall, in the dusk, and leave it on the desk, among the dust. Something in the air seems to answer.

choices.text: Leave it and say a few words aloud

effects.log: You say the elder's name. A faint, warm draught stirs the paper. It is a very small, very exact kind of peace.

choices.text: Bring it back and read it to {b3_peer}

effects.log: The letter says only "I was never angry. Only afraid I would be forgotten." {b3_peer} sits a long while without moving.

events.text: In the great hall of {b3_order}, {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have been reduced, by the third hour of debate, to reciting the same sentence at each other with increasing volume. The sentence is "That is not how it was done." The hall is now a place of great, cheerful noise.

effects.log: The hall empties with relief. In the morning both elders agree it was probably a misunderstanding, and no one can say what.
It does not come. By the sixth hour you are the last person awake, and you have begun to agree with both.
The hall freezes. Then, after a long moment, begins to laugh. The debate resumes at a lower pitch.

events.text: A student of {b3_order} has accused both {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} of the same fault: teaching only what they themselves can do. Both are outraged. Both are right. The student, a small stubborn person, has refused to retract, and has been placed in a room alone with a book on the subject.

effects.log: The student, vindicated, is dazed. Both elders sulk for a year, and then, very quietly, change the way they teach.
The student is gently corrected. The elders feel a little smug and a little unworthy, and the student remembers it forever.

choices.text: Make the student a teacher for a season

effects.log: The student, horrified, discovers that teaching is the hardest thing in the world. They come out very polite and very sure.

events.text: A long-lost banner of {b3_order} is returned by a traveller who found it wrapped round a goat. {b3_elder} says it must be hung in the main hall. {b3_peer} says it should be burned for the shame of having been lost. The goat, which has accompanied the traveller and sits calmly in the courtyard, has no view.

effects.log: It hangs, with a faint, honourable smell. Visitors comment on it. The goat is given a small post in the garden.

choices.text: Burn it in a quiet rite

effects.log: The ashes are scattered. {b3_peer} is satisfied. The goat, fed, wanders off, unconcerned.

choices.text: Keep it in the vault, folded

effects.log: It is never seen again. The goat is occasionally mentioned. The debate is, on the whole, forgotten.

events.text: {b3_elder} wants a statue of the order's founder. {b3_peer} points out that nobody knows what the founder looked like. {b3_elder} says that is an excellent reason to have one, since then nobody can argue. A sculptor has been hired. The sculptor, privately, asks you what the founder was like. You do not know either.

choices.text: Tell the sculptor to make it up kindly

effects.log: The statue is a handsome, thoughtful, vaguely amused figure. It becomes, in a century, exactly what the founder looked like.
{b3_elder} is wounded. {b3_peer} is smug. The sculptor goes home, with a good fee and a faint sense of anticlimax.

choices.text: Commission a statue with a blank face

effects.log: The faceless statue is a sensation. Each disciple sees a different founder in it. It is, strangely, a great comfort.

events.text: There is a dispute about who may serve the order's ceremonial wine. {b3_elder} says the post belongs to the eldest. {b3_peer} says it belongs to the best. The wine is, for the first time in recorded history, going warm. A servant stands holding the jug, with the particular stillness of someone being quietly reasonable.

effects.log: You pour for a hall of old, offended immortals. It is the most humbling hour of your year, and the best-received speech you never gave.

choices.text: Give the post to the servant

effects.log: The servant, astonished, pours. The wine is cold. Nobody says a word. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} drink, and have, at last, nothing to say.
The lot falls on a very young disciple, who drops the jug. The ensuing silence is somehow a kind of unity.

events.text: The order's highest peak is to be re-roofed. {b3_elder} wants tile. {b3_peer} wants thatch. A third party suggests jade. All three quote precedents. The peak has been, for the duration, leaking onto the head of an elderly sage, who sits under a bucket and refuses to move until a decision is made.

choices.text: Choose tile and cover the sage

effects.log: The roof is tiled. The sage, dry, thanks you in a voice like old paper, and does not leave the peak for another century.
{b3_peer}'s thatch is warm and quiet. The sage, now dry, begins to write poems about rain.
It is an absurd, glorious roof. The sage, under jade, is silent for a year, and then says it is too bright to think.

events.text: It is discovered that {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} are the two best players of the order's old board game, and that they have been losing to each other deliberately for five hundred years, each to spare the other's feelings. Both are tired. Both are too polite to say so. The next game is scheduled for tomorrow.

effects.log: Each, told, goes pale, then laughs. They play the next game in earnest, with fury and joy. It lasts a week. Nobody wins. It is perfect.

choices.text: Say nothing and let it go on

effects.log: It goes on. The two, in a lifetime, never learn. It is either tragic or beautiful, and you have, on balance, decided it is the second.

choices.text: Rig the board so one must win

effects.log: The game ends. The winner is dazed, the loser is relieved, and neither forgives you for a decade.

events.text: A courier of {b3_order} brings a letter from another isle that says only: "Which of your two elders is the sane one?" It is unsigned. It is, you think, a joke. It is also, you think, a genuine question from someone who is about to make a decision based on the answer. {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have both noticed you reading.

effects.log: The reply, a week later, is a single line: "Good. Then we will treat with the pair." It is a diplomatic triumph that nobody understands.
{b3_peer} learns of it, as everyone does. The next council is very quiet.

choices.text: Say neither, and invite the writer

effects.log: The writer arrives, a month later, and is revealed as a very ordinary, very shy immortal who just wished to meet them.

events.text: The table of {b3_kin} is long and low, and strength is the only etiquette. You are seated at the end, near the draught. The head of the house, a vast, patient figure, asks you a single question: "What do you want?" The whole table waits. It is not a rhetorical question. They have all been asked it, once.

effects.log: The table nods. They approve of the honesty and disapprove of the shortness. A plate of something dark and good is set before you.
A pause, then a rumble that may be laughter. "Not here," says the head. "But we will leave you alone about it."

choices.text: Say you want to know what they want

effects.log: The head looks at you for a long time. "That," they say, "is a different, better question." The table rearranges itself slightly around you.

events.text: In the Courts of the Demon Dukes, a challenge may be issued over soup. One of the {b3_kin} duellists, a cheerful brute with a very small spoon, has challenged you to a match, in the old style, at dawn, on the sunniest balcony. They are very polite about it. They have apologised twice for the early hour.

ok.log: You win, narrowly, to a roar. The brute is delighted, and brings you tea, and you are, for the first time, treated as kin.

fail.log: You are beaten, thoroughly and cheerfully. The brute helps you up and apologises again, which is somehow worse. You are, nevertheless, respected.

effects.log: The brute shrugs. "Next year." The refusal is accepted, noted, and filed under something a little like "interesting".

events.text: A young demon of {b3_kin} is brought before you for judgement: they have lost a duel and, out of shame, have refused to eat. The old rule says the weak go hungry. The young demon looks at you with an expression of enormous, theatrical suffering. Everyone in the hall is pretending not to watch.

effects.log: You send a bowl. The hall is silent, then a grunt of approval. The young demon eats like a hurricane and is, after that, strangely loyal.

choices.text: Let the rule stand, for a day

effects.log: The young demon fasts, and fights again, and wins. It is the most efficient lesson of the year. You feel, though, a little cold.

choices.text: Challenge them to a rematch, on a full stomach

effects.log: The match is long and good. The young demon loses well. A grudging respect is born, and a very large dinner.

events.text: {b3_kin} keeps an old, fierce custom: on the founder's day, each member must tell the house one thing they are afraid of. It is considered the highest honour of the year. The house waits, with the stillness of a pack at a fire. It is your turn, and you are, you find, quite genuinely afraid.

effects.log: You say what you fear. A very old, very large demon nods and says, "Yes. That one. Everyone has that one." You are, by the end, a member.
The house knows. Nobody says so. Your answer is received with a faintly pitying courtesy, and a small gift of something sharp and honest.

choices.text: Name an enemy instead of a fear

effects.log: A low rumble of approval. They admire the evasion, and you, a little, for it.

events.text: The cook of {b3_kin} produces a dish that everyone swears is the best they have ever tasted, and that nobody can eat more than one spoonful of, because it is also the hottest thing in the isles. You are served a full bowl. The whole table watches, with the focus of a congregation.

ok.log: You finish the bowl, weeping, in perfect silence. The table erupts. You have, in the opinion of the house, become something like family.

fail.log: You manage three spoonfuls and fall over. The table laughs until it must lie down. You are, regardless, adored.

choices.text: Eat half and say it is perfect

effects.log: The table, struck, goes quiet, and then approves. A half-bowl, honestly eaten, is better than a full bowl faked.

events.text: A duke of {b3_kin} summons you at midnight for a talk. It is long, and low, and consists mostly of silence. At the end the duke says: "You are not like us. Why do you stay?" You have, you notice, not decided yet. The candles are low. The question is not a trap. It is, perhaps, the kindest thing anyone has asked you here.

choices.text: Say you stay because it is honest

effects.log: The duke considers. "It is. It is also cruel. Both." They nod. It is the nearest thing to approval the house offers.

choices.text: Say you stay for the people

effects.log: The duke looks, for a moment, almost young. "Then you are one of us after all," they say. It is a compliment of a terrible, warm kind.
The duke nods. "Good. The sure ones die first." They pour you a cup of something black and sweet.

events.text: It is the night of the Duelling Feast of {b3_kin}, and the entertainment is a ritual brawl, performed with a great deal of noise and no malice, in which every member is knocked down once. You have been told you will be knocked down by someone whose name you do not know, and that you must, on no account, get up too fast.

effects.log: You are knocked down by a very small, very old demoness, with a flick of the wrist. The hall cheers. You lie there, and the ceiling is surprisingly beautiful.

choices.text: Resist, and be knocked down harder

effects.log: The old one lets you try, and then does it again, harder. You are grateful for the lesson and quite unable to move.

events.text: A rival house of the Demon Dukes sends a challenge to {b3_kin}: a game of the old sort, played with real pieces and a very long table. You have been picked as {b3_kin}'s champion, on the grounds, the head says, that you are "the only one of us they will not expect to be subtle". The pieces are real. The game lasts a week.

ok.log: You win by a hair, in the last hour, with a move so plain nobody saw it. The rival house toasts you, bitterly and sincerely.

fail.log: You lose by a hair, in the last hour, to a move so plain you never saw it. {b3_kin} thanks you gravely, and says it was the best defeat in forty years.

effects.log: The board is left standing, unfinished, as a monument to a very odd kind of friendship between houses.

events.text: The oldest member of {b3_kin}, a withered demon so ancient that they are mostly a voice, asks to speak to you alone. The voice says: "I was strong once. Now I am only remembered. It is more than I thought possible. Do not become strong for its own benefit. Become remembered." The voice falls silent, and the candle gutters.

choices.text: Ask what they wish to be remembered for

effects.log: A long silence. "For being kind to a very small demon, once, in a storm." You are the only one who ever asks. You remember it.
You leave, thoughtful. The words stay, and in a hundred years you find them wedged in a decision like a stone in a shoe.

events.text: A messenger from another faction comes to {b3_kin} under a flag of truce, bearing a request that is unwelcome: the return of a certain relic, taken three thousand years ago in a war. The head looks at you. "You are the one who reads their scrolls. What does the truce flag mean in their tongue?" You do know. It is not what the messenger claims.

effects.log: The messenger, exposed, goes white. The head, to everyone's surprise, does not strike. "Let them go home," says the head. "They were honest in the end." You have earned a quiet kind of loyalty.

choices.text: Say nothing and watch the head decide

effects.log: The head decides unaided, and well, and later says, "Next time, tell me." You are a little ashamed, and a little proud.

events.text: A child of a rival house has been sent to {b3_kin} as a hostage, to live under its roof for a century. It is the old way. The child is perhaps three hundred years old, thin, furious, and unwilling to eat. You are assigned to look after them. Nobody says "look after". The word used is "watch".
events.arc: The Hostage of the Ash Court

choices.text: Feed the child and say nothing

effects.log: It takes a month. Eventually the child eats, scowling, and says nothing. A bowl is left outside your door, empty, the next morning, which is a thank-you.
The child is watched, and fed, and not spoken to. It is correct. It is also, you feel, a small crime against nobody in particular.

events.text: The hostage of {b3_kin} has begun to follow you everywhere. They have a very small knife, and an even smaller grudge, and they are teaching themselves, from watching you, the way the house fights. It is flattering. It is alarming. The hostage is, you realise, a very good student.
events.arc: The Hostage of the Ash Court

effects.log: You teach them a single, honest form. They practise it all winter, in silence, in the courtyard, at four in the morning. It is the loneliest sound you have heard.
The hostage sulks, and becomes in time extremely independent. Whether it is your doing or the house's you cannot say.

events.text: The century of the hostage ends. The rival house sends an escort. {b3_kin} lines the courtyard to see them go. The hostage, grown taller and quieter, stops in front of you and does the single form you taught, once, perfectly. The head of the house, watching, makes a small noise of surprise. Then the hostage is gone.
events.arc: The Hostage of the Ash Court

effects.log: You bow. The courtyard is silent. For a hundred years afterward the two houses are, if not friends, at least a pair of neighbours who nod.
Your voice carries. The hostage does not turn. But the escort, a little confused, slows. They will remember.

events.text: A member of {b3_kin} has fallen in debt to the Iron Court, and the debt is in the old coin: a service, to be named at the time of collection. They have asked you to stand surety. It is a large honour. It is also, you know, a very real danger. The debtor is looking at the floor with great dignity.
events.arc: The Debt of the Iron Court

effects.log: You sign with a drop of something that is not ink. The debtor weeps, a little, without moving a muscle. You are bound.
The debtor nods, as one who expected it. They are not angry. In the morning they are gone, and you do not hear what became of them.

events.text: The Iron Court names its price. It is a service you are to perform: carry a sealed box to the far edge of the isles, and open it only there. The box is warm. It is very light. The debtor, whose debt you stand for, has asked, in a whisper, that you do not ask what is in it.
events.arc: The Debt of the Iron Court

choices.text: Carry it, and do not open it

effects.log: You carry it, a long, quiet journey. At the far edge you open it. It is a single small seed. The Court wanted a tree planted, somewhere no one would find it.
It is a single small seed, and the moment you look, the box goes cold. The Court, you are told, is not pleased, but it is not very angry either.

events.text: Years pass. The seed you planted at the edge of the isles has grown into a tall, quiet tree, and under it a small crowd of the Iron Court is gathered, in plain robes, on a day of remembrance. The debtor is there, grown very old, and sees you. The debtor does not speak. The debtor raises a cup.
events.arc: The Debt of the Iron Court

effects.log: You drink. The tree rustles. The Court, which does not forgive, nods once. Your name is struck from every ledger of debt it keeps.

choices.text: Sit under the tree a while

effects.log: You sit. It is a very good tree. The leaves turn slowly, and for an hour nobody wants anything of you.

events.text: In {b3_kin}, a rite of passage is held at the cliff's edge: a member steps off and must be caught by the kin who trust them. You have been asked to step off. The cliff is very high, the sea of clouds white and quiet. A line of kin, eleven strong, stands below on the narrow ledge.

ok.log: You step into the white. Eleven hands catch you in a heap of laughter and bad language. You are, now, entirely one of them.

fail.log: You hesitate, and the line, politely, waits. After a long time you step off, late, and are caught anyway. They say nothing of it, and it is deeply kind.

choices.text: Ask to catch someone else first

effects.log: The kin are surprised, then pleased. You catch a young one, who is delighted, and then you step off, and are caught in turn.

events.text: A banquet of {b3_kin}: the dishes arrive in order of the rank of the diner, and yours arrives last. It is a bowl of plain rice. Across the table a very grand demon, who has been eyeing you, slides an entire roast fish down the board with a single, magnificent shove and says: "Eat. I do not like to see anybody hungry. It is bad for the house."

effects.log: You send half onward. It makes a small, surprising chain of generosity, down the board to a very young demon who eats it with a look of pure astonishment.
The grand demon nods, satisfied. At the end of the meal a servant brings you a pair of silver chopsticks, quietly, as a mark of notice.

events.text: A very old law of {b3_kin} says that any member may demand of the head an answer to one question, once in a lifetime, and that the answer will be true. Nobody has ever used it. You have, you realise, the right, and one question. The whole house, who have heard you have remembered, sits very still.

choices.text: Ask what the house is for

effects.log: The head thinks for a long time. "So that nobody has to be alone with being strong," they say. It is the truest thing you have been told in years.
A long hush. The head says a name. It is not what you expected, and it changes how you see the next five centuries.
The house is relieved, and impressed. A question unasked is a kind of trust. You are, quietly, the most respected member of the year.

events.text: A small demon of {b3_kin}, a runner, comes to your door with a dreadful secret: they have overheard the head planning to break a treaty. The runner is shaking. They are asking, with great courage, for advice. They are perhaps a hundred and fifty years old. This is the largest thing that has ever happened to them.

effects.log: The runner nods and goes, and does not forget. In a decade they will be a very quiet, very watchful member of the house, and you will wonder what you did.

choices.text: Tell them you will handle it

effects.log: You go to the head. It is a long, careful, difficult talk. The treaty holds. The runner, who never learns how, feels simply that the world was kinder than feared.

choices.text: Tell them to speak to the head themselves

effects.log: The runner, trembling, goes. They are heard. The head, struck by the courage, delays the plan. It is a good day for runners.

events.text: It is the Year of the Silent Table in {b3_kin}: for twelve months no member may speak at a meal. Everything is done by gesture. The result is a year of astonishing, wordless comedy: jars passed with raised eyebrows, entire quarrels conducted in the angle of a ladle. You discover you are, helplessly, quite good at it.

effects.log: The house learns to watch you at meals. By the year's end you can end a quarrel with a single, perfectly timed pause. It is a rare gift.
You see the whole house in a year as you could not in ten of talk. It is a revelation, and a small, odd mercy.

events.text: A very young duchess of a kindred house visits {b3_kin} on a state visit, and, being young, is bored, and demands to see a real duel. The head looks at you. "Show her something," says the head. It is a very honourable thing to be asked, and a very foolish one to be asked in front of such an audience. She is watching, with a look of grave, bright hunger.

ok.log: You fight a short, fierce, careful bout. The duchess claps once, loudly, and says it was the best she has seen. It is, you suspect, the only one she has.

fail.log: You are beaten in four moves, cleanly. The duchess says it was very instructive, and she means it, and she is not unkind.

choices.text: Offer a demonstration, not a duel

effects.log: You show her a slow, graceful form. She watches, rapt. At the end she asks to be taught. The head allows it, with a very faint smile.

events.text: On the day of the Great Silence, {b3_kin} stops everything for an hour in memory of its dead. It is the one time the house does not boast. You stand in the central courtyard among the stones, and the old ones murmur names, and your own, you notice, is not among them, yet. The air has the weight of a held hand.

choices.text: Say a name of your own dead

effects.log: You say it, softly. The courtyard, which has heard nothing but its own for centuries, listens. A very old demon takes your hand, briefly, and lets go.
You stand. It is simply the hour, and the stones, and the quiet. When it ends, you find your cheeks wet, and nobody mentions it.

events.text: The head of {b3_kin} has a pet, which is a very large, very old, very bad-tempered cloud-beast that is permitted to sleep on any bed it likes. It has chosen yours. It is a hundred times your weight. It is snoring. The head, hearing, says with something like pride: "It has never done that for a guest."

effects.log: You sleep on one corner of your own bed, and are woken in the morning by a warm, immense, patient sigh. The beast has decided you will do.

choices.text: Get up and sleep on the floor

effects.log: You sleep on the floor. In the morning the beast, rising, gives you a thoughtful look, and leaves a small, tidy heap of cloud for you by way of an apology.

events.text: The house of {b3_kin} has one great fear: that its strength will be taken from it, one day, by a gentle thing. A visiting preacher of peace arrives at the gate, unarmed, in a plain robe, and asks for shelter. The house watches you. You are the only one who has ever been, by their reckoning, the least bit gentle.

effects.log: The preacher is fed, and says little. In the morning the preacher leaves, and nothing at all has changed, and the house is, a little, reassured and a little unsettled.
The preacher goes, calm. The house nods. It has, in its own view, been defended. You feel a small cold weight, like a stone in the pocket.

choices.text: Talk with the preacher at the gate

effects.log: It is a long talk and a good one. You part as strangers who understand each other. The house, watching, is nonplussed.

events.text: The first morning at {b3_acad} the bell does not ring. A tutor explains that it rings only for the late, and since nobody has ever been late, it has been unused for four hundred years. The class looks at the bell. The bell, you swear, looks back.

effects.log: You are three breaths late. The bell rings, to great and rusty astonishment, and the tutor writes your name on a plaque that is now your seat.
The bell is oiled and rung twice for ceremony. The tutor says you have an instinct for institutions, which is not a compliment, quite.

events.text: The tutor of {b3_acad} sets one question for the whole year: why do the isles float? Students turn in treatises of three hundred pages. The tutor reads them, weeps once, and gives every student the same mark, a small crescent drawn in red.

choices.text: Argue the isles do not float, the sea sinks

effects.log: The crescent comes back with a tiny question mark beside it. It is the nearest thing to approval the tutor gives.

choices.text: Write one honest page: you do not know

effects.log: The tutor keeps that page and returns the other two hundred and ninety-nine to the pile. You are the only one to graduate that year with a clear head.

events.text: A classmate at {b3_acad}, a thin earnest immortal of two hundred years, asks to copy your notes. Everyone knows the notes are the only thing the academy truly grades, and that copying is both forbidden and the tradition. The classmate does not wish to be caught.

effects.log: They are copied, returned, and quietly improved: the classmate has corrected three of your mistakes. You are somewhat ashamed and very grateful.
It takes the night. At dawn the classmate can do it unaided, and calls you a friend, a word immortals use sparingly.
The classmate nods and goes away. They pass, somehow, and never ask again, and never quite forgive it.

events.text: The dormitory of {b3_acad} is a cloud, and the cloud has moods. On damp days it sulks and your blankets fall through. A senior student hands you a cord, and says to tie yourself to the bed frame before sleeping, with the air of someone confessing something.

effects.log: You rise dry and anchored. The cloud, mollified, gives you the warmest corner for the rest of the year.
You murmur nonsense to the vapour at midnight. It does not answer, but the bed stays up, and a small damp patch in the shape of a smile appears on the wall.

events.text: The Examination of the Third Year at {b3_acad} is oral. The examiner is a hundred-and-forty-year-old crane in spectacles. It asks one question, slowly: "What would you do, if nobody ever asked you to do anything?" Your answer will be written on a scroll and hung.

choices.text: Say you would study the clouds

effects.log: The crane nods and scribbles. Years later a cloud-atlas appears in the library credited, with a modest footnote, to someone with your name.

choices.text: Say you would do nothing, gladly

effects.log: The crane lowers its spectacles and gives you a long look. It scribbles a mark you cannot read, and the scroll goes up with a flourish.

choices.text: Ask the crane the same question

effects.log: The crane stares. Then it laughs, a bark like a door. The examination, unprecedentedly, is adjourned for tea.

events.text: {b3_acad} keeps a library with a floor that is the sky itself. Students move along catwalks of glass. A first-year drops a book through the floor, and the librarian says only, "The sea will return it, in three weeks, and annotated." Nobody can say by whom.

choices.text: Wait for the sea to return it

effects.log: Three weeks later the book is on the doorstep, dry, with a small margin note: "Chapter four is wrong." It is.

choices.text: Drop one of your own books deliberately

effects.log: It returns in three weeks with a note: "Poor, but sincere." You frame it.

events.text: A visiting master of the Jade Void lectures at {b3_acad} on sword theory, and demonstrates by cutting a candle flame in two. The flame, divided, burns. Nobody can say why. The master, flustered, says it is not meant to do that, and the class applauds as if it were planned.

effects.log: The master tries; the flame resists. A long night follows with the master and a dozen students, each pretending it is a scheduled lecture.

choices.text: Take a proper note of what happened

effects.log: Your note is the only record. It is quoted in a footnote for the next four hundred years, to your quiet pleasure.

events.text: {b3_acad} has a tradition: in the second year every student must keep a pet spirit alive for a season. Most choose a mild thing, a dew-sprite or a lamp-moth. You are assigned a very small, very bad-tempered thunder-cat. It regards you with enormous disdain.

effects.log: By autumn it sleeps on your sleeve. It still hisses at everyone else, and you are rather proud of that.

choices.text: Hand it to a senior with a gift for animals

effects.log: The senior is delighted and the cat unimpressed. You pass on a technicality, with the senior's warm notes.

events.text: Graduation at {b3_acad} is a quiet affair: each graduate is walked to the edge of the isle and told to step off. The edge is the bridge to the next place, and it is invisible. Three of your year hesitate. The rite requires that you not wait for them.

effects.log: The air takes your weight, an impossible, familiar firmness. You cross without a sound, and look back to see two of the others follow.
The rite frowns. But the three come, one by one, and you are the last across, with a bruised reputation and three friends.

events.text: The head tutor of {b3_acad} stops you in the cloister. "You are cleverer than your marks," they say, "and kinder than your cleverness. Either will get you through a century. Both together are rare, and we are not sure what to do with it." They look genuinely worried.

effects.log: You are given the hardest reading the academy owns, and a seat by the window. You read until the light turns, and then past it.
The tutor smiles, relieved, and finds you an ordinary desk. It is the best thing they ever did for you.

events.text: A rumour at {b3_acad} says that the old well in the courtyard answers a question for anyone who throws in a true coin. You have only false ones. A group of third-years argue about whether a promise counts. The well, listening, makes a small, interested noise.

effects.log: The well gurgles, and a single word floats up on the water, in handwriting you recognise as your own. You do not tell the third-years.

choices.text: Throw in nothing and ask aloud

effects.log: The well, offended, stays silent. The third-years laugh, then fall quiet, because the courtyard shadows have all shifted a little to listen.

events.text: Your study-mate at {b3_acad} is an ancient demon who took up scholarship out of boredom. They have eaten, by their own account, a dozen smaller scholars. They turn pages with great delicacy, and ask whether you would like the last lemon cake.

effects.log: The demon is moved, nearly to tears. For a century afterward, scholars who share a cake with you are treated gently.
The demon admits it was a metaphor, mostly. You spend a pleasant night on the difference between debate and digestion.

events.text: The Dean of {b3_acad} is blind, and reads the faces of the students by touch before each term. Hands upon your face, the Dean frowns, then smiles. "You are tired," says the Dean. "Take the winter off." It is not a punishment. The Dean says so twice.

effects.log: You sleep for most of it. In spring you wake with the sense that something inside you has been tidied.
The Dean nods and withdraws. You do well, and are tired through the spring, and understand in time what you were offered.

events.text: In the lecture hall of {b3_acad}, a student asks a question which the lecturer cannot answer. The hall, silent, waits. The lecturer says: "I will have it for you in forty years." It is not a joke. The hall settles, resigned, to wait.

effects.log: The forty years are noted in the records. When the answer comes, you are one of eleven in the hall, and the lecturer is very old and very glad.
It takes you six years, in odd corners of the library. The lecturer, on being told, goes pale, and then bursts into delighted tears.

events.text: The kitchen of {b3_acad} serves one dish in every season, named for what the cook is trying to forget. This season the dish is "Lamb Without Regret." It is delicious. Nobody asks. The cook watches from the hatch with the blank face of someone not forgetting.

effects.log: The cook nods, once. In winter you find an extra serving on your tray every day without a word.

choices.text: Ask the cook what the regret was

effects.log: The cook tells you, and it is small and stupid and old. You have a friend for the rest of the century.

events.text: A student at {b3_acad} has been caught writing forged marks on their own scrolls. The Dean asks the class to decide the penalty. The forger is a lonely, brilliant person who simply did not believe they could pass. You are the last to speak.

effects.log: The class agrees, narrowly. The forger sits the examination honestly, and passes by the width of a hair.
The class agrees, with relief. The forger goes quietly, and you will meet them again in a worse room.

choices.text: Say the penalty is the Dean's to decide

effects.log: The Dean sighs. It is the correct answer and nobody likes it. The forger gets a month of copying out the library catalogue.

events.text: Two weeks before the term examinations a student of {b3_acad} falls ill and cannot sit them. The students propose to hide this from the examiners and have the sick student's paper written by committee. Your name is, mysteriously, on the committee.

effects.log: The paper is superb. The examiners are not fooled, but say nothing, and the invalid passes by a margin that makes you all feel peculiar.
The examiners are very quiet. The sick student is given a second sitting, and the committee a lecture, and everyone feels the weight of relief.

events.text: {b3_acad} has a ghost, a former Dean who refuses to leave until the library is properly catalogued. It has been catalogued six times. The ghost finds fault each time. The library is now so thorough it is unusable. The ghost is asking for volunteers.

effects.log: You spend a season cataloguing with a ghost. At the end the ghost pronounces it "adequate" and vanishes, leaving a faint warmth and a small book.

choices.text: Suggest the ghost do it itself

effects.log: The ghost, outraged, begins at once. The library is open to students again by autumn, and you are told, stiffly, never to suggest anything again.

events.text: The Founder's Feast at {b3_acad} requires every student to give a toast in a language they do not speak. Yours has been drawn from a hat. It is a dialect of cloud-speech spoken by about eleven beings. One of them is in the room and visibly alarmed.

choices.text: Give the toast as best you can

effects.log: It is a catastrophe of vowels. The eleven-being nods warmly all the way through, and afterwards teaches you the real word for thanks.

choices.text: Ask the speaker to give it for you

effects.log: The speaker is thrilled, and speaks for ten minutes. Nobody understands, and everybody applauds, and the Founder, you suspect, would have wept.

events.text: The Dean of {b3_acad} announces a new rule: students must spend a year of their study at a post away from the isles, drawn by lot. Yours is a lighthouse on a lone rock in the cloud-sea, kept by one very old keeper who does not like visitors.

effects.log: The keeper says nothing for a month, then a great deal for a night. You come back with a notebook of stories and a new way of looking at the horizon.
You take the friend's easy post and the friend takes the lighthouse. The friend writes you a long letter of complaint that is, by the end, a love letter to the place.

events.text: In its third century {b3_acad} suffers the Great Prank, in which every chair in the lecture hall is turned a quarter-turn overnight. It has been done by someone clever and unsupervised. The Dean has a theory. The Dean's theory is you.

effects.log: The Dean sighs, then asks how you did it. By evening the chairs are the new tradition and you have a surprising reputation.

choices.text: Deny it, because you did not

effects.log: The Dean believes you. The true culprit, a small quiet scholar, thanks you for a decade afterwards.
Your enthusiasm is admitted as evidence. The Dean assigns you a punishment: you must turn all the chairs back, slowly, one a day.

events.text: A paper you wrote at {b3_acad} has been found, centuries later, by a young scholar quoting it at the Dean with wild enthusiasm. You do not recall writing it. It argues something you now think quite wrong. The scholar hands you the copy to sign.

choices.text: Sign it and leave it be

effects.log: You sign. The scholar is happy; the error was beautiful and is reproduced for the next five hundred years.

choices.text: Gently explain where it was wrong

effects.log: The scholar listens, pale then brightening, then writes a better paper. The correction is credited to both of you.

events.text: The reading lamp in your room at {b3_acad} is a gift from the previous occupant, long gone. It burns without oil. It has a dent. When you read late it flickers precisely as the pages need to be turned. You have begun to wonder if it can read.

choices.text: Ask the lamp what it thinks

effects.log: The lamp flares and a small, warm glow settles on the page you were stuck on. You never ask again; it seems unkind to make it show off.
The reply takes eight years and is mostly about weather. But it ends: "Look after the lamp. It is quite brilliant and rather shy."

events.text: {b3_acad} stages a debate every spring between the senior students. This year the motion is "That immortals should die." Everyone is a little uncomfortable. You have been drawn for the affirmative. The Dean, front and centre, is over a thousand years old and keeps very still.

choices.text: Argue it with all your heart

effects.log: You argue beautifully. When it ends, the Dean says quietly, "You put it better than I had." You are not sure it was a compliment.
The hall laughs, and the laughter turns, midway, into something else. The motion is lost, and everyone leaves a little lighter.
You say there is no honest case to make in front of such an audience. The Dean closes the debate with obvious gratitude.

events.text: An old teacher of {b3_acad}, long retired, turns up at the gate asking to audit your lectures. They sit in the back with a flask and a notebook, writing everything. After the third week, you realise they are writing down your mistakes. Neat, polite, numbered.

effects.log: It runs to forty-one items. You correct thirty-eight. The teacher promises to return next year, with another flask.

choices.text: Ask them to teach your class

effects.log: The old teacher is first appalled, then delighted. The lecture that follows is remembered for centuries and your name is on the roster.

events.text: Your thesis at {b3_acad} is on the nature of an immortal grudge. Three readers are assigned: one who despises the subject, one who has lived it, one who is the grudge. You do not discover which is which until the viva.

effects.log: The reader who is the grudge cries, a little. You pass with distinction, and are told you must never publish it.
You win every point and lose the room. The thesis is accepted with a sniff, and the room never entirely forgives you.

events.text: The great telescope at {b3_acad} is turned, once a decade, on a single star chosen by lottery. This decade the lot falls on a small sullen star nobody has attended to for ten thousand years. Your turn at the eyepiece comes. The star, you realise, is looking back.

effects.log: You look until your eyes water. What you see goes into no report, but it changes the way you walk across a courtyard for a century.
There is a small answering flicker. The next observer reports it as an instrument fault. You never correct this.

events.text: A new student of {b3_acad}, a young immortal fresh from the low isles, arrives with a patched robe and a head full of questions. They sit next to you on the first day and ask three before the lecture starts. One of the three is the best question you have heard all year.

effects.log: You do. The young one writes it down and scowls at the page, then at you, then, abruptly, grins. You have made an ally.

choices.text: Say you do not know, and ask them to find out

effects.log: They find out in a week. You are quoted for a decade as the teacher who knew when not to know.

events.text: The last week of term at {b3_acad} is Quiet Week. By custom, the students may not speak. A great deal gets said: the glances, the pointing, the passing of tea. By the end you know the entire dormitory better than you have in months, and nobody has said a word.

choices.text: Keep the vow of silence perfectly

effects.log: You come out the other side oddly clear. Words have a lightness they did not before.

choices.text: Cheat, once, with a whispered joke

effects.log: It travels through the whole building at the speed of suppressed laughter. Nobody tells the tutors. It is the best thing that happens that term.

events.text: The Dean of {b3_acad} announces that a student who failed the year-end exam in the Founder's time has, centuries later, been judged to have been right. The academy owes them a diploma. The student is long dead and represented by a descendant who looks mortified.

effects.log: You carry it to a small grave on a distant isle, and read the old answer aloud. It seems, absurdly, to settle something.
You give a short speech to the descendant and an indifferent goat. It is well received by the goat.

events.text: The Gathering of the Isle Young opens with a parade in which every isle in the sea of clouds sends its three best under-three-hundreds. Yours are the ones in the middle, with the frayed ribbons. The crowd cheers them as if they were kin. For this hour, they are.

choices.text: Walk beside them for the first mile

effects.log: You march in the dust of your own pupils, and the crowd does not notice, and the pupils do. It is perfect.
You watch from the terrace with a cup of tea and say nothing, so as not to make a scene. It is nevertheless the right amount of pride.

events.text: Before the first bout at the Gathering, a young immortal from another isle sidles up to your pupil and offers a pill "for nerves". Your pupil looks at you. The offering youth has a sweet, honest, entirely false face. A tutor from the other isle looks at the sky and whistles.

effects.log: Your pupil hands the pill back with great and awful courtesy. The crowd heard. The other isle remembers.

choices.text: Take the pill and have it examined

effects.log: It is a laxative, ingeniously labelled. The other isle is unaccountably quiet at the banquet.

events.text: The Gathering's referee is a sea-turtle the size of a pavilion, who judges by the mood of the crowd. It has judged for six thousand years and has never been wrong, and has never been right, either. Your pupil fights a bout and the turtle rules with a long, complicated sigh.

effects.log: The turtle, grateful, nods. The ruling stands, and your pupil, for once, thinks a long while about fairness.
The turtle takes the appeal with great seriousness, and rules the opposite, equally gravely. The Gathering is entirely delighted.

events.text: A bout at the Gathering ends with both fighters falling off the platform, to the astonishment of the crowd and the fury of the two isles. Nobody is hurt. Both youths stand up laughing, arms about each other, and refuse to be separated by their tutors.

effects.log: The applause rolls round the platform like weather. The tutors give up, and the pair are carried shoulder-high to the feast.
The referee, relieved, grants the draw. It is the first draw in the Gathering in nine hundred years and goes into the records in red.
