events.text: Your pupil is knocked out in the first round of the Gathering by someone they should have beaten. They sit under the tiered seats, face to the wall, and refuse tea. A very old immortal with a broken sword wanders by and sits on the other side of the wall. You hear a long conversation.

effects.log: The conversation ends with a laugh. Your pupil returns for the evening round with a calmer face and a notch in their philosophy.
You sit between them. Nobody speaks. After an hour the old immortal passes you a pickled plum. It is the best medicine you have taken.

events.text: At the Gathering banquet a young immortal sings a ballad about the isles that is quite terrible and extremely heartfelt. The old masters at the head table gaze fixedly at their plates. Your pupil, with great courage, begins to clap in time.

effects.log: Slowly the hall joins. By the third verse the whole banquet is stamping, and the singer weeps, and the old masters admit it is not their worst.
The singer drinks, is revived, begins a second ballad, and you quietly leave to find the cook.

events.text: The prize at the Gathering this decade is "a boon from the Jade Court," which no one has ever collected, as the Court is slow to define boons. Your pupil, who has won it, is handed a sealed scroll and a dubious smile by a clerk. The clerk says: "Do not open it at home."

effects.log: It is a long form with the single line: "Please state your boon." Your pupil asks for a day off, and the Court, to everyone's horror, grants it.
The scroll stays sealed. It becomes a family heirloom and a threat, and its worth is exactly what people believe it to be.

events.text: On the last evening of the Gathering a storytelling contest is held in the great tent. Every isle sends one who tells of the best bout they saw. Your pupil tells the story of the one they lost. The tent is silent, and then it is not.

effects.log: You cheer so loudly that you are shushed. The telling wins the night, and your pupil learns that losing well is a kind of winning.
They find you after, flushed and shy. You tell them the tale was true, and that it is the only kind worth telling.

events.text: A formal complaint is lodged at the Gathering: your isle's pupils have been seen training at night. The rules forbid it. Your pupils say they were stargazing, and that sparring was a coincidence. The judges, who all trained at night themselves, are very solemn.

effects.log: You defend the stargazing with a straight face. The judges, struggling, rule that it is "technically astronomy," and a rule is born.

choices.text: Own it, and promise to teach them better

effects.log: The judges accept, with a suspicious softness. Next year your pupils are the best-rested youths in the Gathering and the most feared.

events.text: Every pupil at the Gathering carries a lantern lit by their own qi. The lanterns grow with each win and gutter with each loss. By the third day yours burns steadily; the isles watch it, glad and envious. A little spirit asks to carry it for a mile.

effects.log: The spirit walks with great gravity, shining in borrowed light. The isles remember, and are kind to your pupil for it.
You walk the mile in the glow, remembering a Gathering from three centuries back, and your own gutter and its rescue.

events.text: At the closing of the Gathering the isles pledge peace for another ten years in the old words, spoken in a dead dialect by the oldest present. This year the oldest is ill and nobody else knows the words. They all look at you, because a friend once taught them to you, long ago.

effects.log: You stumble, but the words come. When it is done, a ripple of agreement passes through the crowd, and the old one smiles from the cot.

choices.text: Ask the old one to prompt you

effects.log: You and the old one speak it together, in a whisper, from the cot. It is the most beautiful pledge anyone remembers.

events.text: A scout from the Demon Realm watches the Gathering from the highest seat, openly, with a large bag of roasted chestnuts. It is a diplomatic courtesy: he may watch if he is seen watching. Your pupil beats a demon youth and, bowing, receives the scout's nod.

choices.text: Offer the scout a seat of honour

effects.log: The scout, blinking, accepts. A century of cold courtesy between your isle and the Realm thaws, a degree, over the chestnuts.

choices.text: Leave the scout to watch alone

effects.log: The scout watches, eats, and leaves. A note arrives afterward in blunt script: "Good pupils. Do not let them be wasted." It is oddly touching.

events.text: The Gathering opens with a moment of silence for those who did not come home from earlier ones. A name is read for every decade. When your isle's name is called, a tall, frail immortal at the back falls to their knees. They have not been seen on the isles in two hundred years.

effects.log: You kneel. They say a name. It is of someone you also loved. You stay until the crowd has gone.
After, the frail one finds you and takes your hand. No words are needed. The next Gathering, there is a chair for them.

events.text: The Gathering is held on a different isle every decade. This decade it is yours, and the hosting falls to {b3_order}. Banners, benches, a thousand cups of tea, and the matter of where to seat the Demon Realm, who insist on a high dark room, and the Star Sea, who insist on a roof.

effects.log: It takes four days of diplomacy and a very large map. Everyone is seated, nobody is happy, and the Gathering begins on time.
You send your best organiser, who is thrilled. The Gathering is a triumph, and you take none of the blame for the demons' roof.

events.text: A pupil of yours loses the final of the Gathering by a hair, and the winner, a fierce thin girl of the Star Sea, turns round on the dais and bows deeply to your pupil before she accepts the cup. It is not in the rules. The crowd will talk about it for a century.

choices.text: Return the bow to the winner

effects.log: The winner flushes. A friendship starts that will, a thousand years on, hold two isles together through a bad winter.

choices.text: Take your pupil for a walk in the clouds

effects.log: You walk a long time. At the end, your pupil says that was the best fight of their life. It is.

events.text: The Gathering ends and the isles stand around in the sunset, none of them wanting to be first to leave. Someone begins to sing the old song of parting, and by the third line the whole field has taken it up. Your pupil is crying. So, a little, are you.

effects.log: You sing the old song, badly, among thousands. Afterwards the wind carries a handful of voices across the clouds, and then it is only dusk.
You listen to a thousand years of partings from one field. It settles something you had been carrying without noticing.

events.text: The Isle League meets under no roof, on a raft of lashed cloud-wood that drifts between the isles on the third night of the month. By rule, nobody may ask where it will be moored next. You arrive by luck and a small bribe to a ferryman. A Leaguer looks up and kindly pours you tea.

effects.log: The League is mostly smugglers, poets and cartographers. You are made a member of the third kind before the pot is cold.
You watch a long hour of quiet commerce in rumours. They nod to you when you leave, and the raft is a little warmer for your absence.

events.text: A league ferryman owes you a favour, and wants to repay it by taking a letter to the Demon Realm without asking what is in it. He is a short, anxious man who has been refused many things. "Deliver it," he says, "and I will carry your name quietly for a hundred years."

effects.log: It arrives. The reply comes in a week, in an unfamiliar hand, with a pressed flower. The ferryman does not ask. The League smiles into its cups.
He bows low and rows away, slightly hurt. In a decade he will say it was the most honest refusal he ever had.

events.text: The League keeps the one map in the sea of clouds that is always right, because it is redrawn nightly by a committee that does not trust itself. You are asked to contribute a corner. Yours is where the clouds are thinnest, and which isle hides a door in the sea floor.

effects.log: The committee peers at your corner, nods, and amends nothing. For a decade the map is subtly better, and nobody can say why.

choices.text: Draw a false door, on purpose

effects.log: The map now has a decoy, which the League will cheerfully guard for centuries from visitors who need to be wrong.

events.text: A courier of the League is caught by the Ministries with a satchel of forged exit-seals and dragged before a tribunal. The courier is the only League member you ever lent anything to. They look at you across the room, face white.

effects.log: You vouch for them, at some risk to your standing. They are released with a warning, and the League hears of it by evening.
The courier is sentenced to a long and tedious posting in the far end of the Ministries' records. They do not hold it against you, much.

events.text: The League holds an annual auction of things that have no business being sold: a lost note, a river's name, the last meal of a famous duellist. This year the lot is "one mild, honest lie." The auctioneer, a cheerful fox, taps the gavel. The bidding starts at a whisper.

effects.log: You win it for the price of a tea. The lie, when unwrapped, says "I am fine." You keep it in a pocket, as one keeps a coin, for hard days.
You see who wants what lie, and why. It is the most educational auction of your century.

events.text: A League Warden stops you on a raft-walk and asks, very politely, whether you would like to know what the League says about you. They have a file. It is, they promise, short and affectionate. It says: "dependable, sometimes, with tea."

effects.log: It is two lines. The second is a confession of fondness so sincere you read it twice. The Warden looks away, as is only polite.
The Warden nods, pleased. The file is kept. Someday, you suspect, someone will find it and cry.

events.text: A rival league has opened, called the Isle Fellowship, and it is exactly the same with better chairs. They have lured four members of the old raft away with the promise of cushions. The League's head, a stern lady in grey, has called an emergency meeting on the subject of upholstery.

effects.log: The League procures cushions of a quality so impressive the Fellowship folds out of envy. You are credited with saving the League by a margin of foam.

choices.text: Argue that hard seats keep people honest

effects.log: You win the argument and lose four more members. The League is leaner, sharper, and sore in the back.

events.text: The League keeps a safe house on an isle that officially does not exist. A fugitive arrives at it in the dead of night and you are asked to look after them. They are frightened, tired, and wearing the badge of a Ministry that you thought was your friend.

effects.log: You hide them in the cellar behind the preserved plums. They stay three weeks and leave a poem. The Ministries ask, and you say nothing.

choices.text: Send them to the League Warden

effects.log: The Warden takes them, grateful. You never learn what became of them, and the not-knowing gnaws a little.

events.text: A League cartographer asks you to carry a package to the Star Sea, to be delivered "to whoever answers the door." You are not told what is in it. It hums gently, like a cat. The League has a rule against asking questions, and you remember it, at the last moment.

effects.log: A small, solemn child answers the door, takes the package, bows, and closes it. You walk away lighter and puzzled. The League sends a case of excellent plums.
Inside is a ball of wool and a note: "Knit something for yourself." You laugh until you cry, and knit a scarf, and it is the best scarf.

events.text: The League's patron, an old river-spirit who bought a raft in the first age, invites you aboard her private barge. It is lined in books. She asks, as a favour, that you read to her, for her eyes have failed. The book she hands you has no title and no author.

effects.log: It is a gentle history of the League as told by no one. By the end of the night the old spirit is asleep, and the barge, rocked by the wind, hums your name.

choices.text: Read a page and ask what it is

effects.log: The old spirit chuckles. "A book that writes itself while I am awake," she says. "I wanted to see if it did so while someone read." It did.

events.text: The League wishes to hold its next meeting on the Ministries' own roof. Nobody can think why. A bold Leaguer says it is because no one looks up. The Warden says it is because the view is good. You are asked to scout the roof and report on both.

effects.log: The roof is quiet, the view superb, and the guards doze in the sun. You report both. The League meets there. Not one Ministry clerk looks up.
The meeting is held elsewhere. The Warden thanks you drily. For some months you are thought a coward, and then, when a raid fails, a prophet.

events.text: A young Leaguer with a heavy accent from the farthest isle asks you to teach them the League's signs, the secret handshakes and hand-tapped codes. They want to be good at it. They are very bad at it. Their patient, hopeless earnestness fills the room.

effects.log: It takes a year. At the end they can tap one word, and the word is "tea", and it is perfect.

choices.text: Tell them the League is mostly improvisation

effects.log: They are crushed, then relieved, then roaring with laughter. The signs, they decide, are decoration. The League is the people.

events.text: In a hard winter the League's raft is stranded in the ice of a frozen cloud, a rare event, and a hundred Leaguers huddle in their coats. Someone has brought a concertina. The music is atrocious. You find yourself dancing, in boots, on a frozen sea, with an ancient cartographer.

effects.log: You dance until dawn. The cloud thaws just as the sun rises, and the raft drifts free, and nobody in the League will ever admit they were cold.
You play three songs, passably. The League adopts them as anthems. The concertina is yours forever by acclamation.

events.text: The League asks you to settle a dispute between two members over the ownership of a very small, very ugly teapot. Each says it belonged to their grandmother. The teapot is silent on the matter. It is signed on the bottom by an artist neither of them could possibly know.

effects.log: You split it with a very small hammer. The teapot is now two ugly halves. Both claimants are furious, and then, strangely, content.

choices.text: Rule it belongs to the League

effects.log: It goes on a shelf in the raft cabin. Both claimants visit it, quietly, on lonely days, and the dispute is forgotten.

events.text: A message comes through the League's network of rafts, relayed hand to hand, from someone who wishes to remain nameless: "I know where you are, and I mean you no harm. I only wished to say that I enjoyed your last act." You never find out who, or what act.

effects.log: You send a single line: "Thank you." It comes back in a week, sealed, with no words but a small drawn sun.
You change your habits for a season. Nothing happens. The League says that is what good warnings are for.

events.text: A letter comes up the White Stairs from {sect}, the sect you left behind: three pages in a clerk's round hand, a pressed plum blossom, and a postscript from the gatekeeper. The sect has repainted the gate. Your old post is still unfilled, out of sentiment and for lack of volunteers.

effects.log: The reply takes three weeks to cross the sea of clouds, and arrives with a gift of dumplings. The gatekeeper is known to cry in public since.

choices.text: Keep the letter and do not reply

effects.log: You keep the plum blossom in a book. Occasionally you take it out and smell the mortal year it came from.

events.text: {sect} sends word that a disciple of the third rank has taken your old name as a title and hopes you do not mind. The letter is a fond, apologetic scrawl. The disciple trains in your style, poorly. Elder after elder has written to excuse them. The disciple has written to excuse the elders.

effects.log: It reaches them by courier after a year. The disciple takes it for a sign and trains for a century until they too are an immortal, ridiculous and fond.

choices.text: Send a manual of your style

effects.log: You send a single scroll of corrections. The disciple is mortified, thrilled, and best of their generation within a decade.

events.text: A letter from {sect}: the old mountain is being sold. The sect has fallen on thin years and the elders are signing papers. It asks, with great delicacy, whether you might remember the old place in your prayers, now that you are so far above. It does not ask for money. It asks for a sign.

choices.text: Send a sign: a light on the mountain

effects.log: One night a pale lantern burns on the old peak without fuel. The elders see it and tear up the papers. The sect survives another thousand years.

choices.text: Send an anonymous gift of stones

effects.log: The elders find a parcel at the gate. They guess, correctly, and say nothing. The mountain stays.

choices.text: Let it go, with a prayer

effects.log: The mountain is sold. You think of it sometimes, in the evening, with an odd peace.

events.text: The abbot of {sect} writes that they have grown very old and wish, before they die, to see once what the world above looks like. They cannot climb the stairs. Could you perhaps describe it? The letter is long, and ends: "Take your time. I shall wait."

effects.log: It takes a month, and it is a better description than you thought you had. The abbot reads it in the sun, and the letter comes back with a small blot of tea.

choices.text: Go and show them in person

effects.log: You come down in secret and take the abbot up the first white step in a dream. In the morning the abbot is smiling, asleep, and the stairs, for a moment, are gold.

events.text: A letter from {sect}, in a hand like a crow's: there is a quarrel with the neighbouring valley over a spring, and the old people say you once settled such things. The sect asks, if it is not too much, whether the immortal who once swept its floors might wave a hand from above.

effects.log: A mild cloud settles on the contested spring, and its water runs on both sides of the border at once. The valley and the sect stop arguing at dusk.
Your note is nailed to the sect gate and read aloud in the valley. Both sides are shamed into compromise, and a feast follows.

events.text: {sect} writes that a child who looks a good deal like you was born in the village, on a night of falling stars. The letter does not say the child is yours. It says only that the family is poor, the child clever, and the sect would take them in if they had a patron above.

effects.log: You send an unsigned gift and a name for the child to carry. The child grows into a quiet and stubborn scholar. The sect keeps the secret.

choices.text: Offer a place at the White Stairs

effects.log: You send a token of passage. The child will arrive in forty years, bewildered, in a patched coat. You will know them at once.

events.text: A bundle comes from {sect}: your old training sword, rusted, with a note. "We found it in the lumber room under a rice-sack. It still hums a bit. We thought you would want it back, or else the humming is a ghost and we should get it blessed." The humming is audible across the room.

choices.text: Take it back and clean it

effects.log: You oil the blade for a week. It hums a note you remember. The sword hangs on your wall like a small, patient conscience.

choices.text: Send it back with orders to display it

effects.log: It hangs in the sect hall, labelled "this was theirs." Every year new disciples ask what you were like. The elders never say, and the legend grows.

events.text: {sect} sends a message of grave concern: the founding scroll has been misplaced. Without it the elders cannot recall the sect's second rule. They have written down eleven candidates and ask which you remember. You remember, with some embarrassment, that you wrote in its margins when you were bored.

effects.log: The elders are astonished, relieved, and then dismayed: the rule is "Always wash the bowls." They wash them for a generation with a sense of historical duty.

choices.text: Pick the funniest of the eleven

effects.log: The elders adopt it with ceremony. It is a rule against wearing hats indoors. It endures, and so does your small, shameful pride.

events.text: A letter reaches you from {sect}: a dear friend of your mortal years has died, in bed, quietly, aged ninety. They spoke of you in the last week, and left a small box. It was sent up by pigeon-courier and dropped in the clouds. A cloud-crane has found it and brought it to your window.

effects.log: Inside is a wooden spoon, a note, and a pressed leaf. The note says only: "It was a good life. Thank you for the soup." You hold the spoon a long time.

choices.text: Hold the box for a day, then open it

effects.log: You wait a day. When you open it, it is lighter than you feared, and a little warmer. You hang the spoon by the window.

events.text: The head of {sect} writes with great respect to invite you to give the opening lecture at the sect's four-hundredth anniversary. You are the only immortal it ever produced. The letter implies the whole sect is learning your sword-form for the occasion, badly, in rows.

choices.text: Go down and give the lecture

effects.log: You give it from the dais in a cloak borrowed from the gatekeeper. Afterwards you find yourself teaching sweeping to a row of weeping disciples.
It is read aloud by the head in a trembling voice. The lecture is chiselled onto a stone by the gate, misspelled in two places.

events.text: A letter from {sect}: the old tea-seller who sold you cheap tea at the gate when you were a disciple has finally closed their stall. The letter wonders if the immortal remembers. You do. The tea was terrible. You drank it every day for six years, and it was, you realise now, the whole of what you had.

choices.text: Send a pot of the best tea in the isles

effects.log: It arrives in a jar of white jade. The old tea-seller drinks it on the stall's last evening and says it is not as good as their own. They are very happy.

choices.text: Write a poem about the bad tea

effects.log: The poem is nailed up at the gate, where it stays for decades. Disciples read it and drink worse tea in your honour.

events.text: A letter, anonymous, in a trembling script: "The sect is in danger. I cannot say how. The elders will not listen. If you remember us, look down." There is a faint smell of cold ink and old wood. The paper bears a watermark of the sect gate, and a smear of red clay.

effects.log: Through a rift in the haze you see the sect, small and bright. A thin column of smoke rises from the lumber room. You send a cloud to put it out, and the sect never knows.
You write to the abbot, urgently. The abbot has the lumber room cleared and finds a smouldering sack. The sect is saved by a day.

events.text: {sect} writes that there is a new disciple, a boy who asks too many questions and has been put on bowls for it. He has asked, in his first month, why the immortals do not come down. The abbot says the question is above his rank, and would like to know what to say.

effects.log: You send him a single page: "We come down when we are asked properly." The boy reads it, nods gravely, and begins at once to learn how to ask.

choices.text: Tell the abbot to let him ask

effects.log: The abbot, abashed, lets the boy go on asking. By the end of the year the sect is wiser, and the boy is promoted to teaching bowls.

events.text: You receive a letter from {sect} that is entirely a list: every disciple who has trained there since you left, in order, with a small note by each. It runs to forty pages. At the bottom, a line in the abbot's hand: "You asked once who we were. This is the answer."

effects.log: You read it over a week. By the end you know the names and the failures and the small kindnesses of four hundred strangers, and you feel, oddly, like their grandparent.
The last ten names are young. You write to each, a line apiece. The replies fill a drawer, and a year later a basket of pears arrives.

events.text: {sect} writes that the mountain path has been washed away by the rains and the disciples carry water by hand. The abbot is too proud to ask for help. The letter is merely a description of the path. In the margin, someone has drawn a small, sad cloud.

effects.log: One night a pale road of stones appears on the slope, set neatly. The disciples decide it was an ancestor and leave offerings of rice.

choices.text: Send stonemasons and a cart of rice

effects.log: The masons arrive, bewildered, with orders and a bill already paid. The path is mended by spring.

events.text: A letter reaches you from {sect} in a child's writing: "My grandfather says you used to live here and that you are now very important. I would like to be important as well. What do I do?" There is a drawing of a mountain, a sword and what appears to be a goat.

choices.text: Write a kind and honest answer

effects.log: You tell the child to learn one thing well, be kind to the goat, and ask again in ten years. They do, and you write back, again.

choices.text: Send the drawing back with a small addition

effects.log: You add a bird. The child pins it to the wall and tells every visitor an immortal drew it. The village believes this for a hundred years.

events.text: {sect} has been mentioned in a bulletin of the Ministries as a "provincial establishment of modest account." The sect is furious and has not slept. The abbot has written a long letter, mostly crossings-out, asking how best to answer. Your name is dropped, nervously, in the third paragraph.

choices.text: Write a short note to the bulletin

effects.log: The next issue carries a correction: "the sect is the origin of one immortal." The abbot reads it aloud at dinner four nights running.

choices.text: Advise the abbot to say nothing

effects.log: The abbot sulks, then laughs. In a year the bulletin has forgotten, and the sect, undisturbed, is exactly as modest as ever.

events.text: The elders of {sect} have decided, in some alarm, to make you an honorary patriarch. The letter is full of apologies for the haste. The ceremony will go ahead with or without you, in front of your portrait. The portrait, they confess, is rather flattering and has your nose wrong.

effects.log: You are sent a robe. It is too short in the arm. You wear it once, on a feast day, to general astonishment.
The elders are crushed and relieved. The portrait stays up. Your nose is, thereafter, a minor local legend.

events.text: {sect} writes that the old gatekeeper has died and left you a single instruction: "Keep the gate open." The abbot writes that the gate has no hinges now and cannot be closed, and that visitors from the valley have begun walking straight through it. It is nothing sinister. It is rather pleasant.

effects.log: You send word: let the gate stand as it is. The sect becomes, in time, the friendliest on its mountain, and people say it is because of an immortal who never learned to close doors.
The hinges arrive, and the gate is mended. It sticks on every damp day. The disciples find it, quietly, unbearable and wonderful.

events.text: A letter from {sect}, last in a long series. The abbot has written once a year since you left, and this year the handwriting is another's. The old abbot died in the spring. It includes, copied out carefully, the last letter the old abbot never sent. It is two lines long. You read it standing up.

effects.log: You have it framed in plain wood and hung by the door. It says: "I hope you are warm. I hope you are not alone." You are neither, now.

choices.text: Answer it, though there is no one to receive

effects.log: You write a reply, and burn it in a small bowl on the balcony. The smoke rises. For once, the isles are quiet.

events.text: The vault of {b3_order} is lined in a pale, dry wood that smells of paper and mild regret. The keeper hands you a lantern that gives no heat, "so nothing burns". You have an hour. Past a certain shelf the labels switch from names to feelings.

effects.log: You find a shelf labelled "Almost" and sit with it. An hour is ample.

choices.text: Go straight to the lowest shelf

effects.log: It holds a single scroll and a dead moth. The scroll is a recipe. You copy it before the keeper returns.

events.text: Inside {b3_foe} the corridors are bright and the clerks are polite, which you find suspicious. You are asked to wait. The chair is warm, as if someone has just left it. On the table is a half-written letter in your own handwriting. You did not write it.

effects.log: It is a draft of your own report to {b3_order}, from a month from now. It is mostly accurate. You leave a correction on the table.
You are out of the building within a minute, with an odd feeling of having been seen through, politely.

events.text: The head of a department in {b3_foe} invites you to dinner and speaks only of the weather. At the end of the meal they say, "I hope your friends are warm tonight." It is not clear if it is a threat, an offer, or merely cold feet.

effects.log: They look genuinely abashed and say it was only a kindness. Your intelligence on the matter improves, and your appetite does not.
The report is read with great care in {b3_order}, who send a bundle of blankets to everyone for the winter.

events.text: Among the clerks of {b3_foe} you make a friend, a gloomy, funny archivist who has never been promoted. Over many cups they confide that they are bored. You could, with a little care, make their boredom useful to {b3_order}. They would probably thank you for it.

effects.log: You get what you need. The archivist never knows. You carry a small cold weight, and a hundred years pass over it.
You say nothing of your errand and take nothing. The archivist is the only person in {b3_foe} who will ever speak well of you.

events.text: Your cover in {b3_foe} is nearly perfect, except that you cannot stop humming the hymn of {b3_order} in the bath. A colleague has noticed, and asks the name of the tune. It is a fine tune, they say. They would like to learn it.

effects.log: They learn it quickly. Within a month half the corridor hums it. {b3_foe} is, for a season, strangely harmonious.

choices.text: Say it is a folk song, and change it

effects.log: You alter two notes. It becomes a wonderful, entirely false folk song which {b3_foe} will sing for centuries.

events.text: In the matter of {b3_elder} and {b3_peer}, a third party has taken the unusual step of bringing a lamb to the hearing. The lamb is not evidence. It is merely a lamb. The hearing, bewildered, goes on around it. It is, you decide, the only calm party.

effects.log: The lamb is awarded, solemnly, to a small clerk. The quarrel, deprived of its audience, cools a degree.
The lamb eats a corner of the minutes. The record is amended: "partially illegible, lamb."

events.text: {b3_elder} and {b3_peer} have been feuding for six hundred years over an unreturned umbrella. It has become the order's favourite scandal. Neither can recall whose umbrella it was. Both are quite sure the other has the other umbrella. You hold, in your cupboard, a spare.

choices.text: Give each of them an umbrella

effects.log: They are speechless, then furious, then laughing so hard they have to sit down. The feud ends in an hour, after six hundred years.
The feud continues, healthy and beloved, and is added to the order's heritage. You keep the umbrella.
